Chapter 01 / Illustrated summary

Hello, world
of concurrency.

What it means to do more than one thing at a time—and how C++ gives us the tools to do it well.

ANTHONY WILLIAMSC++11 FOUNDATIONS14 PAGES → THE ESSENTIALS
The central idea

Starting a thread is easy. Designing work that runs correctly—and usefully—alongside other work is the real challenge.

01 / What is concurrency?§1.1 · pp. 2–6

Multiple activities. One system.

Concurrency lets independent activities make progress over the same period. It does not require them to execute at exactly the same instant: a single core can interleave tasks, while multiple cores can execute tasks in parallel.

Task switching

One core alternates between tasks. Each context switch costs time: the OS saves and restores execution state, and the CPU may need to reload cached instructions and data.

Hardware concurrency

Multiple cores or hardware threads can support overlapping execution. There can still be more runnable tasks than hardware resources, so task switching remains relevant.

Real schedulers are less tidy than these illustrations. Work chunks vary in size, and even a multicore computer often has many more tasks than it can execute simultaneously.

Two ways to organize concurrent work

Multiple processes

Separate address spaces provide isolation. Communication uses mechanisms such as pipes, sockets, signals, or files, usually with more setup and overhead. Processes can also be distributed across machines.

Multiple threads

Threads in one process share an address space. Starting threads and sharing data are usually cheaper, but coordinating access to that data becomes the programmer’s responsibility.

The book focuses on threads. C++11 standardizes thread-based concurrency, but not a general interprocess communication API.
02 / Why use concurrency?§1.2 · pp. 6–9

Use it for a reason. Not by default.

01. Separate concerns

Give distinct responsibilities their own flow of execution. In the book’s DVD-player example, one thread handles playback while another responds to user input. The code is less intertwined and the interface stays responsive—even on a single core. The design, not the core count, determines this division.

02. Improve performance

Split an algorithm into different tasks (task parallelism), or apply the same operation to different portions of data (data parallelism). The goal may be lower latency for one job, or higher throughput by processing more jobs in the same time.

Independent, naturally parallel work scales especially well. Dependencies between tasks, coordination costs, and limited hardware restrict the gains.

When not to use it

When the benefit does not justify the cost.

Threads take time to launch, need stack memory and OS resources, and introduce scheduling overhead. Tiny jobs may finish faster without them. Too many threads can exhaust resources or reduce performance through excessive context switching.

Concurrent code also costs more to understand, test, and maintain. Use measurements for performance decisions; a clear separation of concerns can independently justify the design. Thread pools can limit resource use, but are not a universal fix.

03 / Concurrency in C++§1.3 · pp. 9–12

From platform extensions to a standard.

Before C++11

C++98 did not define threads or a thread-aware memory model. Applications relied on compiler extensions, operating-system APIs such as POSIX or Windows threads, and libraries such as Boost, ACE, and MFC. RAII-based locks helped manage resources, but portability and memory semantics remained concerns.

What C++11 brought

A thread-aware memory model plus standard facilities to manage threads, protect shared data, synchronize operations, and perform atomic operations. Boost.Thread was a major influence on the library’s design.

Efficiency by design

The library aims for a low abstraction penalty. Lower-level code is not automatically faster; profile first. Reducing contention often matters more than shaving time from an individual lock operation.

An escape hatch

Some library types may expose native_handle() for access to platform-specific facilities. It sacrifices portability and should be considered only when standard facilities are insufficient.

Edition context: this is a summary of the 2012 first edition in C__CON~1.PDF. Its references to the “new standard” mean C++11, not the latest C++ standard.
04 / Getting started§1.4 · pp. 13–14

Hello, Concurrent World.

The chapter compares a single-threaded baseline with one that starts a new thread. Both examples below are from the book; whitespace has been normalized and printed callout markers omitted.

BASELINE · SINGLE THREAD · P. 13
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    std::cout<<"Hello World\n";
}
LISTING 1.1 · TWO THREADS · P. 13
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

void hello()
{
    std::cout<<"Hello Concurrent World\n";
}

int main()
{
    std::thread t(hello);
    t.join();
}
  1. #include <thread> declares the standard thread-management facilities.
  2. hello() is the initial function of the new thread.
  3. std::thread t(hello) starts that thread. The original thread continues in main(); it does not simply call hello() synchronously.
  4. t.join() makes the calling thread wait until the worker finishes.
Correctness detail: removing join() here leaves a joinable std::thread at destruction, which calls std::terminate(). Waiting also ensures the worker completes before main() returns.

Try it locally

Save Listing 1.1 as hello.cpp. With GCC or Clang on Linux:

BUILD & RUN · ADDED STUDY NOTE
g++ -std=c++11 -pthread hello.cpp -o hello
./hello

Expected output: Hello Concurrent World. This is a teaching example, not a performance optimization: the main thread has no useful work to do while waiting.

Interactive walkthrough

Start → wait → finish

main()
launchjoin / waitreturn
hello()
print messagefinish
$ ./hello Waiting to start…

An illustrative sequence, not a C++ runtime. Actual scheduling can vary; join() guarantees waiting, not a particular print-start order.

05 / Take it with you§1.5 · p. 14

A quick knowledge check.

Does concurrency require multiple cores?

No. A single core can interleave activities through task switching. Parallel execution uses hardware resources to run work simultaneously.

Why can more threads make a program slower?

Thread creation, synchronization, context switching, resource consumption, and contention can outweigh the useful work. More threads do not create more hardware capacity.

What is the central trade-off with shared memory?

Threads communicate cheaply through the same address space, but the programmer must coordinate shared access to keep data consistent.

What does join() guarantee in Listing 1.1?

The caller waits for the associated thread to complete. Here, the worker finishes before main returns and the thread object is destroyed.

Chapter in one sentence

Use standard C++ threads when clearer responsibilities or measurable parallel work justify the costs—and design the interactions with care.

Chapter 02 / Illustrated notebook

Managing
threads.

Launch work, control its lifetime, and make ownership explicit. A thread’s execution and its C++ handle are not the same thing.

PRINTED PAGES 15–32PDF PAGES 38–55C++11 · FIRST EDITION
The central rule

Every joinable std::thread needs a deliberate destination: join it, detach it, or transfer its ownership before destruction.

2.1 / Basic thread managementpp. 16–22

Start work. Own the consequences.

Constructing a std::thread starts a new execution using a callable: a function, function object, or lambda. The worker ends when its entry function returns, but the handle can remain joinable even after execution has finished.

A temporary functor in parentheses can look like a function declaration: std::thread t(background_task()); declares a function. Braces—std::thread t{background_task()};—avoid the ambiguity.

join(): wait and release

The caller blocks until the worker finishes. After a successful join, the handle is no longer joinable. It is not a polling or timed-wait interface; later chapters introduce tools for those needs.

detach(): release without waiting

The worker continues independently; the runtime reclaims its thread resources on completion. You cannot later join it through that handle. Detach does not make borrowed data safe or keep the application alive.

Both operations require a joinable handle. Destroying a joinable thread calls std::terminate(), even if the worker has already finished. joinable() means “associated with a thread,” not “currently executing.”

Lifetime safety is part of the design

A detached worker referencing a local variable can access destroyed storage after its launching function returns. Prefer owned data, or join before the referenced data is destroyed. Copying an object containing references does not extend their referents’ lifetimes.

Make cleanup exception-safe

A final join can be skipped by an exception. Listing 2.2 joins in both paths; Listing 2.3 packages the rule into a noncopyable RAII guard. Reverse destruction order ensures the guard waits before the thread and referenced local state are destroyed.

The chapter has no numbered figures or illustrative pictures. All eight numbered listings and its standalone code examples are embedded below. The original four chapter-1 figures remain embedded above.
2.2 / Passing argumentspp. 23–25

Copies, references, and moves.

Constructor arguments are stored as decayed copies or moves for the new thread. A reference parameter in the target function does not by itself request a reference to the caller’s object.

  1. Own the value early. Passing a pointer to a local character buffer copies the pointer, not its contents. Construct std::string(buffer) in the launching thread, before the buffer can disappear.
  2. Share explicitly. Use std::ref(data) for a mutable reference, and keep that object alive until the worker finishes. Reference passing is not synchronization.
  3. Invoke a member. Pass a member-function pointer followed by an object pointer, then the function arguments. The object must remain alive.
  4. Transfer exclusive ownership. Pass std::move(p) to hand a std::unique_ptr to a worker. The source no longer owns the object.
First-edition correction: the book describes its non-const-reference example without std::ref as updating an internal copy. On conforming modern implementations, that particular invocation is ill-formed: the stored argument cannot bind to the required mutable lvalue reference. The correct std::ref solution remains the same.
2.3 / Transferring ownershippp. 25–28

One thread. One owning handle.

std::thread is movable, not copyable. Moving a handle transfers the responsibility to join or detach, without restarting or moving the underlying execution. The moved-from handle no longer represents that thread.

Functions can return a thread or accept one by value; named handles need an explicit std::move when passed onward. Never move-assign into a joinable destination: that calls std::terminate() instead of silently dropping the old thread.

thread_guard

Borrows a reference to a thread. It checks joinable() and joins on destruction. The referenced handle must stay alive.

scoped_thread

Owns the thread by move, validates it on construction, and joins on destruction. Other code cannot independently manage that owned handle.

Movability also permits std::vector<std::thread>: start a collection of workers, then join every member. Production code must also handle partial startup failures.

2.4 / Runtime thread countspp. 28–31

Enough workers. Not too many.

std::thread::hardware_concurrency() is a hint, not a promise; zero means the hint is unavailable. Listing 2.8 uses a fallback of two and limits parallelism based on input size to avoid excessive overhead for small ranges.

  1. Return the initial value for an empty range.
  2. Compute a workload-based thread limit using a nominal 25 elements per thread, then cap it by the hardware hint or fallback.
  3. Allocate one result slot per participating thread, but launch only num_threads - 1 new workers.
  4. Let the original thread process the final block, including any remainder.
  5. Join all workers and combine the partial results with the initial value.
The “25” threshold is illustrative, not a universal tuning rule; its ceiling calculation does not guarantee at least 25 elements in every block. Oversubscription is often costly for CPU-bound work, but thread-count decisions depend on workload. This example is not an exception-safe production parallel algorithm.
Interactive study aid · not a C++ runtime

Explore Listing 2.8’s partitioning

This calculator reproduces the book’s sizing arithmetic. It does not launch threads or measure speed.

2.5 / Identifying threadspp. 31–32

Identity without ownership.

Use t.get_id() for a thread associated with a handle and std::this_thread::get_id() for the current thread. An unassociated handle returns a default std::thread::id, representing “not any thread.”

IDs support comparison, ordering, hashing, and stream output. They can key containers or distinguish a coordinator thread, but their printed representation is implementation-dependent, not a meaningful numerical index. IDs can be reused after a thread ends, so they are not permanent global identities.

Listing 2.1 · Dangling references after detach

Unsafe: the worker can outlive some_local_state. Copying func does not copy the int it references.

Listing 2.1 · Book pp. 18
struct func
{
    int& i;
    func(int& i_):i(i_){}
    void operator()()
    {
        for(unsigned j=0;j<1000000;++j)
        {
            do_something(i);
        }
    }
};
void oops()
{
    int some_local_state=0;
    func my_func(some_local_state);
    std::thread my_thread(my_func);
    my_thread.detach();
}

Listing 2.2 · Join on normal and exceptional exits

The catch-all handler waits, then rethrows. The normal path also joins. Use the full func definition from Listing 2.1; the forward declaration is a cross-reference, not a complete program.

Listing 2.2 · Book pp. 19–20
struct func;
void f()
{
    int some_local_state=0;
    func my_func(some_local_state);
    std::thread t(my_func);
    try
    {
        do_something_in_current_thread();
    }
    catch(...)
    {
        t.join();
        throw;
    }
    t.join();
}

Listing 2.3 · RAII with thread_guard

The guard refers to an existing thread and joins during scope exit. Declare it after the thread so it is destroyed first; the referenced thread must outlive the guard.

Listing 2.3 · Book pp. 20
class thread_guard
{
    std::thread& t;
public:
    explicit thread_guard(std::thread& t_):
        t(t_)
    {}
    ~thread_guard()
    {
        if(t.joinable())
        {
            t.join();
        }
    }
    thread_guard(thread_guard const&)=delete;
    thread_guard& operator=(thread_guard const&)=delete;
};
struct func;
void f()
{
    int some_local_state=0;
    func my_func(some_local_state);
    std::thread t(my_func);
    thread_guard g(t);
    do_something_in_current_thread();
}

Listing 2.4 · Detached document editing

An outline, not a portable GUI implementation. GUI frameworks often require UI operations on their main thread. Detaching also requires a safe shutdown and data-lifetime strategy.

Listing 2.4 · Book pp. 22
void edit_document(std::string const& filename)
{
    open_document_and_display_gui(filename);
    while(!done_editing())
    {
        user_command cmd=get_user_input();
        if(cmd.type==open_new_document)
        {
            std::string const new_name=get_filename_from_user();
            std::thread t(edit_document,new_name);
            t.detach();
        }
        else
        {
            process_user_input(cmd);
        }
    }
}

Listing 2.5 · Returning thread ownership

Returning a local thread transfers ownership by move (or elision). The recipient must still join or detach.

Listing 2.5 · Book pp. 26
std::thread f()
{
    void some_function();
    return std::thread(some_function);
}
std::thread g()
{
    void some_other_function(int);
    std::thread t(some_other_function,42);
    return t;
}

Listing 2.6 · An owning scoped_thread

This original usage line is susceptible to the most vexing parse. Prefer: int some_local_state=0; scoped_thread t{std::thread{func{some_local_state}}};. Supply the full func definition and required headers.

Listing 2.6 · Book pp. 27
class scoped_thread
{
    std::thread t;
public:
    explicit scoped_thread(std::thread t_):
        t(std::move(t_))
    {
        if(!t.joinable())
            throw std::logic_error("No thread");
    }
    ~scoped_thread()
    {
        t.join();
    }
    scoped_thread(scoped_thread const&)=delete;
    scoped_thread& operator=(scoped_thread const&)=delete;
};
struct func;
void f()
{
    int some_local_state;
    scoped_thread t(std::thread(func(some_local_state)));
    do_something_in_current_thread();
}

Listing 2.7 · A group of threads

Twenty threads are started, then joined. This teaching version lacks cleanup if thread creation or vector growth throws after earlier threads were started.

Listing 2.7 · Book pp. 28
void do_work(unsigned id);
void f()
{
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for(unsigned i=0;i<20;++i)
    {
        threads.push_back(std::thread(do_work,i));
    }
    std::for_each(threads.begin(),threads.end(),
                  std::mem_fn(&std::thread::join));
}

Listing 2.8 · A naïve parallel accumulate

This teaching implementation assumes operations do not throw. It needs forward iterators, default-constructible T, and compatible accumulation semantics; regrouped floating-point addition may change the result.

Listing 2.8 · Book pp. 29–30
template<typename Iterator,typename T>
struct accumulate_block
{
    void operator()(Iterator first,Iterator last,T& result)
    {
        result=std::accumulate(first,last,result);
    }
};
template<typename Iterator,typename T>
T parallel_accumulate(Iterator first,Iterator last,T init)
{
    unsigned long const length=std::distance(first,last);
    if(!length)
        return init;
    unsigned long const min_per_thread=25;
    unsigned long const max_threads=
        (length+min_per_thread-1)/min_per_thread;
    unsigned long const hardware_threads=
        std::thread::hardware_concurrency();
    unsigned long const num_threads=
        std::min(hardware_threads!=0?hardware_threads:2,max_threads);
    unsigned long const block_size=length/num_threads;
    std::vector<T> results(num_threads);
    std::vector<std::thread>  threads(num_threads-1);
    Iterator block_start=first;
    for(unsigned long i=0;i<(num_threads-1);++i)
    {
        Iterator block_end=block_start;
        std::advance(block_end,block_size);
        threads[i]=std::thread(
            accumulate_block<Iterator,T>(),
            block_start,block_end,std::ref(results[i]));
        block_start=block_end;
    }
    accumulate_block<Iterator,T>()(
        block_start,last,results[num_threads-1]);
    std::for_each(threads.begin(),threads.end(),
        std::mem_fn(&std::thread::join));
    return std::accumulate(results.begin(),results.end(),init);
}

2.6 / Check your understandingp. 32

The lifetime checklist.

A worker has returned. Can its joinable handle be destroyed?

No. It still needs join() or detach(), or ownership must move elsewhere. Completion alone does not clear joinability.

Does detach() extend the lifetime of a referenced local?

No. Detached work must not outlive the objects it accesses. Own the data or arrange a reliable lifetime and completion protocol.

Why wrap a shared argument in std::ref?

To explicitly pass a reference instead of relying on the constructor’s default storage of decayed copies. Lifetime safety and synchronization remain separate responsibilities.

Why does parallel_accumulate start one fewer worker than its thread count?

The calling thread performs the final block itself. It is already one of the participating threads.

Chapter in one sentence

Make thread ownership, argument ownership, and cleanup on every exit path explicit before trying to scale the work.

Chapter 03 / Illustrated summary

Sharing data
between threads.

Protect invariants, not just variables. Correct shared-state code needs a synchronization protocol, a safe interface, and a plan to avoid waiting forever.

PRINTED PAGES 33–66PDF PAGES 56–8913 LISTINGS · 1 FIGURE · 1 TABLE
The central idea

A mutex protects data only when every access follows the same rules—and the lock covers the whole operation that must stay consistent.

3.1 / The shared-data problempp. 34–37

Never expose a broken invariant.

Reading shared, properly initialized data without modifying it is straightforward. Trouble begins when one thread changes data while another can observe it. An invariant is a relationship that must hold whenever the data is visible as a valid structure.

In a doubly linked list, following a next pointer and then a previous pointer should return to the starting node. Removing a node changes two links. Between those writes, the invariant is temporarily broken; a concurrent reader or remover can see an inconsistent structure.

Race condition

An outcome depends on the ordering of concurrent operations. Some outcomes are acceptable; a problematic race violates the intended behavior, even if every individual access is synchronized.

Data race

Conflicting accesses to the same memory location, at least one a write, without the required ordering and with at least one non-atomic access. In C++, a data race is undefined behavior—not merely an unpredictable result.

Timing-sensitive bugs may disappear under a debugger and reappear under load. Avoid them by protecting intermediate states, designing correct indivisible updates, or using other appropriate synchronization. The chapter mentions lock-free design and software transactional memory as alternatives, but develops mutex-based protection here.

3.2.1–3.2.2 / Mutexes & boundariespp. 37–40

One protocol. Every access.

A std::mutex admits one owning thread at a time. Prefer std::lock_guard<std::mutex> from <mutex> to manual lock/unlock pairs: it acquires in its constructor and releases on scope exit, including exception unwinding.

Keep the mutex close to its protected data, usually as private members of the same class. Every reader and writer must lock the appropriate mutex. A mutex does not automatically attach protection to an object or make unlocked accesses safe.

Don’t leak the protection boundary

Returning a pointer or reference to internal data lets the caller use it after unlocking. Passing internal data to a callback is just as dangerous: the callback can retain an alias, access it later, or re-enter the object. Listing 3.2 demonstrates this escape even though the wrapper itself uses RAII locking.

User-supplied code includes callbacks, virtual functions, and operations on generic element types. Consider what those operations can do while your lock is held—not just what the enclosing function appears to do.
3.2.3 / Races in interfacespp. 40–47

Safe calls can form an unsafe sequence.

Consider a shared stack. A locked empty() says only what was true during that call. Another thread may remove the last item before top(). Even with two items, two threads can both read the top item, then each remove an item: one value is processed twice and another is discarded.

Combine the operation; preserve exception safety

The solution is an interface that checks, obtains, and removes an item under one lock. But if returning or copying the value throws after removal, data can be lost. The book compares four approaches:

  1. Output reference: copy or assign into a caller-provided object before removal; this requires a suitable destination and assignment support.
  2. No-throw return: constrain the element type to a nonthrowing copy or move.
  3. Owning pointer: construct the returned object before removal, then return a std::shared_ptr without another potentially throwing element copy.
  4. Offer alternatives: provide output-reference and value/pointer variants where appropriate.

Listings 3.4–3.5 implement both output-reference and shared-pointer pop(), throwing empty_stack if empty. The copy constructor locks the source; assignment is deleted. The mutable mutex permits locking within const operations. empty() remains a snapshot, not a reservation.

Interactive study aid · Table 3.1

Watch the compound-operation race

Initial stack: bottom [10, 20] top. Each individual call is protected; the question is whether the whole read-and-remove operation is protected.

A deterministic model of operation ordering, not C++ execution or a simulation of undefined behavior. The split example demonstrates a logical race without requiring unsynchronized memory accesses.

3.2.4–3.2.5 / Deadlockpp. 47–54

Don’t build a cycle of waiting.

If thread A owns mutex X and waits for Y, while thread B owns Y and waits for X, neither can proceed. The same cycle can involve joins or other waits, and more than two threads.

Acquire related locks together

For a two-object swap, first handle self-swap so the same nonrecursive mutex is not passed twice. Use std::lock(a, b) to acquire the distinct mutexes without deadlock within that acquisition, then construct guards with std::adopt_lock. If lock acquisition throws, std::lock releases locks it acquired. It does not solve unrelated wait cycles elsewhere in the application.

  1. Avoid nested locking where possible; otherwise acquire the required locks together.
  2. Avoid calling unknown code while holding a lock. It can acquire other locks or call back into the protected object.
  3. Use one consistent order when locks must be acquired separately. Swapping argument order must not change that global order.
  4. Enforce a hierarchy where practical. The sample hierarchical mutex permits only descending numerical levels and stores the current level in thread-local state.
  5. Apply the rule to all waits. In particular, do not join a worker while holding a mutex the worker needs to finish.
The custom hierarchy example is a teaching tool with its own constraints. It prevents acquisition-order cycles only when all relevant locks follow the protocol; it is not a general deadlock detector.
3.2.6–3.2.8 / Ownership & granularitypp. 54–59

Hold enough. Hold it briefly.

lock_guard: fixed scope

Use when a lock should be owned for the whole guard lifetime. Simple RAII; adopt_lock assumes the calling thread already owns the mutex.

unique_lock: flexible scope

Can defer acquisition, unlock and relock, report owns_lock(), and transfer ownership by move. Extra state enables flexibility; use it when that flexibility is needed.

Two deferred std::unique_lock objects can themselves be passed to std::lock. A function can return a unique_lock so its caller continues protected by the same lock. This is transfer between scopes on the owning thread—not permission to unlock a standard mutex on another thread.

Minimize the critical section, not the correctness

Coarse locks are easy to reason about but can serialize unrelated work. Finer locks permit more concurrency but complicate ordering. Do expensive processing or I/O outside the lock when it does not require protection, and revalidate assumptions after reacquiring it.

Listing 3.10 makes two short, independently locked reads and then compares the snapshots. That avoids holding both locks, but it changes the meaning: the values may never have been equal at the same instant. Keep all locks held together if a coherent cross-object snapshot is required.

3.3 / Specialized protectionpp. 59–65

Match the tool to the access pattern.

Initialize once: call_once and local statics

Lazy initialization must be synchronized too. The book’s broken double-checked locking reads an ordinary shared pointer without protection while another thread can write it, producing a data race. Adding an inner mutex does not fix that unlocked read.

std::once_flag plus std::call_once publishes a successfully completed initialization to callers using that same flag. If initialization throws, that call propagates the exception and another invocation can retry. The flag is neither copyable nor movable. This protects initialization only; later use of the initialized resource may still need synchronization.

Since C++11, a function-local static also has synchronized one-time initialization. Returning its reference does not make subsequent mutations automatically safe.

Read-mostly data: reader-writer locks

Many readers can hold shared ownership together, while a writer requires exclusive ownership. The DNS-cache example returns a copy under a shared lock and updates under an exclusive lock. These locks are not automatically faster: measure workloads, contention, and platform behavior.

Edition context: C++11 did not standardize the reader-writer mutex used here, so Listing 3.13 uses Boost. C++14 added std::shared_timed_mutex and std::shared_lock; C++17 added std::shared_mutex. The embedded listing remains faithful to the supplied 2012 edition.

Recursive mutexes: reconsider the design first

std::recursive_mutex allows the owning thread to lock repeatedly, with one unlock required for each lock. It does not repair broken invariants. If one public method needs another, prefer shared private helpers that expect the lock to be held, rather than recursively entering public methods during a half-completed update.

Listing 3.1 · Protecting a list with a mutex

Every list operation shown locks the same mutex. Other accesses must obey the same protocol; the globals themselves do not enforce it.

Listing 3.1 · Book pp. 38
#include <list>
#include <mutex>
#include <algorithm>
std::list<int> some_list;
std::mutex some_mutex;
void add_to_list(int new_value)
{
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> guard(some_mutex);
    some_list.push_back(new_value);
}
bool list_contains(int value_to_find)
{
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> guard(some_mutex);

    return std::find(some_list.begin(),some_list.end(),value_to_find)
        != some_list.end();
}

Listing 3.2 · Accidentally leaking protected data

Intentionally unsafe design: the callback saves a pointer and uses it after the lock is released. Encapsulation and a lock in each method do not prevent this escape.

Listing 3.2 · Book pp. 39–40
class some_data
{
    int a;
    std::string b;
public:
    void do_something();
};
class data_wrapper
{
private:
    some_data data;
    std::mutex m;
public:
    template<typename Function>
    void process_data(Function func)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> l(m);
        func(data);
    }
};
some_data* unprotected;
void malicious_function(some_data& protected_data)
{
    unprotected=&protected_data;
}
data_wrapper x;
void foo()
{
    x.process_data(malicious_function);
    unprotected->do_something();
}

Listing 3.3 · The std::stack interface

Historical interface excerpt, not a complete replacement for std::stack. Individually locked empty(), top(), and pop() still cannot make their combined sequence atomic.

Listing 3.3 · Book pp. 41
template<typename T,typename Container=std::deque<T> >
class stack
{
public:
    explicit stack(const Container&);
    explicit stack(Container&& = Container());
    template <class Alloc> explicit stack(const Alloc&);
    template <class Alloc> stack(const Container&, const Alloc&);
    template <class Alloc> stack(Container&&, const Alloc&);
    template <class Alloc> stack(stack&&, const Alloc&);
    bool empty() const;
    size_t size() const;
    T& top();
    T const& top() const;
    void push(T const&);
    void push(T&&);
    void pop();
    void swap(stack&&);
};

Listing 3.4 · A thread-safe stack outline

Interface only. Both pop overloads check for emptiness as part of the same locked operation; empty() remains just a snapshot.

Listing 3.4 · Book pp. 45
#include <exception>
#include <memory>
struct empty_stack: std::exception
{
    const char* what() const throw();
};
template<typename T>
class threadsafe_stack
{
public:
    threadsafe_stack();
    threadsafe_stack(const threadsafe_stack&);
    threadsafe_stack& operator=(const threadsafe_stack&) = delete;
    void push(T new_value);
    std::shared_ptr<T> pop();
    void pop(T& value);
    bool empty() const;
};

Listing 3.5 · A fleshed-out thread-safe stack

The result is copied or assigned before data.pop(), so a failed copy does not remove the item. Supply a definition for empty_stack::what() before linking a complete program. Stored-type operations run under the mutex and must not re-enter this stack or violate lock ordering.

Listing 3.5 · Book pp. 45–46
#include <exception>
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <stack>
struct empty_stack: std::exception
{
    const char* what() const throw();
};
template<typename T>
class threadsafe_stack
{
private:
    std::stack<T> data;
    mutable std::mutex m;
public:
    threadsafe_stack(){}
    threadsafe_stack(const threadsafe_stack& other)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(other.m);
        data=other.data;
    }
    threadsafe_stack& operator=(const threadsafe_stack&) = delete;
    void push(T new_value)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);
        data.push(new_value);
    }
    std::shared_ptr<T> pop()
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);
        if(data.empty()) throw empty_stack();
        std::shared_ptr<T> const res(std::make_shared<T>(data.top()));
        data.pop();
        return res;
    }
    void pop(T& value)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);
        if(data.empty()) throw empty_stack();
        value=data.top();
        data.pop();
    }
    bool empty() const
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);
        return data.empty();
    }
};

Listing 3.6 · Deadlock-avoiding swap with lock_guard

The identity check avoids locking the same nonrecursive mutex twice. std::lock acquires both locks; adopt_lock tells each guard to manage an already-held lock. some_big_object needs a real definition before it can be stored by value.

Listing 3.6 · Book pp. 48
class some_big_object;
void swap(some_big_object& lhs,some_big_object& rhs);
class X
{
private:
    some_big_object some_detail;
    std::mutex m;
public:
    X(some_big_object const& sd):some_detail(sd){}
    friend void swap(X& lhs, X& rhs)
    {
        if(&lhs==&rhs)
            return;
        std::lock(lhs.m,rhs.m);
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock_a(lhs.m,std::adopt_lock);
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock_b(rhs.m,std::adopt_lock);
        swap(lhs.some_detail,rhs.some_detail);
    }
};

Listing 3.7 · Enforcing a lock hierarchy

The custom mutex permits descending hierarchy values. thread_a follows the rule; thread_b intentionally violates it. hierarchical_mutex is a study type, not part of the standard library.

Listing 3.7 · Book pp. 51
hierarchical_mutex high_level_mutex(10000);
hierarchical_mutex low_level_mutex(5000);
int do_low_level_stuff();
int low_level_func()
{
    std::lock_guard<hierarchical_mutex> lk(low_level_mutex);
    return do_low_level_stuff();
}
void high_level_stuff(int some_param);
void high_level_func()
{
    std::lock_guard<hierarchical_mutex> lk(high_level_mutex);
    high_level_stuff(low_level_func());
}
void thread_a()
{
    high_level_func();
}
hierarchical_mutex other_mutex(100);
void do_other_stuff();
void other_stuff()
{
    high_level_func();
    do_other_stuff();
}
void thread_b()
{
    std::lock_guard<hierarchical_mutex> lk(other_mutex);
    other_stuff();
}

Listing 3.8 · A simple hierarchical mutex

Uses per-thread hierarchy state. Add <mutex>, <stdexcept>, and <climits> in a complete translation unit. Release locks in reverse acquisition order; this simple implementation does not check out-of-order unlocks. Use hierarchy values strictly below ULONG_MAX.

Listing 3.8 · Book pp. 52–53
class hierarchical_mutex
{
    std::mutex internal_mutex;
    unsigned long const hierarchy_value;
    unsigned long previous_hierarchy_value;
    static thread_local unsigned long this_thread_hierarchy_value;
    void check_for_hierarchy_violation()
    {
        if(this_thread_hierarchy_value <= hierarchy_value)
        {
            throw std::logic_error("mutex hierarchy violated");
        }
    }
    void update_hierarchy_value()
    {
        previous_hierarchy_value=this_thread_hierarchy_value;
        this_thread_hierarchy_value=hierarchy_value;
    }
public:
    explicit hierarchical_mutex(unsigned long value):
        hierarchy_value(value),
        previous_hierarchy_value(0)
    {}
    void lock()
    {
        check_for_hierarchy_violation();
        internal_mutex.lock();
        update_hierarchy_value();
    }
    void unlock()
    {
        this_thread_hierarchy_value=previous_hierarchy_value;
        internal_mutex.unlock();
    }
    bool try_lock()
    {
        check_for_hierarchy_violation();
        if(!internal_mutex.try_lock())
            return false;
        update_hierarchy_value();
        return true;
    }
};
thread_local unsigned long
    hierarchical_mutex::this_thread_hierarchy_value(ULONG_MAX);

Listing 3.9 · Deadlock-avoiding swap with unique_lock

defer_lock creates associated but unlocked guards; std::lock then locks the guards together. Each destructor unlocks only if its guard owns the lock. The placeholder object type still needs a complete definition.

Listing 3.9 · Book pp. 54–55
class some_big_object;
void swap(some_big_object& lhs,some_big_object& rhs);
class X
{
private:
    some_big_object some_detail;
    std::mutex m;
public:
    X(some_big_object const& sd):some_detail(sd){}
    friend void swap(X& lhs, X& rhs)
    {
        if(&lhs==&rhs)
            return;
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock_a(lhs.m,std::defer_lock);
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock_b(rhs.m,std::defer_lock);
        std::lock(lock_a,lock_b);
        swap(lhs.some_detail,rhs.some_detail);
    }
};

Listing 3.10 · Comparing separately captured values

Safe individual reads are not a simultaneous snapshot. With concurrent writers, equality can compare values captured at different times and return an answer that never held at one instant.

Listing 3.10 · Book pp. 58
class Y
{
private:
    int some_detail;
    mutable std::mutex m;
    int get_detail() const
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock_a(m);
        return some_detail;
    }
public:
    Y(int sd):some_detail(sd){}
    friend bool operator==(Y const& lhs, Y const& rhs)
    {
        if(&lhs==&rhs)
            return true;
        int const lhs_value=lhs.get_detail();
        int const rhs_value=rhs.get_detail();
        return lhs_value==rhs_value;
    }
};

Listing 3.11 · Mutex-protected lazy initialization

Initialization is protected, but every call still acquires the mutex to check the pointer. After unlocking, do_something() must itself be safe for concurrent use.

Listing 3.11 · Book pp. 60
std::shared_ptr<some_resource> resource_ptr;
std::mutex resource_mutex;
void foo()
{
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(resource_mutex);
    if(!resource_ptr)
    {
        resource_ptr.reset(new some_resource);
    }
    lk.unlock();
    resource_ptr->do_something();
}

Listing 3.12 · Lazy member initialization with call_once

call_once protects open_connection(), not subsequent connection operations. The connection API must permit the concurrent use shown, or have separate synchronization. Placeholder connection types and objects need definitions.

Listing 3.12 · Book pp. 61–62
class X
{
private:
    connection_info connection_details;
    connection_handle connection;
    std::once_flag connection_init_flag;
    void open_connection()
    {
        connection=connection_manager.open(connection_details);
    }
public:
    X(connection_info const& connection_details_):
        connection_details(connection_details_)
    {}
    void send_data(data_packet const& data)
    {
        std::call_once(connection_init_flag,&X::open_connection,this);
        connection.send_data(data);
    }
    data_packet receive_data()
    {
        std::call_once(connection_init_flag,&X::open_connection,this);
        return connection.receive_data();
    }
};

Listing 3.13 · A read-mostly cache with shared_mutex

The original C++11-era example uses Boost: readers take shared locks and updates take exclusive locks. Supply a complete dns_entry definition. Modern standard equivalents are std::shared_timed_mutex (C++14), or std::shared_mutex (C++17), with std::shared_lock; this reproduction retains the original Boost code.

Listing 3.13 · Book pp. 64
#include <map>
#include <string>
#include <mutex>
#include <boost/thread/shared_mutex.hpp>
class dns_entry;
class dns_cache
{
    std::map<std::string,dns_entry> entries;
    mutable boost::shared_mutex entry_mutex;
public:
    dns_entry find_entry(std::string const& domain) const
    {
        boost::shared_lock<boost::shared_mutex> lk(entry_mutex);
        std::map<std::string,dns_entry>::const_iterator const it=
            entries.find(domain);
        return (it==entries.end())?dns_entry():it->second;
    }
    void update_or_add_entry(std::string const& domain,
                             dns_entry const& dns_details)
    {
        std::lock_guard<boost::shared_mutex> lk(entry_mutex);
        entries[domain]=dns_details;
    }
};

Returning ownership of a lock

Process outside the critical section

The mutex is not held during process(). Shared state can change before relocking, so revalidate any assumptions that depended on it.

Book pp. 57 · unnumbered example
void get_and_process_data()
{
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> my_lock(the_mutex);
    some_class data_to_process=get_next_data_chunk();
    my_lock.unlock();
    result_type result=process(data_to_process);
    my_lock.lock();
    write_result(data_to_process,result);
}
3.4 / Check your understandingpp. 65–66

Think in whole operations.

Does a mutex in every method make a container interface safe?

Not necessarily. A sequence such as empty(), top(), pop() can race between calls. Combine the logical operation under one lock, and prevent references from escaping the protected region.

How can RAII coexist with deadlock?

RAII releases a lock when scope exits, but a waiting thread may never reach scope exit. Ordering rules and deadlock-avoiding multi-lock acquisition address that separate problem.

What must adopt_lock and defer_lock mean to the caller?

adopt_lock assumes the calling thread already holds the lock. defer_lock leaves a unique_lock associated with a mutex but initially unlocked; acquire it before touching protected data.

Is call_once enough to protect a database connection?

Only its initialization. Later concurrent operations on the connection need their own thread-safety guarantees or additional synchronization.

Why not keep retrying pop() until it stops throwing empty_stack?

That consumes CPU while doing no useful work and can hinder the producer. Chapter 4 introduces blocking coordination mechanisms for waiting for data or events.

Chapter in one sentence

Protect complete operations with clear boundaries, consistent lock ordering, and synchronization suited to the data’s lifetime and access pattern.

Chapter 04 / Illustrated summary

Synchronizing
concurrent operations.

Don’t just protect data. Coordinate when work can proceed—with condition variables, futures, deadlines, and messages.

PRINTED PAGES 67–102PDF PAGES 90–12516 LISTINGS · 3 FIGURES · 1 TABLE
The central idea

Wait for a meaningful condition or result—not a guessed delay—and make the dependency between operations explicit.

4.1 / Waiting for eventspp. 68–75

Sleep until there is work to do.

Repeatedly checking a shared flag wastes CPU and can contend with the producer. Sleeping between checks reduces polling overhead but trades it for response latency. A condition variable lets a thread block until shared state may allow useful progress.

The predicate is the truth; notification is a prompt

Protect both the shared state and its predicate with the same mutex. A consumer holds a std::unique_lock<std::mutex> and calls cv.wait(lock, predicate). If false, the wait atomically releases the mutex and blocks. On waking, it reacquires the mutex and rechecks; it returns with the lock held only when the predicate is true.

Wakeups can be spurious, and another consumer can take the available work first. Never treat a wakeup alone as proof that an item exists. A notification is not saved as a future event token: the persistent state is what makes an earlier producer update visible to a later waiter.

notify_one()

Wakes one current waiter, if any; which one is unspecified. Useful when one new item enables one worker. It neither transfers the mutex immediately nor guarantees that the selected thread will find the predicate true.

notify_all()

Wakes all current waiters so each can recheck its predicate. Useful for state changes relevant to many threads. They still compete to reacquire the mutex before inspecting the shared state.

std::condition_variable uses a unique_lock on std::mutex. std::condition_variable_any supports other suitable lock types, at potentially higher cost. Predicate checks should be free of externally significant side effects because they may be repeated.

Build the waiting into the queue

Combine reading the front and removing it, just as chapter 3 combined stack operations. try_pop() does not wait for an item (though it may wait to acquire the mutex); wait_and_pop() blocks until one is available. Both return the item without exposing a reference into the queue. Process the item after releasing the queue lock.

The book’s queue illustrates synchronization, not a complete shutdown protocol. Production queues need a plan for closure, exceptions, waiter notification, and joining users before destroying the queue or condition variable.
Interactive study aid · Condition-variable protocol

Wake, recheck, and continue

This deterministic walkthrough includes a spurious wake and a notification sent before waiting. It models the protocol; it does not run C++ threads.

4.2 / One-off resultspp. 76–86

A result you can ask for later.

A future represents a one-off shared state that becomes ready with a value or an exception. Use future<void> for completion without a value. Waiting for readiness does not consume a result; std::future::get() does, leaving that future invalid. A ready state is not reset to represent another event.

std::async

Combines invocation with a returned future. launch::async requests execution on another thread; launch::deferred runs the task on a thread performing a non-timed wait/get. The default permits either policy: concurrency is not guaranteed.

std::packaged_task

Wraps a callable and its result channel. Obtain its future, move the task to an executor or queue, and invoke it there. The wrapper does not start a thread by itself.

std::promise

Provides explicit set_value() or set_exception(). Useful when completion comes from event handling, networking, or more than one possible control-flow path rather than one wrapped function.

std::shared_future

Copyable handles let multiple readers wait for the same result. Move a future into one or call share(). For ordinary T, get() returns a const reference instead of consuming the stored value.

Results and failures travel together

Exceptions from tasks run through async or packaged_task are stored in their shared state and rethrown by get(). A promise needs an explicit set_exception(std::current_exception()) in an appropriate catch handler. Use std::make_exception_ptr to construct an exception value without throwing it first.

Abandoning an unsatisfied promise or packaged task makes its existing shared state ready with future_error(broken_promise). That is different from simply timing out. Satisfy a given promise only once, and obtain its associated future only once.

Share the result, not mutable handle bookkeeping

Give each reader its own shared_future copy before concurrent use. Keep referenced results alive, and separately synchronize any mutable objects reached through a returned pointer. Sharing a future does not automatically make the underlying application object thread-safe.

Async lifetime caveat: releasing the last future referring to an unfinished std::async task launched with launch::async can wait for that task. Discarding the returned future can therefore serialize seemingly asynchronous calls; a timed wait is not cancellation.
4.3 / Time-limited waitingpp. 87–92

A duration is not a deadline.

_for: relative duration

Wait for a span such as chrono::milliseconds(35). Useful for one wait. Restarting an entire relative wait after every spurious wake can accidentally extend a total budget indefinitely.

_until: absolute time point

Wait toward one fixed deadline. Compute it once outside the retry loop, preferably with steady_clock for elapsed-time budgets. All retries use the same endpoint.

Choose the clock intentionally

system_clock represents wall-clock time and may be adjusted. steady_clock is monotonic and suited to elapsed time. high_resolution_clock offers a fine tick period but may alias another clock and need not be steady. A nominal tick period is not a guarantee of measurement accuracy or scheduling precision.

std::chrono::duration<Rep, Period> stores a count and a ratio describing each unit; a time_point is relative to a clock’s epoch. Use duration_cast for explicit conversions that may discard precision. Subtract compatible time points to obtain a duration.

Interpret the result, not just the clock

Condition-variable waits without a predicate report cv_status::timeout or no_timeout, but still require a predicate check. Predicate overloads report the final predicate value. Timed mutex operations report acquisition success. Futures report ready, timeout, or deferred; timed waits do not execute a deferred task.

Timeouts bound the intended wait, not the exact time your thread will run again. Scheduler delays and mutex reacquisition can make the call return later. Timing out neither stops the producer nor cancels an asynchronous operation.

First-edition API notes: the chrono types are std::chrono::duration and std::chrono::time_point, not std::duration or std::time_point. Converting a time_t to a system_clock time point uses system_clock::from_time_t(), not the printed to_time_point(). The original table is preserved above.
4.4.1 / Functional-style dependenciespp. 93–97

Pass inputs in. Return results out.

When each task depends on its inputs rather than mutable external state, dependencies become easier to reason about. Futures carry results between tasks, reducing the amount of shared state that application code must explicitly lock.

The Quicksort example takes a list by value, selects a pivot, partitions the remaining items, recursively sorts lower and higher partitions, and joins the results using splice. The sequential version establishes the structure; the parallel version submits the lower partition through async while sorting the higher one directly.

new_lower.get() is the synchronization point before recombining results. Whether the lower sort actually ran in parallel depends on the launch policy and implementation. The algorithm can create too many tasks, has a sequential partition step, and needs workload cutoffs for practical performance.

The book’s spawn_task wrapper illustrates replacing async with packaged_task plus a thread, but its printed template has syntax errors and starts an unbounded number of detached threads. The original and a clearly labeled corrected illustration are included in the source notebook below. Neither is a production scheduler.
4.4.2 / Message passingpp. 97–102

Make each thread a state machine.

Instead of exposing mutable data across threads, send messages between independently owned components. The chapter relates this discipline to communicating sequential processes and the Actor model. The messaging implementation still synchronizes its queues; C++ does not enforce a ban on other shared memory.

In the ATM example, hardware interaction, bank communication, and ATM logic are separate responsibilities. The logic thread waits for typed messages and executes one state handler at a time: card insertion leads to PIN entry, a full PIN triggers verification, and withdrawal requests lead to bank confirmation before cash is issued or the request is refused.

A member-function pointer selects the current state. A handler records private state, sends messages, and selects the next state. The sample message dispatcher discards unmatched message types; that is a deliberate library policy to examine, not a universal guarantee of message-passing systems.

The chapter gives a partial ATM outline; appendix C contains the supporting messaging framework and more complete example. Message passing moves synchronization into a boundary with explicit protocols—it does not eliminate the need to consider shutdown, delivery, ordering, or failure.

The chapter’s code, embedded.

Listing 4.1 · Waiting for queued data with a condition variable

The queue predicate is checked under mut. wait() releases the mutex while blocked and reacquires it before returning. Processing happens after unlocking. Placeholder functions and data_chunk require definitions; this example uses a last-chunk convention to stop the consumer.

Listing 4.1 · Book pp. 69–70
std::mutex mut;
std::queue<data_chunk> data_queue;
std::condition_variable data_cond;
void data_preparation_thread()
{
    while(more_data_to_prepare())
    {
        data_chunk const data=prepare_data();
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        data_queue.push(data);
        data_cond.notify_one();
    }
}
void data_processing_thread()
{
    while(true)
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        data_cond.wait(
            lk,[]{return !data_queue.empty();});
        data_chunk data=data_queue.front();
        data_queue.pop();
        lk.unlock();
        process(data);
        if(is_last_chunk(data))
            break;
    }
}

Listing 4.2 · The std::queue interface

Historical interface excerpt, not a complete container implementation. Separate front() and pop() calls would expose the same compound-operation races seen in chapter 3.

Listing 4.2 · Book pp. 71–72
template <class T, class Container = std::deque<T> >
class queue {
public:
    explicit queue(const Container&);
    explicit queue(Container&& = Container());
    template <class Alloc> explicit queue(const Alloc&);
    template <class Alloc> queue(const Container&, const Alloc&);
    template <class Alloc> queue(Container&&, const Alloc&);
    template <class Alloc> queue(queue&&, const Alloc&);
    void swap(queue& q);
    bool empty() const;
    size_type size() const;
    T& front();
    const T& front() const;
    T& back();
    const T& back() const;
    void push(const T& x);
    void push(T&& x);
    void pop();
    template <class... Args> void emplace(Args&&... args);

Listing 4.3 · The threadsafe_queue interface

try_pop reports an empty queue without waiting; wait_and_pop blocks for data. Both offer output-reference and shared-pointer variants. The interface explicitly deletes assignment.

Listing 4.3 · Book pp. 72
#include <memory>
template<typename T>
class threadsafe_queue
{
public:
    threadsafe_queue();
    threadsafe_queue(const threadsafe_queue&);
    threadsafe_queue& operator=(
        const threadsafe_queue&) = delete;
    void push(T new_value);
    bool try_pop(T& value);
    std::shared_ptr<T> try_pop();
    void wait_and_pop(T& value);
    std::shared_ptr<T> wait_and_pop();
    bool empty() const;
};

Listing 4.4 · Extracting push and wait_and_pop

The class owns the synchronization details. Consumers need not lock externally. The producer must eventually supply the termination item expected by this illustrative consumer.

Listing 4.4 · Book pp. 73
#include <queue>
#include <mutex>
#include <condition_variable>
template<typename T>
class threadsafe_queue
{
private:
    std::mutex mut;
    std::queue<T> data_queue;
    std::condition_variable data_cond;
public:
    void push(T new_value)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        data_queue.push(new_value);
        data_cond.notify_one();
    }
    void wait_and_pop(T& value)
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        data_cond.wait(lk,[this]{return !data_queue.empty();});
        value=data_queue.front();
        data_queue.pop();
    }
};
threadsafe_queue<data_chunk> data_queue;
void data_preparation_thread()
{
    while(more_data_to_prepare())
    {
        data_chunk const data=prepare_data();
        data_queue.push(data);
    }
}
void data_processing_thread()
{
    while(true)
    {
        data_chunk data;
        data_queue.wait_and_pop(data);
        process(data);
        if(is_last_chunk(data))
            break;
    }
}

Listing 4.5 · A full condition-variable queue

Copying locks the source queue. Every removal checks and extracts under one lock. This teaching implementation has no close/shutdown operation: stop and join all users before destruction. If copying an item throws after a wake, it does not pass the notification to another waiter; robust multi-consumer designs need an exception-handling policy.

Listing 4.5 · Book pp. 74–75
#include <queue>
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <condition_variable>
template<typename T>
class threadsafe_queue
{
private:
    mutable std::mutex mut;
    std::queue<T> data_queue;
    std::condition_variable data_cond;
public:
    threadsafe_queue()
    {}
    threadsafe_queue(threadsafe_queue const& other)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(other.mut);
        data_queue=other.data_queue;
    }
    void push(T new_value)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        data_queue.push(new_value);
        data_cond.notify_one();
    }
    void wait_and_pop(T& value)
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        data_cond.wait(lk,[this]{return !data_queue.empty();});
        value=data_queue.front();
        data_queue.pop();
    }
    std::shared_ptr<T> wait_and_pop()
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        data_cond.wait(lk,[this]{return !data_queue.empty();});
        std::shared_ptr<T> res(std::make_shared<T>(data_queue.front()));
        data_queue.pop();
        return res;
    }
    bool try_pop(T& value)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        if(data_queue.empty())
            return false;
        value=data_queue.front();
        data_queue.pop();
        return true;
    }
    std::shared_ptr<T> try_pop()
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        if(data_queue.empty())
            return std::shared_ptr<T>();
        std::shared_ptr<T> res(std::make_shared<T>(data_queue.front()));
        data_queue.pop();
        return res;
    }
    bool empty() const
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        return data_queue.empty();
    }
};

get() waits if necessary, returns the result (or rethrows its exception), and consumes this future’s shared state. With the default launch policy, the task may be deferred rather than run concurrently. The declared helper functions still need definitions.

Listing 4.7 · Passing arguments to std::async

The original move_only(move_only&&) declaration is missing a trailing semicolon. Add it before compiling. Passing an object copies it; std::ref borrows it. Referenced objects must outlive their use. A discarded async future can block at destruction if the task was actually launched asynchronously.

Listing 4.7 · Book pp. 77–78
#include <string>
#include <future>
struct X
{
    void foo(int,std::string const&);
    std::string bar(std::string const&);
};
X x;
auto f1=std::async(&X::foo,&x,42,"hello");
auto f2=std::async(&X::bar,x,"goodbye");
struct Y
{
    double operator()(double);
};
Y y;
auto f3=std::async(Y(),3.141);
auto f4=std::async(std::ref(y),2.718);
X baz(X&);
std::async(baz,std::ref(x));
class move_only
{
public:
    move_only();
    move_only(move_only&&)
    move_only(move_only const&) = delete;
    move_only& operator=(move_only&&);
    move_only& operator=(move_only const&) = delete;
    void operator()();
};
auto f5=std::async(move_only());

Listing 4.8 · A packaged_task specialization outline

A partial conceptual interface, not a user specialization to add to namespace std. packaged_task is move-only; it cannot be stored directly by value in C++11 std::function, whose target must be copyable. Use a suitable wrapper or a move-aware task container.

Listing 4.8 · Book pp. 79
template<>
class packaged_task<std::string(std::vector<char>*,int)>
{
public:
    template<typename Callable>
    explicit packaged_task(Callable&& f);
    std::future<std::string> get_future();
    void operator()(std::vector<char>*,int);
};

Listing 4.9 · Posting tasks to a GUI thread

This is an outline with polling and placeholder GUI hooks, not a complete event loop. Execute tasks outside the queue lock, respect the framework’s required UI thread, and provide thread shutdown/joining. Do not block that UI thread waiting for a task only it can execute.

Listing 4.9 · Book pp. 80
#include <deque>
#include <mutex>
#include <future>
#include <thread>
#include <utility>
std::mutex m;
std::deque<std::packaged_task<void()> > tasks;
bool gui_shutdown_message_received();
void get_and_process_gui_message();
void gui_thread()
{
    while(!gui_shutdown_message_received())
    {
        get_and_process_gui_message();
        std::packaged_task<void()> task;
        {
            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m);
            if(tasks.empty())
                continue;
            task=std::move(tasks.front());
            tasks.pop_front();
        }
        task();
    }
}
std::thread gui_bg_thread(gui_thread);
template<typename Func>
std::future<void> post_task_for_gui_thread(Func f)
{
    std::packaged_task<void()> task(f);
    std::future<void> res=task.get_future();
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m);
    tasks.push_back(std::move(task));
    return res;
}

Listing 4.10 · Promises for multiple connections

Incoming payloads satisfy matching promises; outgoing operations signal completion through a promise. Networking types are placeholders. Real code needs failure handling, queue consumption, and a precisely defined meaning for successful transmission.

Listing 4.10 · Book pp. 82
#include <future>
void process_connections(connection_set& connections)
{
    while(!done(connections))
    {
        for(connection_iterator
                connection=connections.begin(),end=connections.end();
            connection!=end;
            ++connection)
        {
            if(connection->has_incoming_data())
            {
                data_packet data=connection->incoming();
                std::promise<payload_type>& p=
                    connection->get_promise(data.id);
                p.set_value(data.payload);
            }
            if(connection->has_outgoing_data())
            {
                outgoing_packet data=
                    connection->top_of_outgoing_queue();
                connection->send(data.payload);
                data.promise.set_value(true);
            }
        }
    }
}

Listing 4.11 · A fixed-deadline condition-variable wait

The deadline is computed once with steady_clock, outside the loop. Spurious wakes do not restart the full budget. Accesses to done must use m; returning may still be delayed by scheduling or mutex reacquisition, so this is not a hard real-time guarantee.

Listing 4.11 · Book pp. 90–91
#include <condition_variable>
#include <mutex>
#include <chrono>
std::condition_variable cv;
bool done;
std::mutex m;
bool wait_loop()
{
    auto const timeout= std::chrono::steady_clock::now()+
        std::chrono::milliseconds(500);
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m);
    while(!done)
    {
        if(cv.wait_until(lk,timeout)==std::cv_status::timeout)
            break;
    }
    return done;
}

Listing 4.12 · Sequential functional-style Quicksort

The public interface takes and returns a list by value; the implementation uses partition, splice, and moves to avoid unnecessary copying. Add <list>, <algorithm>, and <utility>. It is a teaching sort, not a replacement for a tuned sorting library.

Listing 4.12 · Book pp. 94–95
template<typename T>
std::list<T> sequential_quick_sort(std::list<T> input)
{
    if(input.empty())
    {
        return input;
    }
    std::list<T> result;
    result.splice(result.begin(),input,input.begin());
    T const& pivot=*result.begin();

    auto divide_point=std::partition(input.begin(),input.end(),
            [&](T const& t){return t<pivot;});
    std::list<T> lower_part;
    lower_part.splice(lower_part.end(),input,input.begin(),
        divide_point);
    auto new_lower(
        sequential_quick_sort(std::move(lower_part)));
    auto new_higher(
        sequential_quick_sort(std::move(input)));
    result.splice(result.end(),new_higher);
    result.splice(result.begin(),new_lower);
    return result;
}

Listing 4.13 · Parallel Quicksort using futures

The lower partition is submitted to std::async while the current thread sorts the higher one. Default policy permits deferred execution, so actual parallelism is not guaranteed. Unbounded recursive task creation may oversubscribe resources; production versions need workload cutoffs and scheduling control.

Listing 4.13 · Book pp. 95–96
template<typename T>
std::list<T> parallel_quick_sort(std::list<T> input)
{
    if(input.empty())
    {
        return input;
    }
    std::list<T> result;
    result.splice(result.begin(),input,input.begin());
    T const& pivot=*result.begin();
    auto divide_point=std::partition(input.begin(),input.end(),
            [&](T const& t){return t<pivot;});
    std::list<T> lower_part;
    lower_part.splice(lower_part.end(),input,input.begin(),
        divide_point);
    std::future<std::list<T> > new_lower(
        std::async(&parallel_quick_sort<T>,std::move(lower_part)));
    auto new_higher(
        parallel_quick_sort(std::move(input)));
    result.splice(result.end(),new_higher);
    result.splice(result.begin(),new_lower.get());
    return result;
}

Listing 4.14 · A sample spawn_task implementation

Original code has missing typename before dependent std::result_of<...>::type uses and an extra closing parenthesis in task(std::move(f))). It will not compile as printed. A corrected C++11 illustration appears below. std::result_of was deprecated in C++17 and removed in C++20; newer code uses std::invoke_result. The simple detached-thread design is not a thread pool.

Listing 4.14 · Book pp. 97
template<typename F,typename A>
std::future<std::result_of<F(A&&)>::type>
    spawn_task(F&& f,A&& a)
{
    typedef std::result_of<F(A&&)>::type result_type;
    std::packaged_task<result_type(A&&)>
        task(std::move(f)));
    std::future<result_type> res(task.get_future());
    std::thread t(std::move(task),std::move(a));
    t.detach();
    return res;
}

Listing 4.15 · A message-driven ATM logic class

A partial class, not a standalone program. It relies on the messaging library, message types, and additional states from appendix C. The loop dispatches the current state; message handlers update that state. No real banking operation is implemented here.

Listing 4.15 · Book pp. 99–100
struct card_inserted
{
    std::string account;
};
class atm
{
    messaging::receiver incoming;
    messaging::sender bank;
    messaging::sender interface_hardware;
    void (atm::*state)();
    std::string account;
    std::string pin;
    void waiting_for_card()
    {
        interface_hardware.send(display_enter_card());
        incoming.wait()
            .handle<card_inserted>(
                [&](card_inserted const& msg)
                {
                    account=msg.account;
                    pin="";
                    interface_hardware.send(display_enter_pin());
                    state=&atm::getting_pin;
                }
                );
    }
    void getting_pin();
public:
    void run()
    {
        state=&atm::waiting_for_card;
        try
        {
            for(;;)
            {
                (this->*state)();
            }
        }
        catch(messaging::close_queue const&)
        {
        }
    }
};

Listing 4.16 · Handling PIN-entry messages

This member definition extends the ATM outline. Digit, delete-last, and cancel messages determine the next state; four digits trigger a verification request. The messaging framework handles blocking and dispatch. Message types and the remaining states still require definitions.

Listing 4.16 · Book pp. 101
void atm::getting_pin()
{
    incoming.wait()
        .handle<digit_pressed>(
            [&](digit_pressed const& msg)
            {
                unsigned const pin_length=4;
                pin+=msg.digit;
                if(pin.length()==pin_length)
                {
                    bank.send(verify_pin(account,pin,incoming));
                    state=&atm::verifying_pin;
                }
            }
            )
        .handle<clear_last_pressed>(
            [&](clear_last_pressed const& msg)
            {
                if(!pin.empty())
                {
                    pin.resize(pin.length()-1);
                }
            }
            )
        .handle<cancel_pressed>(
            [&](cancel_pressed const& msg)
            {
                state=&atm::done_processing;
            }
            );
}

Corrected C++11 spawn_task illustration

Added study aid, not a verbatim book listing. Fixes the dependent-type declarations and extra parenthesis and uses forwarding for the supplied callable and argument. It still creates a detached thread per call; ensure borrowed data outlives the task and do not treat it as a bounded executor.

Added study aid · corrected C++11 example
#include <future>
#include <thread>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

template<typename F, typename A>
std::future<typename std::result_of<F(A&&)>::type>
spawn_task(F&& f, A&& a)
{
    typedef typename std::result_of<F(A&&)>::type result_type;
    std::packaged_task<result_type(A&&)> task(std::forward<F>(f));
    std::future<result_type> res(task.get_future());
    std::thread t(std::move(task), std::forward<A>(a));
    t.detach();
    return res;
}

Additional unnumbered examples

The remaining standalone snippets appear below. Table 4.1’s API fragments are preserved in the table image, not concatenated into a runnable program.

Polling with a short sleep

All flag updates must also lock m. Sleeping reduces busy-waiting but adds a latency/CPU trade-off; this is the baseline, not the preferred event-waiting design.

Book p. 68 · unnumbered example
bool flag;
std::mutex m;
void wait_for_flag()
{
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m);
    while(!flag)
    {
        lk.unlock();
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(100));
        lk.lock();
    }
}

Choosing a launch policy

These names continue Listing 4.7. launch::async requests asynchronous execution; launch::deferred runs on the thread performing a non-timed wait/get. The combined policy leaves the choice to the implementation.

Book p. 78 · unnumbered example
auto f6=std::async(std::launch::async,Y(),1.2);
auto f7=std::async(std::launch::deferred,baz,std::ref(x));
auto f8=std::async(
   std::launch::deferred | std::launch::async,
   baz,std::ref(x));
auto f9=std::async(baz,std::ref(x));
f7.wait();

A calculation that throws

Add <cmath> and <stdexcept>, and use std::sqrt in portable code. This defines the function used by the next two examples.

Book p. 83 · unnumbered example
double square_root(double x)
{
    if(x<0)
    {
        throw std::out_of_range("x<0");
    }
    return sqrt(x);
}

Calling directly

The negative argument throws to the caller immediately.

Book p. 83 · unnumbered example
double y=square_root(-1);

Calling through a future

The asynchronous task stores its exception in the shared state; get() rethrows it on the thread retrieving the result.

Book p. 83 · unnumbered example
std::future<double> f=std::async(square_root,-1);
double y=f.get();

Passing the current exception to a promise

Call set_exception(std::current_exception()) from a catch handler. This fragment belongs inside a function; calculate_value and some_promise need definitions.

Book p. 84 · unnumbered example
extern std::promise<double> some_promise;
try
{
    some_promise.set_value(calculate_value());
}
catch(...)
{
    some_promise.set_exception(std::current_exception());
}

Constructing an exception for a promise

First-edition name correction: std::copy_exception is not a C++11 standard API. Use std::make_exception_ptr(std::logic_error("foo ")) instead.

Book p. 84 · unnumbered example
some_promise.set_exception(std::copy_exception(std::logic_error("foo ")));

Moving a future into shared_future

The original future becomes invalid after moving its shared state; the shared_future becomes valid. Give each reader its own shared_future handle.

Book p. 85 · unnumbered example
std::promise<int> p;
std::future<int> f(p.get_future());
assert(f.valid());
std::shared_future<int> sf(std::move(f));
assert(!f.valid());
assert(sf.valid());

Implicit transfer from a temporary

The temporary future returned by get_future() can transfer its state directly to a shared_future.

Book p. 86 · unnumbered example
std::promise<std::string> p;
std::shared_future<std::string> sf(p.get_future());

Deducing a shared future type

share() transfers the state out of the original future and returns a copyable shared_future. The map parameter types are placeholders.

Book p. 86 · unnumbered example
std::promise< std::map< SomeIndexType, SomeDataType, SomeComparator,
    SomeAllocator>::iterator> p;
auto sf=p.get_future().share();

Converting durations

54802 milliseconds becomes 54 whole seconds: duration_cast truncates the fractional part rather than rounding.

Book p. 89 · unnumbered example
std::chrono::milliseconds ms(54802);
std::chrono::seconds s=
    std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::seconds>(ms);

Waiting briefly for a future

wait_for can report ready, timeout, or deferred. A deferred result is not made ready by a timed wait; decide when to call get()/wait() to execute it.

Book p. 89 · unnumbered example
std::future<int> f=std::async(some_task);
if(f.wait_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(35))==std::future_status::ready)
    do_something_with(f.get());

Timing a block of work

Original type correction: std::chrono::duration<double,std::chrono::seconds> is invalid because the second template argument must be a ratio, not a duration type. Use std::chrono::duration<double>(stop-start).count(). Prefer steady_clock for elapsed-time measurement; high_resolution_clock need not be steady.

Book p. 90 · unnumbered example
auto start=std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
do_something();
auto stop=std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
std::cout<<"do_something() took "
  <<std::chrono::duration<double,std::chrono::seconds>(stop-start).count()
  <<" seconds"<<std::endl;
4.5 / Check your understandingp. 102

Choose the right waiting contract.

Why is a condition-variable notification not enough?

A wake can be spurious, another consumer may have taken the work, or a notification may occur before a waiter exists. The mutex-protected predicate records whether progress is possible; always check it.

Does wait() keep the queue mutex locked while sleeping?

No. It atomically releases the lock and blocks, then reacquires the mutex before checking the predicate or returning. Keeping the mutex locked would prevent a producer from making progress.

Which future producer should I use?

Use async for a task with a returned result, packaged_task when controlling where a callable runs, and promise when explicitly reporting a value or exception from event-driven control flow.

What does a deferred timed-wait result mean?

The async task has not started and is deferred. A non-timed wait/get can execute it on the calling thread; repeatedly using wait_for does not start that work.

Does wait_for timing out cancel the operation?

No. It ends that wait attempt. Cancellation and task lifetime need a separate protocol; destruction of an async future can still wait for an unfinished asynchronously launched task.

Why compute a deadline outside the wait loop?

It preserves one overall budget through repeated wakeups. Restarting the full relative duration after each wake can extend the total wait unexpectedly.

Chapter in one sentence

Coordinate progress through predicates, one-off result channels, fixed deadlines, and explicit messages instead of repeated polling or hidden shared-state assumptions.
