Chapter 05 / Illustrated summary

The C++
memory model.

Atomicity prevents torn operations. Ordering establishes when other data can be read safely. They are related guarantees—not the same guarantee.

PRINTED PAGES 103–147PDF PAGES 126–17013 LISTINGS · 7 FIGURES · 3 TABLES
The central idea

To publish data safely, prove the path: write the payload → release → acquire that observes the publication → read the payload.

5.1 / Memory model basicspp. 104–106

Start with locations, not cache folklore.

The memory model defines the abstract guarantees a correct C++ program can rely on, regardless of the compiler and processor. Objects can contain subobjects; a scalar object is a memory location, while adjacent nonzero-width bit-fields can share one location. Distinct fields are not necessarily independently writable if they are packed bit-fields.

Two conflicting accesses to the same memory location, at least one non-atomic and at least one a write, need the required happens-before ordering. Without it, cross-thread conflicting accesses form a data race and cause undefined behavior. “The hardware writes an int in one instruction” is not a C++ synchronization argument.

Atomic accesses avoid a data race on that atomic object, but do not automatically fix a logical race or protect other data. Each atomic object has its own modification order: a total order of its modifications, consistent with the language’s coherence constraints. Separate atomic objects do not automatically share a single order.

Modification order is an order of writes, not a promise that every read sees the latest wall-clock value or that successive reads must see a strictly later write. Reading the same value again, or skipping intermediate modifications, may be permitted. Construction and publication must also be safe before concurrent use.
5.2 / Atomic types & operationspp. 107–119

Indivisible operations. Explicit contracts.

<atomic> supplies std::atomic<T>, specializations, aliases, and related free functions. Atomic objects are not copyable in the ordinary sense. Loading one and storing into another is two operations, not an atomic transaction over both objects.

atomic_flag

The C++11 building block provides clear() and test_and_set(); test_and_set returns the previous state. Its operations are guaranteed lock-free. The book uses it to build a spinlock—not a general recommendation to busy-wait.

atomic<bool> and generic atomics

Support load, store, exchange, and compare/exchange. Most atomic types are not guaranteed lock-free; use is_lock_free() where that property matters. Atomic does not mean wait-free or necessarily faster.

Atomic integers

Add fetch_add/sub, fetch_and/or/xor, increment/decrement, and corresponding compound operators. Named fetch operations return the old value; compound assignment returns the new one. Two atomic operations are still two operations.

Atomic pointers

Support pointer updates and element-based fetch_add/sub. Making the pointer atomic does not own the pointee, extend its lifetime, or solve reclamation. Do not dereference a pointer without a valid lifetime protocol.

The generic primary template requires a suitable trivially copyable type, not an arbitrary class such as std::vector. Compare/exchange compares representations rather than calling a user-defined operator==; padding, floating-point representations, and the applicable standard version matter.

Compare/exchange: expected is an input and an output

compare_exchange_weak(expected, desired) conditionally replaces the stored value. On an ordinary mismatch it updates expected with the observed value and returns false. Weak CAS may also fail spuriously; strong CAS does not have that spurious-failure permission. Loops must recompute a dependent desired value when expected changes.

Success is a read-modify-write; failure is a load. The failure order cannot be release or acq_rel. In the chapter’s C++11 rules it also cannot be stronger than success. For the one-order overload, acq_rel success maps to acquire failure, while release success maps to relaxed failure.

Free functions usually take a pointer to the atomic object, use an atomic_ prefix, and add _explicit for a memory-order argument. The chapter also shows C++11 atomic free functions for shared_ptr. These protect the handle, not arbitrary changes to the pointed-to data.

Edition context: the 2012 chapter describes C++11. Later standards expanded these APIs: C++20 added atomic waiting/notification, more atomic_flag operations, floating-point atomic arithmetic, and atomic<shared_ptr<T>>. The original tables are preserved as historical reference. In particular, C++11 atomic integers do not have *=, /=, or shift compound operations despite a stray broader claim in the prose.
5.3.1–5.3.2 / The ordering chainpp. 119–123

Build a happens-before proof.

Sequenced-before orders operations within a thread. A matching synchronizes-with relationship bridges threads. For ordinary release/acquire synchronization, combining those edges transitively gives a happens-before path from the producer’s data writes to the consumer’s data reads.

In Listing 5.2, the writer fills a vector and then stores true into an atomic flag. The reader waits until it observes that publication before reading the vector. Default sequentially consistent operations include the required release/acquire effects, so the ordinary vector access can be safe in this one-shot protocol.

For the direct handoff, the acquire must read from the relevant release store, or from a qualifying release sequence. Merely placing release and acquire operations somewhere in two functions is not enough. If the acquire reads an unrelated or initial value, that publication edge has not been established.

Do not read “happens-before” as a timestamp or an instruction-fence diagram. It is a language relation defining permitted observations. Mutex unlock/lock and other standard facilities also specify synchronization directly; the standard does not require them to be implemented using a particular atomic instruction.
5.3.3 / Memory-order choicespp. 123–140

Choose guarantees before choosing speed.

Sequentially consistent: the default

memory_order_seq_cst is the easiest starting point. When all relevant atomic operations are SC, they fit a single total order consistent with the required sequencing and coherence rules. This rules out outcomes that would require a cycle in that order. It does not turn several operations into one transaction, eliminate all logical races, or repair a nonatomic data race.

Relaxed: atomicity and coherence, not publication

memory_order_relaxed preserves atomicity and per-object coherence but does not by itself create a cross-thread synchronization edge. Seeing ready=true through a relaxed load does not force a later load of a different atomic payload to observe the producer’s earlier update.

The notebook analogy gives each atomic its own write history, with different readers at different positions in it. A reader cannot go backward in a single location’s modification order for properly sequenced repeated loads, but there is no implied global ordering across unrelated atomic objects.

Release/acquire: publish through an observed handoff

A release store synchronizes with an acquire load that reads its value, including the applicable release-sequence cases. Earlier writes in the producer become ordered before later reads in the consumer. Payload accesses may themselves be relaxed atomics, or ordinary accesses if the protocol orders all conflicting uses.

memory_order_acq_rel gives an RMW both sides of the handoff. Release is not a valid plain-load order; acquire/acq_rel are not valid plain-store orders. Pairwise synchronization is not a universal SC order: the independent writers in Listing 5.7 can still lead both readers to miss the other flag.

Transitive relays

A middle thread can acquire the producer’s publication, then release another flag for a final consumer to acquire. The chain carries the earlier data visibility even when the relay never reads that data. Listing 5.9 demonstrates this; the following CAS variant combines the relay states into one atomic variable.

Consume: historical dependency ordering

The chapter’s consume model orders operations that depend on a published pointer, not an unrelated load. In Listing 5.10, the pointed-to members have a dependency path; the independent atomic a does not have the same historical guarantee.

For new code, prefer acquire rather than trying to exploit consume. Implementations generally strengthen consume to acquire, and memory_order_consume and kill_dependency are deprecated in C++26. This summary preserves the chapter’s dependency explanation as historical context, not as a recommended optimization technique.
Interactive study aid / Publication proofBased on Listings 5.5 & 5.8

What did the ready flag actually promise?

One writer sets payload=42, then ready=true. One reader observes ready=true and reads payload. Both objects begin initialized (payload=0, ready=false); there are no later writes or resets. This model assumes that successful ready observation, not that any spin loop is guaranteed to finish.

This is a fixed language-rule explanation, not a hardware simulator, C++ runtime, or exhaustive memory-model checker. Undefined behavior is deliberately not assigned a set of numeric outcomes. Tests on one machine cannot prove a weak-order outcome impossible.

5.3.4 / Release sequencespp. 141–142

A publication can survive an RMW chain.

After a release operation on an atomic, a qualifying contiguous chain of read-modify-write modifications in that atomic’s modification order can carry the publication forward. An acquire reading a value from that sequence can synchronize with the head release, even when intermediate RMWs are relaxed.

The queue-count example publishes a filled buffer with a release store. Consumers claim indexes using acquire fetch_sub operations. Later claims read values produced by earlier claims, but still acquire the producer’s publication through the release sequence. The claims do not need to release data to one another just to make the original buffer contents visible.

Standard-version distinction: C++11 release sequences could also contain qualifying same-thread writes after the head release; since C++20, the post-head sequence is limited to RMW modifications. The RMW-only chain used here illustrates the common case. An intervening plain store can break the chain under current rules; do not generalize it into “any later read sees every earlier release.”

Ordering publication does not make buffer reuse safe. Consumers need exclusive index ownership, valid element lifetimes, and a shutdown/repopulation protocol. Listing 5.11 leaves these concerns and the waiting implementation incomplete.

5.3.5–5.3.6 / Fences & ordinary datapp. 143–146

Fences need a communication path.

std::atomic_thread_fence constrains ordering without itself reading or writing the publication variable. In Listing 5.12, a release fence follows the payload write and precedes a relaxed flag store. A consumer reads that flag store, then executes an acquire fence before reading the payload. That connected path orders the payload accesses.

A fence is not a global cache flush and does not synchronize unrelated threads merely because both executed one. Placement matters: moving the release fence before the payload write removes the publication guarantee for that write.

Listing 5.13 makes the payload an ordinary bool. It remains safe because all its conflicting accesses are ordered by the atomic flag and fences. Without that ordering, the same ordinary-data handoff can contain a data race. It would be incorrect to describe its failure merely as “sometimes reading the old value.”

Back to a mutex

The spinlock’s successful acquire test-and-set can read the false written by the preceding owner’s release clear. The owner’s critical-section writes then happen-before the next owner’s reads. Higher-level facilities package such synchronization contracts so most application code can avoid manually proving low-level atomic protocols.

Practical default

Use higher-level synchronization first. If atomics are necessary, start with clear lifetime rules and sequential consistency; weaken ordering only with a proof and a measured reason.

The chapter’s code, embedded.

Transcribed from the supplied PDF with whitespace normalized, smart quotation marks converted to ASCII, callout annotations omitted, and multi-page listings joined. The original source includes placeholder functions, missing headers, obsolete spellings, and demonstrations with assertions that are not guaranteed. Notes distinguish those cases; these are not 13 independent production-ready programs.

Listing 5.1 · A spinlock built from atomic_flag

Add <atomic> in a complete translation unit. Acquire test-and-set pairs with release clear. This mutex busy-waits, is not recursive or fair, and can perform badly under contention or when its owner is descheduled; prefer a standard mutex unless measured requirements justify otherwise.

Listing 5.1 · Book pp. 111–112
class spinlock_mutex
{
    std::atomic_flag flag;
public:
    spinlock_mutex():
        flag(ATOMIC_FLAG_INIT)
    {}
    void lock()
    {
        while(flag.test_and_set(std::memory_order_acquire));
    }
    void unlock()
    {
        flag.clear(std::memory_order_release);
    }
};

Listing 5.2 · Publishing ordinary data through an atomic flag

The printed std::this_thread::sleep(std::milliseconds(1)) is not a standard C++11 call. Use std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(1)) and add <thread> and <chrono>. With the default sequentially consistent flag operations, observing true orders the earlier vector write before the reader’s access. Do not mutate the vector again concurrently.

Listing 5.2 · Book pp. 120
#include <vector>
#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
std::vector<int> data;
std::atomic<bool> data_ready(false);
void reader_thread()
{
    while(!data_ready.load())
    {
        std::this_thread::sleep(std::milliseconds(1));
    }
    std::cout<<"The answer="<<data[0]<<"\n";
}
void writer_thread()
{
    data.push_back(42);
    data_ready=true;
}

Listing 5.3 · Unspecified function-argument evaluation order

The two get_num() function executions produce 1 and 2, but which function parameter receives which is unspecified. This is not a multithreaded test; do not confuse it with directly writing two unsequenced increments of the same scalar in older C++ versions.

Listing 5.3 · Book pp. 122
#include <iostream>
void foo(int a,int b)
{
    std::cout<<a<<","<<b<<std::endl;
}
int get_num()
{
    static int i=0;
    return ++i;
}
int main()
{
    foo(get_num(),get_num());
}

Listing 5.4 · Sequential consistency supplies a total order

On completion, the assertion is guaranteed by the sequentially consistent ordering: z can be 1 or 2, but not 0. Both readers observing the other flag as false would require a cycle in the single SC order.

Listing 5.4 · Book pp. 125
#include <atomic>
#include <thread>
#include <assert.h>
std::atomic<bool> x,y;
std::atomic<int> z;
void write_x()
{
    x.store(true,std::memory_order_seq_cst);
}
void write_y()
{
    y.store(true,std::memory_order_seq_cst);
}
void read_x_then_y()
{
    while(!x.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst));
    if(y.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst))
        ++z;
}
void read_y_then_x()
{
    while(!y.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst));
    if(x.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst))
        ++z;
}
int main()
{
    x=false;
    y=false;
    z=0;
    std::thread a(write_x);
    std::thread b(write_y);
    std::thread c(read_x_then_y);
    std::thread d(read_y_then_x);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    c.join();
    d.join();
    assert(z.load()!=0);
}

Listing 5.5 · Relaxed operations do not publish other variables

Intentionally not a guaranteed assertion: z can be 0 because observing the relaxed y store does not synchronize the x access. All shared variables here are atomic, so this permitted outcome is not a data race. A particular CPU or test run may never exhibit it.

Listing 5.5 · Book pp. 127–128
#include <atomic>
#include <thread>
#include <assert.h>
std::atomic<bool> x,y;
std::atomic<int> z;
void write_x_then_y()
{
    x.store(true,std::memory_order_relaxed);
    y.store(true,std::memory_order_relaxed);
}
void read_y_then_x()
{
    while(!y.load(std::memory_order_relaxed));
    if(x.load(std::memory_order_relaxed))
        ++z;
}
int main()
{
    x=false;
    y=false;
    z=0;
    std::thread a(write_x_then_y);
    std::thread b(read_y_then_x);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    assert(z.load()!=0);
}

Listing 5.6 · Several independent atomic modification orders

Each atomic has its own coherent modification order; the three values in a printed triplet are separate loads, not one snapshot. The go flag starts the workers but does not impose one global order on later relaxed x/y/z operations.

Listing 5.6 · Book pp. 129–130
#include <thread>
#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
std::atomic<int> x(0),y(0),z(0);
std::atomic<bool> go(false);
unsigned const loop_count=10;
struct read_values
{
    int x,y,z;
};
read_values values1[loop_count];
read_values values2[loop_count];
read_values values3[loop_count];
read_values values4[loop_count];
read_values values5[loop_count];
void increment(std::atomic<int>* var_to_inc,read_values* values)
{
    while(!go)
        std::this_thread::yield();
    for(unsigned i=0;i<loop_count;++i)
    {
        values[i].x=x.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        values[i].y=y.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        values[i].z=z.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        var_to_inc->store(i+1,std::memory_order_relaxed);
        std::this_thread::yield();
    }
}
void read_vals(read_values* values)
{
    while(!go)
        std::this_thread::yield();
    for(unsigned i=0;i<loop_count;++i)
    {
        values[i].x=x.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        values[i].y=y.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        values[i].z=z.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        std::this_thread::yield();
    }
}
void print(read_values* v)
{
    for(unsigned i=0;i<loop_count;++i)
    {
        if(i)
            std::cout<<",";
        std::cout<<"("<<v[i].x<<","<<v[i].y<<","<<v[i].z<<")";
    }
    std::cout<<std::endl;
}
int main()
{
    std::thread t1(increment,&x,values1);
    std::thread t2(increment,&y,values2);
    std::thread t3(increment,&z,values3);
    std::thread t4(read_vals,values4);
    std::thread t5(read_vals,values5);
    go=true;
    t5.join();
    t4.join();
    t3.join();
    t2.join();
    t1.join();
    print(values1);
    print(values2);
    print(values3);
    print(values4);
    print(values5);
}

Listing 5.7 · Acquire/release is not a universal total order

Intentionally not a guaranteed assertion: z can be 0. The separate writers do not provide a chain that forces either reader to observe the other flag. Pairwise acquire/release synchronization is weaker than one SC order over all these operations.

Listing 5.7 · Book pp. 133
#include <atomic>
#include <thread>
#include <assert.h>
std::atomic<bool> x,y;
std::atomic<int> z;
void write_x()
{
    x.store(true,std::memory_order_release);
}
void write_y()
{
    y.store(true,std::memory_order_release);
}
void read_x_then_y()
{
    while(!x.load(std::memory_order_acquire));
    if(y.load(std::memory_order_acquire))
        ++z;
}
void read_y_then_x()
{
    while(!y.load(std::memory_order_acquire));
    if(x.load(std::memory_order_acquire))
        ++z;
}
int main()
{
    x=false;
    y=false;
    z=0;
    std::thread a(write_x);
    std::thread b(write_y);
    std::thread c(read_x_then_y);
    std::thread d(read_y_then_x);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    c.join();
    d.join();
    assert(z.load()!=0);
}

Listing 5.8 · Publishing a relaxed payload with release/acquire

The reader waits until its acquire load of y reads true from the release store. The prior relaxed write to x then happens-before the later relaxed load of x; with no other writer, the assertion must hold on completion.

Listing 5.8 · Book pp. 134–135
#include <atomic>
#include <thread>
#include <assert.h>
std::atomic<bool> x,y;
std::atomic<int> z;
void write_x_then_y()
{
    x.store(true,std::memory_order_relaxed);
    y.store(true,std::memory_order_release);
}
void read_y_then_x()
{
    while(!y.load(std::memory_order_acquire));
    if(x.load(std::memory_order_relaxed))
        ++z;
}
int main()
{
    x=false;
    y=false;
    z=0;
    std::thread a(write_x_then_y);
    std::thread b(read_y_then_x);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    assert(z.load()!=0);
}

Listing 5.9 · Transitive synchronization through a relay

Supply <atomic>, <thread>, <cassert>, and a driver that launches and joins these functions. The relay acquires sync1 before releasing sync2, so the final consumer observes the producer’s earlier data stores even though the relay never reads those elements.

Listing 5.9 · Book pp. 136–137
std::atomic<int> data[5];
std::atomic<bool> sync1(false),sync2(false);
void thread_1()
{
    data[0].store(42,std::memory_order_relaxed);
    data[1].store(97,std::memory_order_relaxed);
    data[2].store(17,std::memory_order_relaxed);
    data[3].store(-141,std::memory_order_relaxed);
    data[4].store(2003,std::memory_order_relaxed);
    sync1.store(true,std::memory_order_release);
}
void thread_2()
{
    while(!sync1.load(std::memory_order_acquire));
    sync2.store(true,std::memory_order_release);
}
void thread_3()
{
    while(!sync2.load(std::memory_order_acquire));
    assert(data[0].load(std::memory_order_relaxed)==42);
    assert(data[1].load(std::memory_order_relaxed)==97);
    assert(data[2].load(std::memory_order_relaxed)==17);
    assert(data[3].load(std::memory_order_relaxed)==-141);
    assert(data[4].load(std::memory_order_relaxed)==2003);
}

Listing 5.10 · Historical consume ordering and dependencies

First-edition example: pointer-dependent member reads are ordered under the historical consume rules, but the independent a assertion is not guaranteed by those rules. Modern implementations generally strengthen consume to acquire; prefer acquire in new code. The printed this_thread::sleep call should be sleep_for; add required headers, and delete the allocated X after both threads join in a complete example.

Listing 5.10 · Book pp. 139–140
struct X
{
    int i;
    std::string s;
};
std::atomic<X*> p;
std::atomic<int> a;
void create_x()
{
    X* x=new X;
    x->i=42;
    x->s="hello";
    a.store(99,std::memory_order_relaxed);
    p.store(x,std::memory_order_release);
}
void use_x()
{
    X* x;
    while(!(x=p.load(std::memory_order_consume)))
        std::this_thread::sleep(std::chrono::microseconds(1));
    assert(x->i==42);
    assert(x->s=="hello");
    assert(a.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)==99);
}
int main()
{
    std::thread t1(create_x);
    std::thread t2(use_x);
    t1.join();
    t2.join();
}

Listing 5.11 · A release sequence for claiming queue items

An incomplete, nonterminating teaching outline: add <vector> and define process()/wait_for_more_items(). Each successful fetch_sub claim reads through the release sequence to the publication store. This does not supply shutdown, safe buffer reuse, bounded negative-count handling, or a general concurrent queue implementation.

Listing 5.11 · Book pp. 141–142
#include <atomic>
#include <thread>
std::vector<int> queue_data;
std::atomic<int> count;
void populate_queue()
{
    unsigned const number_of_items=20;
    queue_data.clear();
    for(unsigned i=0;i<number_of_items;++i)
    {
        queue_data.push_back(i);
    }

    count.store(number_of_items,std::memory_order_release);
}
void consume_queue_items()
{
    while(true)
    {
        int item_index;
        if((item_index=count.fetch_sub(1,std::memory_order_acquire))<=0)
        {
            wait_for_more_items();
            continue;
        }
        process(queue_data[item_index-1]);
    }
}
int main()
{
    std::thread a(populate_queue);
    std::thread b(consume_queue_items);
    std::thread c(consume_queue_items);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    c.join();
}

Listing 5.12 · Ordering relaxed operations with fences

The relaxed load of y must read the published true for the fence-to-fence synchronization path. The release fence is after the x write; the acquire fence is before the x read. Under these conditions the assertion holds on completion. Fences do not independently broadcast data.

Listing 5.12 · Book pp. 143–144
#include <atomic>
#include <thread>
#include <assert.h>
std::atomic<bool> x,y;
std::atomic<int> z;
void write_x_then_y()
{
    x.store(true,std::memory_order_relaxed);
    std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_release);
    y.store(true,std::memory_order_relaxed);
}
void read_y_then_x()
{
    while(!y.load(std::memory_order_relaxed));
    std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acquire);
    if(x.load(std::memory_order_relaxed))
        ++z;
}
int main()
{
    x=false;
    y=false;
    z=0;
    std::thread a(write_x_then_y);
    std::thread b(read_y_then_x);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    assert(z.load()!=0);
}

Listing 5.13 · Ordering a nonatomic payload with fences

x is an ordinary bool, but its accesses are ordered through the release fence, atomic y handoff, and acquire fence, so there is no data race in this one-shot protocol. Removing the necessary synchronization can make the ordinary payload access undefined behavior, not just return an old value.

Listing 5.13 · Book pp. 145
#include <atomic>
#include <thread>
#include <assert.h>
bool x=false;
std::atomic<bool> y;
std::atomic<int> z;
void write_x_then_y()
{
    x=true;
    std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_release);
    y.store(true,std::memory_order_relaxed);
}
void read_y_then_x()
{
    while(!y.load(std::memory_order_relaxed));
    std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acquire);
    if(x)
        ++z;
}
int main()
{
    x=false;
    y=false;
    z=0;
    std::thread a(write_x_then_y);
    std::thread b(read_y_then_x);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    assert(z.load()!=0);
}

Additional unnumbered examples and sample output

All remaining standalone source snippets and the sample output from Listing 5.6 are included below. Code-like text inside Figures 5.1–5.7 and Tables 5.1–5.3 remains embedded in those original images.

Initializing atomic_flag

C++11 spelling for an initially clear flag. C++20 added further atomic_flag operations and guaranteed clear default initialization; the original C++11 example is retained.

Book pp. 110 · unnumbered example
std::atomic_flag f=ATOMIC_FLAG_INIT;

Clearing and setting a flag

clear is a store operation; test_and_set is an atomic read-modify-write returning the previous flag value.

Book pp. 111 · unnumbered example
f.clear(std::memory_order_release);
bool x=f.test_and_set();

Constructing and assigning an atomic Boolean

Assignment from an ordinary bool stores atomically. It does not mean copying another atomic object is permitted.

Book pp. 112 · unnumbered example
std::atomic<bool> b(true);
b=false;

Load, store, and exchange

Initialize the local atomic before its first load in C++11: for example std::atomic<bool> b(false). The printed default-constructed local b has no initialized value in that edition.

Book pp. 113 · unnumbered example
std::atomic<bool> b;
bool x=b.load(std::memory_order_acquire);
b.store(true);
x=b.exchange(false,std::memory_order_acq_rel);

Retrying a weak compare/exchange

The printed atomic<bool> needs std:: qualification unless introduced elsewhere. expected is updated when the comparison fails; a weak operation can also fail spuriously. The external b must be defined and initialized.

Book pp. 113 · unnumbered example
bool expected=false;
extern atomic<bool> b; // set somewhere else
while(!b.compare_exchange_weak(expected,true) && !expected);

Success and failure memory orders

These are alternative calls, not an initialized standalone program. Initialize b and expected first and qualify memory_order_acq_rel/acquire with std::. For the chapter’s C++11 rules, failure cannot be release/acq_rel or stronger than success.

Book pp. 114 · unnumbered example
std::atomic<bool> b;
bool expected;
b.compare_exchange_weak(expected,true,
    memory_order_acq_rel,memory_order_acquire);
b.compare_exchange_weak(expected,true,memory_order_acq_rel);

Atomic pointer arithmetic

fetch_add returns the old pointer; compound subtraction returns the new pointer. Atomicity of the pointer does not provide ownership or safe lifetime management of pointed-to objects.

Book pp. 115 · unnumbered example
class Foo{};
Foo some_array[5];
std::atomic<Foo*> p(some_array);
Foo* x=p.fetch_add(2);
assert(x==some_array);
assert(p.load()==&some_array[2]);
x=(p-=1);
assert(x==&some_array[1]);
assert(p.load()==&some_array[1]);

An explicitly ordered pointer update

This is a read-modify-write operation. A release order supplies no acquire semantics for the read part; the pointed-to data needs its own lifetime and synchronization protocol.

Book pp. 115 · unnumbered example
p.fetch_add(3,std::memory_order_release);

Atomic free functions for shared_ptr

The example uses the C++11 shared_ptr atomic free functions to protect the pointer handle, not arbitrary mutation of my_data. All concurrent accesses to that handle must use the required atomic API. C++20 added std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> as the modern approach.

Book pp. 119 · unnumbered example
std::shared_ptr<my_data> p;
void process_global_data()
{
    std::shared_ptr<my_data> local=std::atomic_load(&p);
    process_data(local);
}
void update_global_data()
{
    std::shared_ptr<my_data> local(new my_data);
    std::atomic_store(&p,local);
}

A compare/exchange relay

The ellipses stand for omitted data access. Reset expected=1 after failed comparisons so the relay waits for state 1 before publishing state 2. The successful RMW uses both acquire and release semantics.

Book pp. 137–138 · unnumbered example
std::atomic<int> sync(0);
void thread_1()
{
    // ...
    sync.store(1,std::memory_order_release);
}
void thread_2()
{
    int expected=1;
    while(!sync.compare_exchange_strong(expected,2,
                                        std::memory_order_acq_rel))
        expected=1;
}
void thread_3()
{
    while(sync.load(std::memory_order_acquire)<2);
    // ...

Breaking a historical dependency chain

Illustrative fragment with an ellipsis in its array initializer, not compilable as printed. It assumes global_data is already safely initialized and read-only. Do not remove a dependency that is needed to make a mutable payload access safe; prefer acquire instead of consume for new code.

Book pp. 140 · unnumbered example
int global_data[]={ … };
std::atomic<int> index;
void f()
{
    int i=index.load(std::memory_order_consume);
    do_something_with(global_data[std::kill_dependency(i)]);
}

A release fence in the wrong place

Deliberately weaker than Listing 5.12: the x write occurs after the release fence, so the fence does not publish that write through y. Keeping the consumer from Listing 5.12 no longer guarantees its assertion.

Book pp. 144–145 · unnumbered example
void write_x_then_y()
{
    std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_release);
    x.store(true,std::memory_order_relaxed);
    y.store(true,std::memory_order_relaxed);
}
5.4 / Check your understandingp. 147

Prove the edges. Then trust the result.

Does atomic mean lock-free?

No. Most atomic types may use implementation-internal locks. atomic_flag operations are guaranteed lock-free, but a spinlock built with them still blocks other threads from entering a critical section and does not guarantee fair or bounded progress.

Can two atomic variables be read as one snapshot?

Not automatically. Each load is an individual operation, even with seq_cst. A coherent multi-object snapshot needs an appropriate protocol.

What must an acquire read observe to publish the writer’s data?

It must read from the relevant release operation or a qualifying release sequence, with the payload writes sequenced before publication and reads after acquisition. An acquire reading an unrelated initial value does not establish that handoff.

Can a relaxed counter be useful?

Yes, if its own atomicity and coherence are all the algorithm needs, for example certain independent statistics with an appropriate surrounding lifetime protocol. It must not be treated as publishing unrelated mutable state without additional synchronization.

What is the difference between Listings 5.5 and 5.13?

Listing 5.5 allows a surprising result with atomic objects and insufficient publication ordering. Listing 5.13 deliberately supplies the required fence/atomic handoff to order an ordinary payload safely. Removing that handoff from the latter risks undefined behavior.

Can repeated successful test runs prove a relaxed outcome forbidden?

No. Compiler choices, hardware, and scheduling may hide permitted outcomes indefinitely. Tests help catch defects, but the guarantee needs a language-level proof or appropriate formal analysis.

Chapter in one sentence

Atomic operations protect individual accesses; a correct ordering and lifetime protocol is what makes the surrounding shared data safe.

Chapter 06 / Illustrated summary

Designing
lock-based structures.

A container can be safe yet force every operation to take turns. Design its representation and interface so independent work can actually overlap.

PRINTED PAGES 148–179PDF PAGES 171–20213 LISTINGS · 1 FIGURE
The central idea

Reduce serialization without weakening the invariants: choose complete operations, partition ownership carefully, and prove the lock protocol.

6.1 / Designing for concurrencypp. 149–150

Thread safety is the starting line.

A concurrent data structure must preserve its invariants, avoid problematic races, and define which combinations of operations are safe. But making every method take one global mutex only provides safe serialization. The next goal is to let operations on independent regions proceed together.

  1. Specify the contract. State which reads, writes, copies, and whole-container operations may overlap. Construction, publication, destruction, and shutdown remain explicit lifetime responsibilities.
  2. Expose complete operations. Do not force clients to combine separately locked checks and mutations such as empty(), front(), and pop().
  3. Review exceptions and callbacks. Know which steps allocate, copy, move, destroy, hash, or call user code; RAII unlocks a mutex but does not undo an already modified payload.
  4. Minimize serialization. Prepare allocations outside locks, separate independent regions, and distinguish read-only access from modification.
  5. Prove every multi-lock path. Smaller locks add opportunities for concurrency, but also lock-order, lifetime, and publication obligations.
Fine-grained locking is not automatically faster. Lock overhead, allocation, contention, memory locality, workload distribution, and long callbacks all affect the result. Benchmark a correct design under realistic use.
6.2.1–6.2.2 / Stacks & single-lock queuespp. 151–157

Begin with the contract you can prove.

The stack retains a single mutex and combined pop operations. empty() is just a snapshot; pop rechecks while locked and reports an empty stack. All accesses are safe under the protocol, but only one operation can manipulate the structure at a time. The stack has no built-in waiting mechanism.

The condition-variable queue adds wait_and_pop() as well as try_pop(). The blocking version waits on a predicate while releasing the mutex so producers can work. try_pop() does not wait for an element, although mutex acquisition can still block.

Exceptions can affect both state and progress

If notify_one wakes a consumer that throws during extraction, a queued item may remain while other consumers stay asleep. The chapter discusses notifying all waiters, passing notification onward after failure, or moving payload allocation to push and storing shared_ptr values.

Storing shared_ptr values lets a pointer-returning pop copy the owning handle without moving T. It also moves payload allocation before the push lock, shortening the critical section. Output-reference overloads still invoke T’s assignment and need their own exception guarantees.

The first edition overstates some exception guarantees. Moving from an element can change it before throwing, even if the container has not yet removed its node. “No leak and intact links” is weaker than “the original value is unchanged.” The printed stack and queue examples are annotated accordingly below.
6.2.3 / Finer-grained queuespp. 158–169

Change the representation to separate the work.

A singly linked queue naturally removes at the head and appends at the tail. Simply adding one lock at each end is insufficient: with one real node, the head and tail refer to the same node, so a producer’s next-link write can conflict with a consumer’s next-link read.

The dummy tail is part of the algorithm

Keep an always-present empty tail node. For an empty queue, head and tail both refer to that dummy. Pushing fills the old dummy with the payload and links a newly allocated dummy after it. Popping a nonempty queue removes a real head node without removing the dummy tail.

Producer side

Prepare the new payload and dummy node without holding the queue locks. Under tail_mutex, fill the old dummy, link the new dummy, and advance tail. Only the pointer-update portion is serialized among producers.

Consumer side

Hold head_mutex while deciding and advancing head. Read tail through get_tail(), which briefly locks tail_mutex. Then the removed node can be processed and destroyed outside the head lock.

One lock order, two jobs for the tail lock

Where both locks are needed, the order is head_mutex then tail_mutex. push takes only tail_mutex, so it does not create the reverse edge. The tail lock not only protects the pointer: its release/acquire synchronization also makes the producer’s node updates visible to the consumer.

Read tail after acquiring head_mutex. The deliberately broken alternative snapshots tail first; other consumers can then advance the head past the old boundary before the caller obtains its lock. A lock protecting a read is not enough if the snapshot later becomes invalid for the operation.

Adding blocking operations requires another proof

The book splits the blocking queue across Listings 6.7–6.10. A helper waits until head differs from the safely read tail and returns the held head lock, keeping extraction and head removal in the same critical section. The output-reference form assigns the value before unlinking the node.

Important first-edition caveat: as printed, the producer changes the condition under tail_mutex, while the consumer performs its final predicate check and waits using head_mutex. The producer can enqueue and notify after a false predicate check but before the consumer has entered the wait. That notification can be missed, leaving an item queued and the consumer asleep. A correct blocking adaptation must coordinate the predicate-to-wait transition with the producer, or use another correctly designed waiting protocol; merely moving notify_one before or after unlocking tail_mutex does not fix it.

The queue is unbounded: it grows until resources are exhausted. A bounded queue additionally needs a capacity protocol and producer waiting/failure behavior to provide backpressure. Neither form automatically supplies a close operation or safe destruction while consumers are waiting.

6.3.1 / A thread-safe lookup tablepp. 169–174

Shard by a stable property of the key.

Use a fixed array of hash buckets so a key’s hash identifies its lock without modifying shared topology. Each bucket stores a list of key/value pairs and has a reader-writer mutex. Reads take a shared lock; additions, updates, and removals take an exclusive lock for that bucket.

Different buckets can be updated concurrently. Multiple readers can also share one bucket, but writers in that bucket must exclude both readers and other writers. This is an opportunity for concurrency, not a guaranteed N-fold speedup: collisions, hot keys, lock implementation, and callback cost still matter.

A deliberately smaller interface

The table returns values, not iterators into mutable internal storage. An add-or-update operation avoids a separate existence check followed by mutation. Lookup may return a supplied default value; that contract can blur “missing” and “present with the default,” so applications may prefer a separate status result.

Bucket count and hash behavior must remain stable during access, and the bucket count must be positive. A stateful custom hasher must itself be safe to call concurrently. Hashing, equality, assignment, allocation, and destruction remain user-code and exception-safety concerns.

A whole-table snapshot needs whole-table coordination

To copy a coherent map snapshot, acquire all bucket locks in the same global order and retain them throughout the copy. Copying each bucket separately without retaining earlier locks would not describe one consistent table state. This larger operation deliberately blocks the otherwise independent updates.

Edition context: the original code uses Boost shared_mutex/shared_lock. Modern standard alternatives include shared_timed_mutex (C++14) and shared_mutex (C++17) with shared_lock. Listings 6.11–6.12 also need the const-iterator, template, pointer-access, and access-control corrections described beside the original source.
Interactive study aid / Bucket contentionBased on §6.3.1

Which operations really need to wait?

This illustrative table uses nonnegative integer keys and bucket = key % bucket_count. It is not a simulation of std::hash, an actual lock scheduler, or a throughput benchmark.

“May overlap” describes lock compatibility, not a promise of simultaneous execution or a fairness guarantee. Whole-table snapshots and callbacks taking additional locks are outside this simplified model.

6.3.2 / A per-node locked listpp. 175–179

Move the lock with the traversal.

Ordinary iterators can outlive the protection of the node they reference. The chapter instead supplies container-controlled operations: push_front(), for_each(), find_first_if(), and remove_if(). Each node owns a mutex, a shared payload pointer, and unique ownership of its next node.

Traversal uses hand-over-hand locking: hold the current node, acquire the next node’s lock, then release the old one. Always moving in the same direction maintains a consistent order and prevents another operation from deleting a node before the traversal has secured it.

Removal holds both predecessor and target locks while unlinking the target. It then releases the removed node’s mutex before destroying that node, while still protecting the predecessor so no new traversal can enter the removed link. Other threads can work on different parts of the list, but cannot pass a slow traversal holding a node they need.

Callbacks are a documented trust boundary

The user-supplied function or predicate runs while a node is locked. It must not re-enter the same structure in a way that reacquires its locks, take incompatible external locks, or retain references for unsynchronized later access. Slow callbacks serialize following traversals at that node.

find_first_if returns a shared_ptr to the payload. That keeps the payload alive after node removal, but does not keep its node locked. Reading or mutating that payload while a callback modifies it requires an additional safe application contract. Traversal is not automatically a coherent snapshot of the whole list.

Source notebook / All 13 listingspp. 151–177

The chapter’s code, embedded.

Transcribed from the supplied PDF with whitespace normalized, typographic quotes converted to ASCII, printed callouts omitted, and multi-page listings joined. Source typos, incomplete fragments, and intentionally unsafe alternatives are preserved with notes. Different queue revisions reuse the same class names and are alternatives, not code to concatenate into one file.

Listing 6.1 · A mutex-protected stack

Supply <stack>, <mutex>, <memory>, <utility>, and a definition for empty_stack::what(). Unlike chapter 3, this version moves from the stored value: a throwing move can change that value before pop() is reached. Preserving structure is not the same as preserving the original element; strong exception guarantees require appropriate element-type guarantees.

Listing 6.1 · Book pp. 151–152
#include <exception>
struct empty_stack: std::exception
{
    const char* what() const throw();
};
template<typename T>
class threadsafe_stack
{
private:
    std::stack<T> data;
    mutable std::mutex m;
public:
    threadsafe_stack(){}
    threadsafe_stack(const threadsafe_stack& other)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(other.m);
        data=other.data;
    }
    threadsafe_stack& operator=(const threadsafe_stack&) = delete;
    void push(T new_value)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);
        data.push(std::move(new_value));
    }
    std::shared_ptr<T> pop()
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);
        if(data.empty()) throw empty_stack();
        std::shared_ptr<T> const res(
           std::make_shared<T>(std::move(data.top())));
        data.pop();
        return res;
    }
    void pop(T& value)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);
        if(data.empty()) throw empty_stack();
        value=std::move(data.top());
        data.pop();
    }
    bool empty() const
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);
        return data.empty();
    }
};

Listing 6.2 · A single-lock queue with blocking pop

Printed push() uses std::move(data), but its parameter is new_value: use std::move(new_value). Add required standard headers. A throwing extraction after notify_one can leave other consumers asleep despite available data; consider notification recovery or a different storage/extraction policy. There is no close/shutdown operation.

Listing 6.2 · Book pp. 154–155
template<typename T>
class threadsafe_queue
{
private:
    mutable std::mutex mut;
    std::queue<T> data_queue;
    std::condition_variable data_cond;
public:
    threadsafe_queue()
    {}
    void push(T new_value)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        data_queue.push(std::move(data));
        data_cond.notify_one();
    }
    void wait_and_pop(T& value)
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        data_cond.wait(lk,[this]{return !data_queue.empty();});
        value=std::move(data_queue.front());
        data_queue.pop();
    }
    std::shared_ptr<T> wait_and_pop()
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        data_cond.wait(lk,[this]{return !data_queue.empty();});
        std::shared_ptr<T> res(
            std::make_shared<T>(std::move(data_queue.front())));
        data_queue.pop();
        return res;
    }
    bool try_pop(T& value)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        if(data_queue.empty())
            return false;
        value=std::move(data_queue.front());
        data_queue.pop();
        return true;
    }
    std::shared_ptr<T> try_pop()
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        if(data_queue.empty())
            return std::shared_ptr<T>();
        std::shared_ptr<T> res(
            std::make_shared<T>(std::move(data_queue.front())));
        data_queue.pop();
        return res;
    }
    bool empty() const
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        return data_queue.empty();
    }
};

Listing 6.3 · A queue storing shared_ptr payloads

Allocate the payload before taking the queue lock. The shared-pointer-returning pop overloads avoid element copying/moving during extraction. The output-reference overloads still move-assign T and can throw or modify its state; they do not inherit a universal no-throw guarantee. Stop and join all users before destruction.

Listing 6.3 · Book pp. 156–157
template<typename T>
class threadsafe_queue
{
private:
    mutable std::mutex mut;
    std::queue<std::shared_ptr<T> > data_queue;
    std::condition_variable data_cond;
public:
    threadsafe_queue()
    {}
    void wait_and_pop(T& value)
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        data_cond.wait(lk,[this]{return !data_queue.empty();});
        value=std::move(*data_queue.front());
        data_queue.pop();
    }
    bool try_pop(T& value)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        if(data_queue.empty())
            return false;
        value=std::move(*data_queue.front());
        data_queue.pop();
        return true;
    }
    std::shared_ptr<T> wait_and_pop()
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        data_cond.wait(lk,[this]{return !data_queue.empty();});
        std::shared_ptr<T> res=data_queue.front();
        data_queue.pop();
        return res;
    }
    std::shared_ptr<T> try_pop()
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        if(data_queue.empty())
            return std::shared_ptr<T>();
        std::shared_ptr<T> res=data_queue.front();
        data_queue.pop();
        return res;
    }
    void push(T new_value)
    {
        std::shared_ptr<T> data(
            std::make_shared<T>(std::move(new_value)));
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        data_queue.push(data);
        data_cond.notify_one();
    }
    bool empty() const
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(mut);
        return data_queue.empty();
    }
};

Listing 6.4 · A simple single-threaded linked queue

Not thread-safe and defective as printed even for ordinary automatic objects: tail is not initialized, and removing the final node does not reset tail. Initialize tail to nullptr and clear it when head becomes empty before treating this as a usable single-threaded baseline.

Listing 6.4 · Book pp. 158–159
template<typename T>
class queue
{
private:
    struct node
    {
        T data;
        std::unique_ptr<node> next;
        node(T data_):
            data(std::move(data_))
        {}
    };
    std::unique_ptr<node> head;
    node* tail;
public:
    queue()
    {}
    queue(const queue& other)=delete;
    queue& operator=(const queue& other)=delete;
    std::shared_ptr<T> try_pop()
    {
        if(!head)
        {
            return std::shared_ptr<T>();
        }
        std::shared_ptr<T> const res(
            std::make_shared<T>(std::move(head->data)));
        std::unique_ptr<node> const old_head=std::move(head);
        head=std::move(old_head->next);
        return res;
    }
    void push(T new_value)
    {
        std::unique_ptr<node> p(new node(std::move(new_value)));
        node* const new_tail=p.get();
        if(tail)
        {
            tail->next=std::move(p);
        }
        else
        {
            head=std::move(p);
        }
        tail=new_tail;
    }
};

Listing 6.5 · A single-threaded queue with a dummy node

The dummy tail node is always present. A push stores the payload in the old dummy and appends a new dummy. This version establishes the representation but has no locks and is not safe for concurrent access.

Listing 6.5 · Book pp. 160–161
template<typename T>
class queue
{
private:
    struct node
    {
        std::shared_ptr<T> data;
        std::unique_ptr<node> next;
    };
    std::unique_ptr<node> head;
    node* tail;
public:
    queue():
        head(new node),tail(head.get())
    {}
    queue(const queue& other)=delete;
    queue& operator=(const queue& other)=delete;
    std::shared_ptr<T> try_pop()
    {
        if(head.get()==tail)
        {
            return std::shared_ptr<T>();
        }
        std::shared_ptr<T> const res(head->data);
        std::unique_ptr<node> old_head=std::move(head);
        head=std::move(old_head->next);
        return res;
    }
    void push(T new_value)
    {
        std::shared_ptr<T> new_data(
            std::make_shared<T>(std::move(new_value)));
        std::unique_ptr<node> p(new node);
        tail->data=new_data;
        node* const new_tail=p.get();
        tail->next=std::move(p);
        tail=new_tail;
    }
};

Listing 6.6 · A nonblocking-in-interface, two-lock queue

try_pop does not wait for an item, but it does acquire mutexes: this is not a nonblocking or lock-free algorithm. get_tail() must be called while head_mutex is held, and its tail_mutex acquisition also publishes the producer’s writes. Allocation precedes the producer lock; removed-node destruction happens outside the consumer lock.

Listing 6.6 · Book pp. 161–162
template<typename T>
class threadsafe_queue
{
private:
    struct node
    {
        std::shared_ptr<T> data;
        std::unique_ptr<node> next;
    };
    std::mutex head_mutex;
    std::unique_ptr<node> head;
    std::mutex tail_mutex;
    node* tail;
    node* get_tail()
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> tail_lock(tail_mutex);
        return tail;
    }
    std::unique_ptr<node> pop_head()
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> head_lock(head_mutex);

        if(head.get()==get_tail())
        {
            return nullptr;
        }
        std::unique_ptr<node> old_head=std::move(head);
        head=std::move(old_head->next);
        return old_head;
    }
public:
    threadsafe_queue():
        head(new node),tail(head.get())
    {}
    threadsafe_queue(const threadsafe_queue& other)=delete;
    threadsafe_queue& operator=(const threadsafe_queue& other)=delete;
    std::shared_ptr<T> try_pop()
    {
        std::unique_ptr<node> old_head=pop_head();
        return old_head?old_head->data:std::shared_ptr<T>();
    }
    void push(T new_value)
    {
        std::shared_ptr<T> new_data(
            std::make_shared<T>(std::move(new_value)));
        std::unique_ptr<node> p(new node);
        node* const new_tail=p.get();
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> tail_lock(tail_mutex);
        tail->data=new_data;
        tail->next=std::move(p);
        tail=new_tail;
    }
};

Listing 6.7 · The split-lock blocking queue interface

This is the interface portion of a class assembled across Listings 6.7–6.10, not a separate complete definition. The printed void empty() must be bool empty(). The helpers and member bodies in the later listings must be merged into this class rather than compiled as repeated class definitions.

Listing 6.7 · Book pp. 166
template<typename T>
class threadsafe_queue
{
private:
    struct node
    {
        std::shared_ptr<T> data;
        std::unique_ptr<node> next;
    };
    std::mutex head_mutex;
    std::unique_ptr<node> head;
    std::mutex tail_mutex;
    node* tail;
    std::condition_variable data_cond;
public:
    threadsafe_queue():
        head(new node),tail(head.get())
    {}
    threadsafe_queue(const threadsafe_queue& other)=delete;
    threadsafe_queue& operator=(const threadsafe_queue& other)=delete;
    std::shared_ptr<T> try_pop();
    bool try_pop(T& value);
    std::shared_ptr<T> wait_and_pop();
    void wait_and_pop(T& value);
    void push(T new_value);
    void empty();
};

Listing 6.8 · Pushing into the split-lock queue

This out-of-class push definition belongs to the assembled queue. It updates under tail_mutex and then notifies, but never coordinates with head_mutex. Combined with the consumer’s final predicate check and wait, this can miss a notification; see the warning beside the queue summary. It is not a production-ready blocking protocol as printed.

Listing 6.8 · Book pp. 166
template<typename T>
void threadsafe_queue<T>::push(T new_value)
{
    std::shared_ptr<T> new_data(
        std::make_shared<T>(std::move(new_value)));
    std::unique_ptr<node> p(new node);
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> tail_lock(tail_mutex);
        tail->data=new_data;
        node* const new_tail=p.get();
        tail->next=std::move(p);
        tail=new_tail;
    }
    data_cond.notify_one();
}

Listing 6.9 · Waiting and popping with transferred lock ownership

A class fragment containing helper and member definitions. wait_for_data returns the held head lock so extraction stays protected. Returning head_lock directly permits implicit move; the explicit std::move is unnecessary. The wait protocol needs a fix for the missed-wakeup window, and output-reference extraction needs an exception policy.

Listing 6.9 · Book pp. 167
template<typename T>
class threadsafe_queue
{
private:
    node* get_tail()
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> tail_lock(tail_mutex);
        return tail;
    }
    std::unique_ptr<node> pop_head()
    {
        std::unique_ptr<node> old_head=std::move(head);
        head=std::move(old_head->next);
        return old_head;
    }
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> wait_for_data()
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> head_lock(head_mutex);
        data_cond.wait(head_lock,[&]{return head.get()!=get_tail();});
        return std::move(head_lock);
    }
    std::unique_ptr<node> wait_pop_head()
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> head_lock(wait_for_data());
        return pop_head();
    }
    std::unique_ptr<node> wait_pop_head(T& value)
    {
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> head_lock(wait_for_data());
        value=std::move(*head->data);
        return pop_head();
    }
public:
    std::shared_ptr<T> wait_and_pop()
    {
        std::unique_ptr<node> const old_head=wait_pop_head();
        return old_head->data;
    }
    void wait_and_pop(T& value)
    {
        std::unique_ptr<node> const old_head=wait_pop_head(value);
    }
};

Listing 6.10 · try_pop and empty for the split-lock queue

Merge this fragment with Listings 6.7–6.9. Correct void empty() to bool empty() in both declaration and definition. In bool try_pop(T&), use return static_cast<bool>(old_head) or old_head != nullptr; unique_ptr’s explicit conversion does not permit the printed return old_head to convert implicitly to bool.

Listing 6.10 · Book pp. 168–169
template<typename T>
class threadsafe_queue
{
private:
    std::unique_ptr<node> try_pop_head()
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> head_lock(head_mutex);
        if(head.get()==get_tail())
        {
            return std::unique_ptr<node>();
        }
        return pop_head();
    }
    std::unique_ptr<node> try_pop_head(T& value)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> head_lock(head_mutex);
        if(head.get()==get_tail())
        {
            return std::unique_ptr<node>();
        }
        value=std::move(*head->data);
        return pop_head();
    }
public:
    std::shared_ptr<T> try_pop()
    {
        std::unique_ptr<node> old_head=try_pop_head();
        return old_head?old_head->data:std::shared_ptr<T>();
    }
    bool try_pop(T& value)
    {
        std::unique_ptr<node> const old_head=try_pop_head(value);
        return old_head;
    }
    void empty()
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> head_lock(head_mutex);
        return (head.get()==get_tail());
    }
};

Listing 6.11 · A bucket-locked lookup table

Uses Boost shared_mutex/shared_lock because this is C++11-era code. find_entry_for() is const but returns a mutable iterator from a const list, so add const and non-const helper overloads with matching iterator types (and use a const_iterator in value_for). Require num_buckets>0 before hashing. Hash/equality/value operations must obey the documented concurrency and callback constraints.

Listing 6.11 · Book pp. 171–173
template<typename Key,typename Value,typename Hash=std::hash<Key> >
class threadsafe_lookup_table
{
private:
    class bucket_type
    {
    private:
        typedef std::pair<Key,Value> bucket_value;
        typedef std::list<bucket_value> bucket_data;
        typedef typename bucket_data::iterator bucket_iterator;
        bucket_data data;
        mutable boost::shared_mutex mutex;

        bucket_iterator find_entry_for(Key const& key) const
        {
            return std::find_if(data.begin(),data.end(),
                                [&](bucket_value const& item)
                                {return item.first==key;});
        }
    public:
        Value value_for(Key const& key,Value const& default_value) const
        {
            boost::shared_lock<boost::shared_mutex> lock(mutex);
            bucket_iterator const found_entry=find_entry_for(key);
            return (found_entry==data.end())?
                default_value:found_entry->second;
        }
        void add_or_update_mapping(Key const& key,Value const& value)
        {
            std::unique_lock<boost::shared_mutex> lock(mutex);
            bucket_iterator const found_entry=find_entry_for(key);
            if(found_entry==data.end())
            {
                data.push_back(bucket_value(key,value));
            }
            else
            {
                found_entry->second=value;
            }
        }
        void remove_mapping(Key const& key)
        {
            std::unique_lock<boost::shared_mutex> lock(mutex);
            bucket_iterator const found_entry=find_entry_for(key);
            if(found_entry!=data.end())
            {
                data.erase(found_entry);
            }
        }
    };
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<bucket_type> > buckets;
    Hash hasher;
    bucket_type& get_bucket(Key const& key) const
    {
        std::size_t const bucket_index=hasher(key)%buckets.size();
        return *buckets[bucket_index];
    }
public:
    typedef Key key_type;
    typedef Value mapped_type;
    typedef Hash hash_type;
    threadsafe_lookup_table(
        unsigned num_buckets=19,Hash const& hasher_=Hash()):
        buckets(num_buckets),hasher(hasher_)
    {
        for(unsigned i=0;i<num_buckets;++i)
        {
            buckets[i].reset(new bucket_type);
        }
    }
    threadsafe_lookup_table(threadsafe_lookup_table const& other)=delete;
    threadsafe_lookup_table& operator=(
        threadsafe_lookup_table const& other)=delete;
    Value value_for(Key const& key,
                    Value const& default_value=Value()) const
    {
        return get_bucket(key).value_for(key,default_value);
    }
    void add_or_update_mapping(Key const& key,Value const& value)
    {
        get_bucket(key).add_or_update_mapping(key,value);
    }
    void remove_mapping(Key const& key)
    {
        get_bucket(key).remove_mapping(key);
    }
};

Listing 6.12 · Taking a whole-table snapshot

Conceptual extension, not compilable as printed. It needs a template-qualified class definition and declaration, pointer access through buckets[i]->, a suitable bucket iterator type, and legal access to the nested bucket’s private mutex/data (for example an explicit friendship or helper interface). Acquire every bucket in the same order and keep all locks until copying finishes.

Listing 6.12 · Book pp. 174
std::map<Key,Value> threadsafe_lookup_table::get_map() const
{
    std::vector<std::unique_lock<boost::shared_mutex> > locks;
    for(unsigned i=0;i<buckets.size();++i)
    {
        locks.push_back(
            std::unique_lock<boost::shared_mutex>(buckets[i].mutex));
    }
    std::map<Key,Value> res;
    for(unsigned i=0;i<buckets.size();++i)
    {
        for(bucket_iterator it=buckets[i].data.begin();
            it!=buckets[i].data.end();
            ++it)
        {
            res.insert(*it);
        }
    }
    return res;
}

Listing 6.13 · A list with per-node locks and traversal operations

The destructor predicate is printed as [](node const&){return true;}, but remove_if invokes the predicate on T. Use [](T const&){return true;} for the intended generic list. Callbacks run under node locks; do not re-enter, retain references for unlocked use, or violate lock ordering. A returned shared_ptr keeps T alive, but does not keep its node mutex held or make concurrent mutations of T safe.

Listing 6.13 · Book pp. 176–177
template<typename T>
class threadsafe_list
{
    struct node
    {
        std::mutex m;
        std::shared_ptr<T> data;
        std::unique_ptr<node> next;
        node():
            next()
        {}
        node(T const& value):
            data(std::make_shared<T>(value))
        {}
    };
    node head;
public:
    threadsafe_list()
    {}
    ~threadsafe_list()
    {
        remove_if([](node const&){return true;});
    }
    threadsafe_list(threadsafe_list const& other)=delete;
    threadsafe_list& operator=(threadsafe_list const& other)=delete;
    void push_front(T const& value)
    {
        std::unique_ptr<node> new_node(new node(value));
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(head.m);
        new_node->next=std::move(head.next);
        head.next=std::move(new_node);

    }
    template<typename Function>
    void for_each(Function f)
    {
        node* current=&head;
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(head.m);
        while(node* const next=current->next.get())
        {
            std::unique_lock<std::mutex> next_lk(next->m);
            lk.unlock();
            f(*next->data);
            current=next;
            lk=std::move(next_lk);
        }
    }
    template<typename Predicate>
    std::shared_ptr<T> find_first_if(Predicate p)
    {
        node* current=&head;
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(head.m);
        while(node* const next=current->next.get())
        {
            std::unique_lock<std::mutex> next_lk(next->m);
            lk.unlock();
            if(p(*next->data))
            {
                return next->data;
            }
            current=next;
            lk=std::move(next_lk);
        }
        return std::shared_ptr<T>();
    }
    template<typename Predicate>
    void remove_if(Predicate p)
    {
        node* current=&head;
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(head.m);
        while(node* const next=current->next.get())
        {
            std::unique_lock<std::mutex> next_lk(next->m);
            if(p(*next->data))
            {
                std::unique_ptr<node> old_next=std::move(current->next);
                current->next=std::move(next->next);
                next_lk.unlock();
            }
            else
            {
                lk.unlock();
                current=next;
                lk=std::move(next_lk);
            }
        }
    }
};

A value-or-default lookup signature

6.4 / Check your understandingp. 179

Ask what the lock actually protects.

Why isn’t one mutex enough for maximum concurrency?

It may be enough for correctness, but it serializes unrelated operations. A proven partition into independently protected regions can allow overlap; smaller locks alone do not prove safety or better performance.

Why keep an empty dummy tail node?

It separates the node being appended from a real head node being removed. The representation makes safe head-side and tail-side ownership possible, with a short cross-check under the tail lock.

Why must get_tail() happen while head_mutex is held?

It keeps other consumers from advancing head while this consumer establishes its tail boundary. The tail lock also orders producer node updates before the consumer uses them.

Does notify_one() guarantee a queued item will be consumed?

No. Predicate checks, waiting transitions, producer updates, exceptions, shutdown, and scheduling all matter. The printed split-lock blocking queue has a missed-wakeup window that needs a corrected protocol.

When can two writes proceed in the bucket table?

When they address different buckets and no larger operation or external constraint blocks them. Different keys in the same bucket still share its exclusive lock.

Does shared_ptr make a found list element thread-safe?

No. It preserves lifetime, not synchronization of later accesses to T. Node locking no longer protects a caller after the lookup returns.

Chapter in one sentence

Design the representation so independent operations can overlap, then prove the interface, lock order, exception behavior, waiting protocol, and object lifetimes together.
