Chapter 07 / Illustrated summary

Designing
lock-free structures.

Removing a mutex is the easy part. Proving progress, publishing nodes safely, and knowing when memory can be reused are the real design problems.

PRINTED PAGES 180–223PDF PAGES 203–24621 LISTINGS · 1 FIGURE
The central idea

A successful pointer update does not prove a node is safe to dereference—or safe to delete. Progress, ordering, and reclamation each need their own argument.

7.1 / Definitions & consequencespp. 181–184

“No mutex” is not a progress guarantee.

Blocking

A stalled participant can prevent others from completing an operation. A spinlock still has an owner that everyone else needs to release the flag, even though it makes no sleeping OS call.

Lock-free

Under the algorithm’s execution and primitive assumptions, the system as a whole keeps completing operations despite a delayed participant. An individual thread can still starve through repeated failed retries.

Wait-free

Each operation completes within a bounded number of its own steps, regardless of interference. This is stronger than lock-free, but is not a promise about wall-clock latency or CPU scheduling.

Check the whole call path

Atomic operations may use internal locks, and allocators, deleters, reference counting, or callbacks can block. A lock-free pointer-update algorithm does not automatically make the public operation end-to-end lock-free.

The chapter contrasts a spinlock with retry-based updates. Its loose use of “nonblocking” for code without blocking library calls should not be confused with formal nonblocking progress guarantees. A loop that simply waits for one particular thread to finish is still an obstruction to progress.

Potential advantages include less owner-dependent waiting and more opportunities for overlap. Costs include complicated proofs, atomic contention, cache traffic, reclamation overhead, and worse throughput on some workloads. Measure against a lock-based alternative rather than assuming lock-free means faster.

A correct lock-free algorithm rules out an infinite execution in which active participants collectively retry forever without completing operations, subject to its assumptions. Per-thread starvation is still possible. Also, arbitrary thread termination, exceptions, or process failures are not automatically made harmless by a lock-free update loop.
7.2.1 / A stack without a mutexpp. 184–188

Publish a prepared node with CAS.

Construct a node privately, set its next pointer to the observed head, and use compare/exchange to make it the new head only if the observation still matches. On failure, CAS refreshes the expected head so the thread can retry without discarding another thread’s update.

A pop similarly tries to replace head with its successor. The successful CAS identifies the winner that removes that node. Returning a shared_ptr payload prepared during push avoids allocating or copying a potentially throwing T after removal.

Removal does not grant exclusive lifetime knowledge

Another pop may already have loaded the same head and be about to read its next link. Deleting the node immediately after your successful CAS can therefore produce a use-after-free. An atomic head pointer does not make that later dereference safe.

The first examples deliberately leak nodes to isolate the update logic. That removes immediate deletion from the demonstration, but does not provide a usable memory-management policy. Empty checks, initialized atomic state, destruction, and exceptions still need explicit treatment.

7.2.2 / Deferred reclamationpp. 188–192

Unlinked is not the same as unreferenced.

The first strategy counts active pop calls and retires removed nodes until a safe point. When a caller appears to be alone, it claims a retired batch and rechecks the active count before deciding whether the batch can be deleted or must be deferred again.

The figure shows why sampling “one active caller” and then deleting a later batch is not enough: other threads can enter and retire newly referenced nodes between those actions. Correctness requires a protocol connecting the batch being reclaimed to the relevant quiescence observation.

This approach can retain memory indefinitely under sustained activity without suitable safe points. It also needs to protect retired-list metadata itself: delaying deletion is not permission to overwrite fields other active operations can still read.

The printed machinery has additional hazards, including a null retired-node path and reuse of a next link while readers may still inspect it. This summary explains the reclamation goal and the figure’s schedule, but does not endorse Listings 7.4–7.5 as a verified library.
7.2.3 / Hazard pointerspp. 193–200

Announce protection before dereferencing.

  1. Read a candidate pointer from the shared structure.
  2. Publish that candidate in a registered hazard slot.
  3. Read the shared source again. If it changed, retry protection before accessing the candidate’s fields.
  4. While protection is valid, attempt the removal; retry validation if the candidate changes.
  5. Clear protection after the protected access is finished. Retire removed nodes and reclaim only when the protocol proves they are no longer protected.

The sample uses a fixed table of thread-owned hazard slots and a thread-local owner object. Retired nodes carry type-erased deleters. A scanner takes a retired batch, deletes entries with no outstanding hazards under the full protocol, and puts protected entries back for a future pass.

Batching trades memory for scanning cost

Scanning every hazard for every retired node on every pop is expensive. The chapter suggests batching reclamation and using thread-local retired lists to reduce shared contention. This changes memory bounds and exit/shutdown handling, so those costs belong in the design too.

Hazards protect selected objects’ lifetimes, not all application-level invariants. Slot exhaustion, nested operations needing several slots, allocation failure during retirement, delayed readers, and safe shutdown are not optional details.

Historical context: the chapter’s pointer-validity discussion and patent/licensing discussion reflect the 2012 text, not a current portability or legal determination. Prefer a maintained, vetted reclamation implementation for the target platform; do not infer current licensing obligations or blanket safety for arbitrary dangling-pointer use from this summary.
7.2.4–7.2.5 / Reference counts & orderingpp. 200–209

Acquire the reference before touching the node.

Atomic shared_ptr operations can combine safe handle acquisition with lifetime management, greatly simplifying the stack. But those operations are not guaranteed lock-free. The chapter’s alternative is a split-reference scheme: keep an external count alongside the shared pointer value and an internal count in the node.

Incrementing the external count with CAS protects and validates the pointer before dereferencing it. Removing the shared pointer source transfers its outstanding references into internal accounting. A failed remover releases its temporary reference; whichever path proves the final count has reached zero may delete the node.

The pointer and external count must change together. Loading a raw pointer and only then incrementing a counter inside the node leaves exactly the lifetime window this scheme is meant to close. Wider pointer/count atomics may not be lock-free on the chosen platform.

Relax memory orders only after proving the relationships

Start from sequential consistency. The counted stack then uses release to publish the prepared node, acquire when obtaining protection before reading node fields, and suitable ordering when the final reference can trigger deletion. Release sequences let later RMW observations inherit a publication without every operation carrying the strongest ordering.

Counter ranges, wraparound, padding and representation-sensitive CAS, safe initialization, payload ownership, and reclamation paths remain part of the proof. Narrower counters or unused pointer bits are platform-specific engineering choices—not portable shortcuts.

The printed stack revisions are fragments with repeated class names, missing initialization, and several syntax/API typos. They are reproduced with local notes below, not combined into an allegedly verified production stack.
7.2.6 / From SPSC to a helping queuepp. 209–221

The supported callers are part of the algorithm.

First: one producer, one consumer

Listing 7.13 retains a dummy node and uses atomic head and tail pointers. One producer fills the current dummy and publishes a new tail. One consumer checks the published boundary, removes a real head node, and then deletes it. The one-producer/one-consumer restriction is essential to the proof.

Two producers could write the same node members concurrently. Two consumers could claim and delete the same node. Replacing endpoint mutexes with atomic pointers does not, by itself, create a multi-producer/multi-consumer queue.

Then: protect both ends and all reference sources

The generalization gives the payload pointer a CAS-based claim and protects loaded endpoints with external references before dereferencing them. The internal node counter tracks both individual references and how many external counter sources remain, because the same node can be referenced through more than one shared location.

Releasing a temporary reference and releasing an entire external-counter source are different operations. Updating their accounting separately can let multiple threads incorrectly conclude that they own the final deletion.

Finally: help stalled producers

If one producer claims a payload field and pauses before installing the successor and updating tail, other producers must not simply spin waiting for it. That would hide an owner-dependent lock inside a CAS loop.

The helping design makes the successor pointer atomic. Another producer can install an equivalent dummy successor and help advance tail. The original producer can detect that work has already been completed and use the shared result rather than waiting for its own node to be chosen.

The later queue listings are partial revisions, not independent classes. They omit complete construction/shutdown and contain issues such as the missing empty-pop reference release in Listing 7.20. Allocation and cleanup inside helping paths also need review. The study notes do not certify this multi-producer/multi-consumer implementation.
7.3 / Guidelines & ABApp. 221–223

The same address may not mean the same state.

In the ABA problem, a thread observes head=A and derives a successor from it. Other work changes head to B and then back to an A-valued pointer, while changing the structure or reusing an address. A pointer-only CAS accepts the same bits even though the original reasoning is stale.

A version tag compared atomically with the pointer can detect the intervening change, provided the tag has not wrapped and the representation is supported. Tags do not replace safe memory reclamation: a failed CAS cannot undo an earlier invalid dereference. Likewise, lifetime protection alone does not solve every logical ABA caused by reinserting a still-live node.

Interactive study aid / A → B → A

A stale observation that looks current

This abstract schedule retains symbolic nodes and does not dereference freed memory. It demonstrates a logical stale-successor error, not an actual unsafe C++ run.

The version tag is assumed not to wrap in this example. A real tagged-pointer design needs atomic support, representation and overflow analysis, plus a valid lifetime protocol.

The chapter’s four design rules

  1. Prototype with seq_cst. Weaker ordering is an optimization that requires a complete proof, not merely successful tests.
  2. Plan reclamation from the start. Account for delayed readers, safe retirement, resource exhaustion, and final cleanup.
  3. Audit ABA and reuse. Compare state identity, not just address equality, when the algorithm depends on history.
  4. Help rather than wait for an owner. Make unfinished shared work completable by another participant when progress requires it.

Listing 7.1 · A spinlock is still a lock

Add <atomic>. This is a counterexample to “uses atomic operations, therefore lock-free.” If the owning thread stops running while holding the flag, other callers keep spinning without acquiring it. It is not a lock-free mutex.

Listing 7.1 · Book pp. 181
class spinlock_mutex
{
    std::atomic_flag flag;
public:
    spinlock_mutex():
        flag(ATOMIC_FLAG_INIT)
    {}
    void lock()
    {
        while(flag.test_and_set(std::memory_order_acquire));
    }
    void unlock()
    {
        flag.clear(std::memory_order_release);
    }
};

Listing 7.2 · Publishing a stack node with compare/exchange

A push-only teaching fragment: initialize head to nullptr before use in C++11, add required headers, and supply lifetime/cleanup rules. Successful CAS publishes the prepared node; failure updates new_node->next. It does not yet supply pop or reclamation.

Listing 7.2 · Book pp. 185
template<typename T>
class lock_free_stack
{
private:
    struct node
    {
        T data;
        node* next;
        node(T const& data_):
            data(data_)
        {}
    };
    std::atomic<node*> head;
public:
    void push(T const& data)
    {
        node* const new_node=new node(data);
        new_node->next=head.load();
        while(!head.compare_exchange_weak(new_node->next,new_node));
    }
};

Listing 7.3 · A stack that deliberately leaks nodes

Checks empty before dereferencing, and returns a shared_ptr payload after successful removal. Removed nodes are deliberately never deleted. Initialize head explicitly for ordinary C++11 objects. This is not a complete usable reclamation strategy or a bounded-memory container.

Listing 7.3 · Book pp. 187–188
template<typename T>
class lock_free_stack
{
private:
    struct node
    {
        std::shared_ptr<T> data;
        node* next;
        node(T const& data_):
            data(std::make_shared<T>(data_))
        {}
    };
    std::atomic<node*> head;
public:
    void push(T const& data)
    {
        node* const new_node=new node(data);
        new_node->next=head.load();
        while(!head.compare_exchange_weak(new_node->next,new_node));
    }
    std::shared_ptr<T> pop()
    {
        node* old_head=head.load();
        while(old_head &&
            !head.compare_exchange_weak(old_head,old_head->next));
        return old_head ? old_head->data : std::shared_ptr<T>();
    }
};

Listing 7.4 · Counting active pop calls

Class fragment extending the earlier stack. Increment the active-pop count before reading head and balance it on every exit. Initialize head, threads_in_pop, and deferred-list state explicitly. The reference count here counts active calls, not per-node owners.

Listing 7.4 · Book pp. 189
template<typename T>
class lock_free_stack
{
private:
    std::atomic<unsigned> threads_in_pop;
    void try_reclaim(node* old_head);
public:
    std::shared_ptr<T> pop()
    {
        ++threads_in_pop;
        node* old_head=head.load();
        while(old_head &&
              !head.compare_exchange_weak(old_head,old_head->next));
        std::shared_ptr<T> res;
        if(old_head)
        {
            res.swap(old_head->data);
        }
        try_reclaim(old_head);
        return res;
    }
};

Listing 7.5 · A deferred reclamation list

Historical teaching fragment requiring the stack/node definitions. It has no guard against chain_pending_node(nullptr) after an empty pop in the multiple-caller branch. Reusing a removed node’s ordinary next link for the retired list also needs a race audit while another pop may still read that link; delayed deletion alone does not prove safe concurrent mutation. Do not deploy this transcription as a verified reclaimer.

Listing 7.5 · Book pp. 189–190
template<typename T>
class lock_free_stack
{
private:
    std::atomic<node*> to_be_deleted;
    static void delete_nodes(node* nodes)
    {
        while(nodes)
        {
            node* next=nodes->next;
            delete nodes;
            nodes=next;
         }
    }
    void try_reclaim(node* old_head)
    {
        if(threads_in_pop==1)
        {
            node* nodes_to_delete=to_be_deleted.exchange(nullptr);
            if(!--threads_in_pop)
            {
                delete_nodes(nodes_to_delete);
            }
            else if(nodes_to_delete)
            {
                chain_pending_nodes(nodes_to_delete);
            }
            delete old_head;
        }
        else
        {
            chain_pending_node(old_head);
            --threads_in_pop;
        }
    }
    void chain_pending_nodes(node* nodes)
    {
        node* last=nodes;
        while(node* const next=last->next)
        {
            last=next;
        }
        chain_pending_nodes(nodes,last);
    }
    void chain_pending_nodes(node* first,node* last)
    {
        last->next=to_be_deleted;
        while(!to_be_deleted.compare_exchange_weak(
                  last->next,first));
    }
    void chain_pending_node(node* n)
    {
        chain_pending_nodes(n,n);
    }
};

Listing 7.6 · Protecting stack pop with a hazard pointer

Requires hazard registration, scans, retirement helpers, the stack type, and initialized atomics. Publish the hazard and validate head again before dereferencing; repeat after each failed removal. The simple reclaim_later allocation can throw after the node has been removed, so exception handling and final cleanup also need a production policy.

Listing 7.6 · Book pp. 194–195
std::shared_ptr<T> pop()
{
    std::atomic<void*>& hp=get_hazard_pointer_for_current_thread();
    node* old_head=head.load();
    do
    {
        node* temp;
        do
        {
            temp=old_head;
            hp.store(old_head);
            old_head=head.load();
        } while(old_head!=temp);
    }
    while(old_head &&
          !head.compare_exchange_strong(old_head,old_head->next));
    hp.store(nullptr);
    std::shared_ptr<T> res;
    if(old_head)
    {
        res.swap(old_head->data);
        if(outstanding_hazard_pointers_for(old_head))
        {
            reclaim_later(old_head);
        }
        else
        {
            delete old_head;
        }
        delete_nodes_with_no_hazards();
    }
    return res;
}

Listing 7.7 · Registering a per-thread hazard slot

The fixed table supports at most 100 concurrently owned slots. Add headers and initialization appropriate to the chosen C++ version; atomic<thread::id> support and lock-freedom are implementation-sensitive. Slots are released at thread exit. This single cached hazard slot is not suitable for arbitrary nested operations that need independent simultaneous protections.

Listing 7.7 · Book pp. 195–196
unsigned const max_hazard_pointers=100;
struct hazard_pointer
{
    std::atomic<std::thread::id> id;
    std::atomic<void*> pointer;
};
hazard_pointer hazard_pointers[max_hazard_pointers];
class hp_owner
{
    hazard_pointer* hp;

public:
    hp_owner(hp_owner const&)=delete;
    hp_owner operator=(hp_owner const&)=delete;
    hp_owner():
        hp(nullptr)
    {
        for(unsigned i=0;i<max_hazard_pointers;++i)
        {
            std::thread::id old_id;
            if(hazard_pointers[i].id.compare_exchange_strong(
                old_id,std::this_thread::get_id()))
            {
                hp=&hazard_pointers[i];
                break;
            }
        }
        if(!hp)
        {
            throw std::runtime_error("No hazard pointers available");
        }
    }
    std::atomic<void*>& get_pointer()
    {
        return hp->pointer;
    }
    ~hp_owner()
    {
        hp->pointer.store(nullptr);
        hp->id.store(std::thread::id());
    }
};
std::atomic<void*>& get_hazard_pointer_for_current_thread()
{
    thread_local static hp_owner hazard;
    return hazard.get_pointer();
}

Listing 7.8 · Retiring and scanning hazard-protected nodes

A separate retired-list wrapper stores a type-erased deleter. A scan claims a batch by exchange, deletes only unprotected objects, and republishes protected ones. Registration/validation, retirement ordering, allocation failure, domain lifetime, and shutdown are part of the proof; this helper fragment alone is not a hazard-pointer library.

Listing 7.8 · Book pp. 197–198
template<typename T>
void do_delete(void* p)
{
    delete static_cast<T*>(p);
}
struct data_to_reclaim
{
    void* data;
    std::function<void(void*)> deleter;
    data_to_reclaim* next;
    template<typename T>
    data_to_reclaim(T* p):
        data(p),
        deleter(&do_delete<T>),
        next(0)
    {}
    ~data_to_reclaim()
    {
        deleter(data);
    }
};
std::atomic<data_to_reclaim*> nodes_to_reclaim;
void add_to_reclaim_list(data_to_reclaim* node)
{
    node->next=nodes_to_reclaim.load();
    while(!nodes_to_reclaim.compare_exchange_weak(node->next,node));
}
template<typename T>
void reclaim_later(T* data)
{
    add_to_reclaim_list(new data_to_reclaim(data));
}
void delete_nodes_with_no_hazards()
{
    data_to_reclaim* current=nodes_to_reclaim.exchange(nullptr);
    while(current)
    {
        data_to_reclaim* const next=current->next;
        if(!outstanding_hazard_pointers_for(current->data))
        {
            delete current;
        }
        else
        {
            add_to_reclaim_list(current);
        }
        current=next;
    }
}

Listing 7.9 · Reference counting with atomic shared_ptr operations

Printed new_node->next=head.load() is invalid because head is a shared_ptr: use std::atomic_load(&head). All concurrent accesses to head must use the appropriate atomic API. Atomic shared_ptr operations are not guaranteed lock-free, and allocation/deallocation can block even if the head update primitive is lock-free.

Listing 7.9 · Book pp. 200–201
template<typename T>
class lock_free_stack
{
private:
    struct node
    {
        std::shared_ptr<T> data;
        std::shared_ptr<node> next;
        node(T const& data_):
            data(std::make_shared<T>(data_))
        {}
    };
    std::shared_ptr<node> head;
public:
    void push(T const& data)
    {
        std::shared_ptr<node> const new_node=std::make_shared<node>(data);
        new_node->next=head.load();
        while(!std::atomic_compare_exchange_weak(&head,
                  &new_node->next,new_node));
    }
    std::shared_ptr<T> pop()
    {
        std::shared_ptr<node> old_head=std::atomic_load(&head);
        while(old_head && !std::atomic_compare_exchange_weak(&head,
                  &old_head,old_head->next));
        return old_head ? old_head->data : std::shared_ptr<T>();
    }
};

Listing 7.10 · A stack with split reference counts: push

Combine this class fragment with Listing 7.11, explicitly initialize the counted head to an empty value, and supply standard headers. Pointer-plus-counter atomic operations may require a wider atomic primitive or internal locks. Finite counters, representation padding, and overflow require an implementation-specific audit.

Listing 7.10 · Book pp. 201–202
template<typename T>
class lock_free_stack
{
private:
    struct node;
    struct counted_node_ptr
    {
        int external_count;
        node* ptr;
    };
    struct node
    {
        std::shared_ptr<T> data;
        std::atomic<int> internal_count;
        counted_node_ptr next;
        node(T const& data_):
            data(std::make_shared<T>(data_)),
            internal_count(0)
        {}
    };
    std::atomic<counted_node_ptr> head;
public:
    ~lock_free_stack()
    {
        while(pop());
    }
    void push(T const& data)
    {
        counted_node_ptr new_node;
        new_node.ptr=new node(data);
        new_node.external_count=1;
        new_node.ptr->next=head.load();
        while(!head.compare_exchange_weak(new_node.ptr->next,new_node));
    }
};

Listing 7.11 · A stack with split reference counts: pop

Merge into the earlier stack rather than redefining it. Remove the printed stray # after pop(). Obtain the external reference before dereferencing a node, then transfer counts or release the temporary reference on each path. This is not an ordinary shared_ptr control block.

Listing 7.11 · Book pp. 203–204
template<typename T>
class lock_free_stack
{
private:
    void increase_head_count(counted_node_ptr& old_counter)
    {
        counted_node_ptr new_counter;
        do
        {
            new_counter=old_counter;
            ++new_counter.external_count;
        }
        while(!head.compare_exchange_strong(old_counter,new_counter));
        old_counter.external_count=new_counter.external_count;
    }
public:
    std::shared_ptr<T> pop()#
    {
        counted_node_ptr old_head=head.load();
        for(;;)
        {
            increase_head_count(old_head);
            node* const ptr=old_head.ptr;
            if(!ptr)
            {
                return std::shared_ptr<T>();
            }
            if(head.compare_exchange_strong(old_head,ptr->next))
            {
                std::shared_ptr<T> res;
                res.swap(ptr->data);
                int const count_increase=old_head.external_count-2;
                if(ptr->internal_count.fetch_add(count_increase)==
                   -count_increase)
                {
                    delete ptr;
                }
                return res;
            }
            else if(ptr->internal_count.fetch_sub(1)==1)
            {
                delete ptr;
            }
        }
    }
};

Listing 7.12 · Weaker memory orders for the counted stack

The printed push is missing a semicolon after head.load(std::memory_order_relaxed). Initialize the counted head explicitly. Publication, node dereference, release sequences, and deletion each need a separate ordering argument. Wide atomic lock-freedom and representation/counter limits remain relevant; passing tests does not certify these subtle algorithms.

Listing 7.12 · Book pp. 207–209
template<typename T>
class lock_free_stack
{
private:
    struct node;
    struct counted_node_ptr
    {
        int external_count;
        node* ptr;
    };
    struct node
    {
        std::shared_ptr<T> data;
        std::atomic<int> internal_count;
        counted_node_ptr next;
        node(T const& data_):
            data(std::make_shared<T>(data_)),
            internal_count(0)
        {}
    };
    std::atomic<counted_node_ptr> head;
    void increase_head_count(counted_node_ptr& old_counter)
    {
        counted_node_ptr new_counter;
        do
        {
            new_counter=old_counter;
            ++new_counter.external_count;
        }
        while(!head.compare_exchange_strong(old_counter,new_counter,
                                            std::memory_order_acquire,
                                            std::memory_order_relaxed));
        old_counter.external_count=new_counter.external_count;
    }
public:
    ~lock_free_stack()
    {
        while(pop());
    }
    void push(T const& data)
    {
        counted_node_ptr new_node;
        new_node.ptr=new node(data);
        new_node.external_count=1;
        new_node.ptr->next=head.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)
        while(!head.compare_exchange_weak(new_node.ptr->next,new_node,
                                          std::memory_order_release,
                                          std::memory_order_relaxed));
    }
    std::shared_ptr<T> pop()
    {
        counted_node_ptr old_head=
            head.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        for(;;)
        {
            increase_head_count(old_head);
            node* const ptr=old_head.ptr;
            if(!ptr)
            {
                return std::shared_ptr<T>();
            }
            if(head.compare_exchange_strong(old_head,ptr->next,
                                            std::memory_order_relaxed))
            {
                std::shared_ptr<T> res;
                res.swap(ptr->data);
                int const count_increase=old_head.external_count-2;
                if(ptr->internal_count.fetch_add(count_increase,
                       std::memory_order_release)==-count_increase)
                {
                    delete ptr;
                }
                return res;
            }
            else if(ptr->internal_count.fetch_add(-1,
                        std::memory_order_relaxed)==1)
            {
                ptr->internal_count.load(std::memory_order_acquire);
                delete ptr;
            }
        }
    }
};

Listing 7.13 · A single-producer, single-consumer queue

Only one producer may call push and only one consumer may call pop concurrently. The dummy node and tail publication order protect ordinary node members under that constraint. Join both users before destruction. Adding a second producer or consumer breaks the proof; general-purpose allocation and shared_ptr handling are outside a strict end-to-end lock-free guarantee.

Listing 7.13 · Book pp. 209–210
template<typename T>
class lock_free_queue
{
private:
    struct node
    {
        std::shared_ptr<T> data;
        node* next;
        node():
            next(nullptr)
        {}
    };
    std::atomic<node*> head;
    std::atomic<node*> tail;
    node* pop_head()
    {
        node* const old_head=head.load();
        if(old_head==tail.load())
        {
            return nullptr;
        }
        head.store(old_head->next);
        return old_head;
    }
public:
    lock_free_queue():
        head(new node),tail(head.load())
    {}
    lock_free_queue(const lock_free_queue& other)=delete;
    lock_free_queue& operator=(const lock_free_queue& other)=delete;
    ~lock_free_queue()
    {
        while(node* const old_head=head.load())
        {
            head.store(old_head->next);
            delete old_head;
        }
    }
    std::shared_ptr<T> pop()
    {
        node* old_head=pop_head();
        if(!old_head)
        {
            return std::shared_ptr<T>();
        }
        std::shared_ptr<T> const res(old_head->data);
        delete old_head;
        return res;
    }
    void push(T new_value)
    {
        std::shared_ptr<T> new_data(std::make_shared<T>(new_value));
        node* p=new node;
        node* const old_tail=tail.load();
        old_tail->data.swap(new_data);
        old_tail->next=p;
        tail.store(p);
    }
};

Broken intermediate attempt. It loads a tail pointer and dereferences it without first obtaining lifetime protection; another thread can advance the queue and reclaim that node. It also relies on partial, changing type definitions. Do not run it as a safe queue.

Listing 7.14 · Book pp. 212
void push(T new_value)
{

Listing 7.15 · A queue with a counted tail

An incomplete class fragment with later helper definitions and initialization omitted. Initialize every atomic payload pointer and both counted endpoints. It protects the loaded tail, but after one producer claims the data field the others still wait for that producer to complete: the chapter later adds helping to address that progress problem.

Listing 7.15 · Book pp. 212–213
template<typename T>
class lock_free_queue
{
private:
    struct node;
    struct counted_node_ptr
    {
        int external_count;
        node* ptr;
    };
    std::atomic<counted_node_ptr> head;
    std::atomic<counted_node_ptr> tail;
    struct node_counter
    {
        unsigned internal_count:30;
        unsigned external_counters:2;
    };
    struct node
    {
        std::atomic<T*> data;
        std::atomic<node_counter> count;
        counted_node_ptr next;
        node()
        {
            node_counter new_count;
            new_count.internal_count=0;
            new_count.external_counters=2;
            count.store(new_count);

            next.ptr=nullptr;
            next.external_count=0;
        }
    };
public:
    void push(T new_value)
    {
        std::unique_ptr<T> new_data(new T(new_value));
        counted_node_ptr new_next;
        new_next.ptr=new node;
        new_next.external_count=1;
        counted_node_ptr old_tail=tail.load();
        for(;;)
        {
            increase_external_count(tail,old_tail);
            T* old_data=nullptr;
            if(old_tail.ptr->data.compare_exchange_strong(
               old_data,new_data.get()))
            {
                old_tail.ptr->next=new_next;
                old_tail=tail.exchange(new_next);
                free_external_counter(old_tail);
                new_data.release();
                break;
            }
            old_tail.ptr->release_ref();
        }
    }
};

Listing 7.16 · Popping with counted queue references

Class fragment to merge with the queue representation and helper definitions. Empty-return, success, and retry paths must each release the references they acquired. The node stub shown here is not a replacement for the complete node definition.

Listing 7.16 · Book pp. 214–215
template<typename T>
class lock_free_queue
{
private:
    struct node
    {
        void release_ref();
    };
public:
    std::unique_ptr<T> pop()
    {
        counted_node_ptr old_head=head.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        for(;;)
        {
            increase_external_count(head,old_head);
            node* const ptr=old_head.ptr;
            if(ptr==tail.load().ptr)
            {
                ptr->release_ref();
                return std::unique_ptr<T>();
            }
            if(head.compare_exchange_strong(old_head,ptr->next))
            {
                T* const res=ptr->data.exchange(nullptr);
                free_external_counter(old_head);
                return std::unique_ptr<T>(res);
            }
            ptr->release_ref();
        }
    }
};

Listing 7.17 · Releasing a temporary node reference

The packed counters are updated together by CAS, and deletion is conditional on both reaching zero. Atomicity of these bit-fields comes from wrapping the complete counter structure in atomic, not from the individual bit-fields. Counter ranges and representation must be audited.

Listing 7.17 · Book pp. 215
template<typename T>
class lock_free_queue
{
private:
    struct node
    {
        void release_ref()
        {
            node_counter old_counter=
                count.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
            node_counter new_counter;
            do
            {
                new_counter=old_counter;
                --new_counter.internal_count;
            }
            while(!count.compare_exchange_strong(
                  old_counter,new_counter,
                  std::memory_order_acquire,std::memory_order_relaxed));
            if(!new_counter.internal_count &&
               !new_counter.external_counters)
            {
                delete this;
            }
        }
    };
};

Listing 7.18 · Obtaining an external reference

A helper class fragment. CAS increments the count and validates the pointer in one atomic update before the caller dereferences it. A plain load followed by incrementing a count inside the node would leave a reclamation window.

Listing 7.18 · Book pp. 216
template<typename T>
class lock_free_queue
{
private:
    static void increase_external_count(
        std::atomic<counted_node_ptr>& counter,
        counted_node_ptr& old_counter)
    {
        counted_node_ptr new_counter;
        do
        {
            new_counter=old_counter;
            ++new_counter.external_count;
        }
        while(!counter.compare_exchange_strong(
              old_counter,new_counter,
              std::memory_order_acquire,std::memory_order_relaxed));
        old_counter.external_count=new_counter.external_count;
    }
};

Listing 7.19 · Releasing an external counter

Transfers the external count into the node’s internal accounting while dropping an external-counter source. Both fields change together. Deletion, counter limits, and every failure path must agree with the rest of the queue algorithm.

Listing 7.19 · Book pp. 216–217
template<typename T>
class lock_free_queue
{
private:
    static void free_external_counter(counted_node_ptr &old_node_ptr)
    {
        node* const ptr=old_node_ptr.ptr;
        int const count_increase=old_node_ptr.external_count-2;
        node_counter old_counter=
            ptr->count.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        node_counter new_counter;
        do
        {
            new_counter=old_counter;
            --new_counter.external_counters;
            new_counter.internal_count+=count_increase;
        }
        while(!ptr->count.compare_exchange_strong(
              old_counter,new_counter,
              std::memory_order_acquire,std::memory_order_relaxed));
        if(!new_counter.internal_count &&
           !new_counter.external_counters)
        {
            delete ptr;
        }
    }
};

Listing 7.20 · Adapting pop for a helping queue

Partial revision with atomic next. Unlike Listing 7.16, the printed empty-return path omits ptr->release_ref(); restore balanced reference release when auditing an assembled implementation. Constructor, destructor, helpers, and initialization must also be supplied. This fragment is not a validated complete queue.

Listing 7.20 · Book pp. 218
template<typename T>
class lock_free_queue
{
private:
    struct node
    {
        std::atomic<T*> data;
        std::atomic<node_counter> count;
        std::atomic<counted_node_ptr> next;
    };
public:
    std::unique_ptr<T> pop()
    {
        counted_node_ptr old_head=head.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        for(;;)
        {
            increase_external_count(head,old_head);
            node* const ptr=old_head.ptr;
            if(ptr==tail.load().ptr)
            {
                return std::unique_ptr<T>();
            }
            counted_node_ptr next=ptr->next.load();
            if(head.compare_exchange_strong(old_head,next))
            {
                T* const res=ptr->data.exchange(nullptr);
                free_external_counter(old_head);
                return std::unique_ptr<T>(res);
            }
            ptr->release_ref();
        }
    }
};

Listing 7.21 · Helping another producer finish push

Other producers can install a dummy successor and advance tail on behalf of a stalled producer. Merge with the matching atomic-next representation and count helpers. Allocation can fail even inside the helping path after partial work; review reference/resource cleanup and end-to-end progress rather than treating this as production-ready source.

Listing 7.21 · Book pp. 219–220
template<typename T>
class lock_free_queue
{
private:
    void set_new_tail(counted_node_ptr &old_tail,
                      counted_node_ptr const &new_tail)
    {
        node* const current_tail_ptr=old_tail.ptr;
        while(!tail.compare_exchange_weak(old_tail,new_tail) &&
              old_tail.ptr==current_tail_ptr);
        if(old_tail.ptr==current_tail_ptr)
            free_external_counter(old_tail);
        else
            current_tail_ptr->release_ref();
    }
public:
    void push(T new_value)
    {
        std::unique_ptr<T> new_data(new T(new_value));
        counted_node_ptr new_next;
        new_next.ptr=new node;
        new_next.external_count=1;
        counted_node_ptr old_tail=tail.load();
        for(;;)
        {
            increase_external_count(tail,old_tail);
            T* old_data=nullptr;
            if(old_tail.ptr->data.compare_exchange_strong(
                   old_data,new_data.get()))
            {
                counted_node_ptr old_next={0};
                if(!old_tail.ptr->next.compare_exchange_strong(
                       old_next,new_next))
                {
                    delete new_next.ptr;
                    new_next=old_next;
                }
                set_new_tail(old_tail, new_next);
                new_data.release();
                break;
            }
            else
            {
                counted_node_ptr old_next={0};
                if(old_tail.ptr->next.compare_exchange_strong(
                       old_next,new_next))
                {
                    old_next=new_next;
                    new_next.ptr=new node;
                }
                set_new_tail(old_tail, old_next);
            }
        }
    }
};

Additional unnumbered examples

The chapter’s five remaining standalone source fragments are embedded below. The figure’s code-like labels remain in the original embedded image.

The first unsafe pop sketch

A deliberately incomplete stack fragment. It dereferences old_head without checking for an empty stack, leaks nodes, and can lose an item if assigning the result throws after removal.

Book pp. 186–187 · unnumbered example
template<typename T>
class lock_free_stack
{
public:
    void pop(T& result)
    {
        node* old_head=head.load();
        while(!head.compare_exchange_weak(old_head,old_head->next));
        result=old_head->data;
    }
};

Publish a hazard, then validate

A partial pop outline. Do not dereference the loaded pointer until hazard publication and source revalidation have succeeded under the required memory-ordering protocol. The omitted removal/reclamation code is essential.

Book pp. 193 · unnumbered example
std::shared_ptr<T> pop()
{
    std::atomic<void*>& hp=get_hazard_pointer_for_current_thread();
    node* old_head=head.load();
    node* temp;
    do
    {
        temp=old_head;
        hp.store(old_head);
        old_head=head.load();
    } while(old_head!=temp);
    // ...
}

Scanning the hazard-pointer slots

Used by the retirement machinery. A scan by itself is not permission to delete a reachable node: the full protect/validate/unlink/retire protocol and its ordering must hold.

Book pp. 197 · unnumbered example
bool outstanding_hazard_pointers_for(void* p)
{
    for(unsigned i=0;i<max_hazard_pointers;++i)
    {
        if(hazard_pointers[i].pointer.load()==p)
        {
            return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}

Relaxing the push publication order

Add the missing semicolon after head.load(std::memory_order_relaxed). This is an alternative member body for the counted stack, not a standalone program. Successful publication uses release; failed CAS and the preliminary load use relaxed ordering.

Book pp. 205 · unnumbered example
void push(T const& data)
{
    counted_node_ptr new_node;
    new_node.ptr=new node(data);
    new_node.external_count=1;
    new_node.ptr->next=head.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)
    while(!head.compare_exchange_weak(new_node.ptr->next,new_node,
        std::memory_order_release,std::memory_order_relaxed));
}

Acquiring protection before node access

An alternative increase_head_count helper. Its successful acquire CAS both protects the pointer’s lifetime through the count and acquires the node’s publication. Failure is retried without dereferencing the unprotected candidate.

Book pp. 206 · unnumbered example
void increase_head_count(counted_node_ptr& old_counter)
{
    counted_node_ptr new_counter;
    do
    {
        new_counter=old_counter;
        ++new_counter.external_count;
    }
    while(!head.compare_exchange_strong(old_counter,new_counter,
        std::memory_order_acquire,std::memory_order_relaxed));
    old_counter.external_count=new_counter.external_count;
}
7.4 / Check your understandingp. 223

Prove safety and progress separately.

Why is a spinlock not lock-free?

Its owner can pause while everyone else spins forever waiting for that specific owner. Using a lock-free atomic flag does not give the enclosing algorithm a lock-free progress guarantee.

Does winning a pop CAS mean I can delete the node?

No. Other threads may still have loaded it and need to inspect its fields. Unlinking gives one thread the logical item, but safe reclamation requires a separate lifetime protocol.

Why validate after publishing a hazard?

The node may have been removed between the initial load and hazard publication. Rechecking the shared source under the full hazard protocol establishes whether protection is valid before dereferencing.

Why keep counts next to the shared pointer?

Acquiring the external reference and validating the pointer in one atomic update closes the window in which a raw loaded pointer could be reclaimed before an in-node count is incremented.

Does a version tag make arbitrary pointer use safe?

No. It can detect a stale comparison when it has not wrapped, but it does not keep memory alive or repair a dereference performed before the comparison.

What is helping supposed to guarantee?

Another active participant can complete the necessary shared steps of an interrupted operation rather than waiting for one specific thread to resume. The surrounding algorithm and primitives must still satisfy the claimed progress guarantee.

Chapter in one sentence

Lock-free design is a joint proof of atomic updates, publication ordering, safe reclamation, and progress—even when a participant pauses at the worst possible point.

Chapter 08 / Illustrated summary

Designing
concurrent code.

Safe building blocks are only the beginning. Choose the work, data layout, lifetime rules, and performance goal so threads can spend their time doing useful work.

PRINTED PAGES 224–272PDF PAGES 247–29513 LISTINGS · 3 FIGURES
The central idea

Concurrency is a design choice, not a thread count. Minimize unnecessary communication, preserve ownership on failures, and measure the outcome that matters: latency, throughput, or responsiveness.

8.1 / Dividing workpp. 225–233

Generalists, specialists, or both?

The chapter’s house-building analogy separates two questions: how many workers should participate, and what responsibility should each have? Threads can perform the same operation on separate data, discover new subtasks recursively, or specialize in different stages.

Partition before starting

Assign contiguous ranges to workers, process them independently, then combine results. Good for uniform, known-size data. Too many tiny ranges waste scheduling effort; unequal per-item costs can leave workers idle.

Partition recursively

Quicksort discovers partitions while processing a pivot. Independent branches can become tasks. Limit execution resources rather than spawning a fresh OS thread at every branch; a waiting worker can help execute queued tasks.

Separate responsibilities

A GUI thread, filesystem scanner, and compute worker have different jobs. Heavy sharing and frequent mutual waits may indicate the boundary is wrong: combine tightly coupled work or give one component clear ownership.

Build a pipeline

Each stage transforms an item and sends it to the next stage’s queue. Multiple items can occupy different stages simultaneously. Balance stage capacity, bound queues, and define end-of-input, cancellation, and backpressure.

Latency and completion cadence are not the same

In the book’s ideal example, 20 items each need four 3-second steps. Four data-parallel workers finish items in batches of four every 12 seconds, completing all 20 in 60 seconds. A four-stage pipeline still takes 12 seconds for its first item, then completes one every 3 seconds, finishing in 69 seconds. The pipeline is smoother, not faster for this finite batch.

Listing 8.1 illustrates helping while waiting: instead of blocking on the lower partition’s future, the waiting caller tries to sort a queued chunk. The printed worker-vector management has a data race, so use the idea to understand task scheduling—not as a ready-made pool.

Modern precision: default-policy std::async permits deferred or asynchronous execution. The standard does not require a global task scheduler, reuse of worker threads, or a hardware-based concurrency cap, despite the chapter’s optimistic language. Explicit async can fail to launch; a properly designed bounded executor/pool gives a different resource-control contract.
8.2 / What limits performance?pp. 233–239

More runnable threads can mean less progress.

Hardware capacity is a hint, not a reservation

hardware_concurrency() may return zero, describes an implementation’s concurrency hint, and need not match physical cores or the CPU budget available to a process. Independent components that each create that many workers can oversubscribe the same machine. Account for the whole application, external load, topology, and CPU limits.

True contention and cache ping-pong

A hot shared counter forces updates through one atomic modification order. Even relaxed fetch_add still performs a read-modify-write on that shared object; weaker ordering does not eliminate coherence traffic. A mutex and even reader-lock bookkeeping can become similarly hot synchronization state.

False sharing

Different threads may legally update distinct objects that happen to share one cache line. Hardware then transfers or invalidates the line despite the logical independence. This is a performance effect, not by itself a C++ data race. Read-only sharing is usually much less troublesome than competing writes.

Locality versus isolation

Keep data used by the same thread close together, but separate frequently written data owned by different threads. Spreading everything out wastes cache capacity; keeping everything adjacent invites false sharing. Task migration, NUMA placement, bandwidth, and working-set size can change the tradeoff.

Oversubscription

Many existing threads are fine when most are blocked. Too many CPU-ready threads increase scheduling and cache costs. Extra workers may hide I/O waits, but only until a different bottleneck—storage, memory bandwidth, locks, or scheduling—dominates. Measure under realistic load.

The text simplifies hardware stalls. Modern out-of-order execution, SMT, cache hierarchies, coherence protocols, and mutex implementations differ; a cache miss does not universally prevent every other hardware thread on a core from progressing. Treat fixed cache-line sizes and timing claims as architecture-dependent illustrations.
8.3 / Layout & access patternspp. 239–243

Assign memory ownership, not just loop indices.

For row-major matrix multiplication, a result entry uses one input row and one input column. Assigning output rows gives each worker mostly contiguous writes; assigning scattered columns can cause many shared boundary lines. Rectangular output tiles can reduce the distinct input working set each worker needs, improving reuse when the traversal is also chosen carefully.

The chapter compares a 1,000 × 1,000 problem on 100 workers. Ten output rows per worker require a source footprint of about 1,010,000 elements; a 100 × 100 output tile needs about 200,000 distinct source elements. These are distinct elements needed, not a guarantee of five times fewer physical memory reads or five times faster execution. Cache reuse, loop order, alignment, and repeated loads matter.

“An exact number of cache lines” is insufficient unless the block boundaries are also aligned. Row boundaries, element size, base alignment, and allocation all affect whether adjacent writers share a line.

Beyond arrays

A tree naturally partitions into subtrees, but uneven sizes and scattered allocations can hurt balance and locality. Separating routing metadata from a larger payload may avoid fetching unused or frequently modified data during traversal. Keeping a mutex beside its protected payload helps the owner’s locality, but contending lockers may invalidate that same line.

The book’s 64 KiB padding experiments exaggerate separation to investigate a suspected bottleneck. They are not a recommended memory layout, nor does a timing improvement alone isolate false sharing. Confirm with repeated controlled measurements and, where available, hardware counters.

8.4.1 / Exception safetypp. 243–250

Two obligations: transport errors and own threads.

Worker exceptions

An exception escaping a raw std::thread entry function terminates the process. packaged_task captures it in a future; a promise can explicitly carry exception_ptr. The caller must retrieve the failure according to the API’s error policy.

Caller exceptions

Launching another thread, copying an iterator, or processing the caller’s final block may throw after workers already exist. Destroying a joinable std::thread terminates. Establish an RAII joiner as soon as ownership begins.

Listings 8.2–8.4 evolve from unguarded worker calls to packaged tasks and finally join_threads. Future::get waits for the result and rethrows a stored exception; joining ensures that the worker itself is no longer accessing borrowed state. Those are related but distinct responsibilities.

Declare objects so the joiner runs before the thread vector and any state workers still reference are destroyed. The joiner does not stop workers, guarantee they finish, or undo work already performed. Arbitrary user callbacks need a documented basic/strong guarantee and an explicit policy when several workers fail.

Async simplifies ownership, not every policy

A future created for an async-launched task can wait when the last reference to its shared state is released. That protects referenced data during unwinding in these recursive examples. Deferred tasks need not start when discarded, and an ordinary promise/packaged-task future does not automatically join a thread.

Exception delivery still requires get(). If one branch fails while another result is returned without retrieving its future, the unobserved failure is not magically propagated. Likewise, waiting in a destructor may make an otherwise “quick” early return take longer.

8.4.2–8.4.4 / Scale, latency & responsivenesspp. 250–254

Choose the metric before the thread count.

For a fixed workload with serial fraction f and N processors, ideal Amdahl speedup is S(N) = 1 / (f + (1 − f) / N). Its limit is 1/f when f is positive. One-third serial work caps ideal speedup at three, no matter how many processors are added.

The model assumes a perfectly divisible parallel portion and ignores launch, synchronization, bandwidth, load imbalance, and other overheads. Growing the input changes the workload and can change the serial fraction; that is a different scaling experiment.

Interactive study aid / Fixed-workload Amdahl model

How much can more processors help?

A mathematical model—not a benchmark, prediction for this browser, or recommendation to launch this many threads. No real parallel C++ is executed.

Hide latency without multiplying contention

When workers wait for I/O, a few extra workers or asynchronous I/O can keep CPUs busy. When they wait for an unstarted task, helping may be better than sleeping. A bounded pool must not let all workers block on queued dependencies that no worker remains free to execute.

Keep the event loop responsive

Move long-running work off the GUI thread, post results back through the framework’s event mechanism, and make cancellation cooperative at safe points. Listing 8.6 is only an outline: repeated start, stop before start, normal completion, cancellation/completion races, worker errors, and quit all need explicit states. Joining a slow task in an event handler can still freeze the interface.

8.5 / Algorithms in practicepp. 255–271

Each algorithm brings a different contract.

for_each: independent work, unordered effects

Assign separate contiguous blocks or recursively split the range. A void future still matters: it transports errors. Shared captures, aliases, external I/O, packed proxy elements, and output ordering may violate the assumption of independent operations even when the indices differ.

find: preserve early stopping, define “found”

A shared atomic done flag tells workers to stop at their next check. The promise version arbitrates a winning value or exception and joins all workers before deciding “not found.” Otherwise, waiting on an unset promise after an unsuccessful search could hang forever.

These examples may return any winning match, not the earliest match promised by sequential std::find. Stopping also does not mean all comparisons cease instantaneously: some workers are already in flight. The recursive version can discard an unobserved branch exception after finding a match elsewhere.

partial_sum: dependencies change the shape of the work

A scan cannot simply sum blocks independently. One strategy performs local scans, then adds the cumulative total from previous blocks. Publish the adjusted last element first so the next block can begin its adjustment while this block finishes updating its remaining elements.

For the input 1…9 split three ways, local scans are {1,3,6}, {4,9,15}, {7,15,24}. Propagating offsets gives {1,3,6}, {10,15,21}, {28,36,45}. The text’s isolated “55” at the end of this worked example is an arithmetic typo; the total is 45.

A second strategy doubles the dependency distance each round: add from 1 away, then 2, then 4, and so on. The example alternates buffers and synchronizes phases with a barrier. It performs O(N log N) work with O(log N) ideal rounds, compared with the linear-work block strategy. More parallelism can justify more total operations when hardware and problem sizes fit.

Barriers couple failure and lifetime

A generation counter prevents a fast participant from confusing the next round with the previous one. Dropping decreases both the future cohort and the current arrivals still owed. A participant that exits without completing the required phase protocol can strand everyone else.

Listing 8.13’s thread-per-element design is deliberately extreme, not a suitable default for large CPU workloads. A failed launch leaves an unfilled barrier seat; a throwing participant can terminate the process or hang the joiner. Capturing exception_ptr alone is not recovery: remaining participants also need a safe route through or out of the synchronization protocol.

Numeric contracts matter. Regrouping arithmetic changes floating-point rounding and is unsuitable for non-associative operations without a defined policy. Signed integer overflow remains undefined behavior. The sample “25 elements” thresholds are teaching constants, not portable optimal grain sizes. These algorithms are C++11 teaching implementations, not specifications of later standard execution-policy overloads.
