Listing 8.1 · Quicksort with a shared stack of tasks

Requires a compatible thread_safe_stack that supports move-only promise-bearing chunks; the printed boost::shared_ptr spelling must agree with that stack API. This historical example has unsynchronized concurrent access to the shared threads vector from recursive worker calls, so it is not a safe thread-pool implementation. hardware_concurrency()==0 also underflows the unsigned “minus one” limit. Exceptions in sort_chunk need capture into the promise and safe worker shutdown; thread construction/vector insertion and partial construction need a separate ownership policy. Do not deploy it unchanged.

Listing 8.1 · Book pp. 228–230
template<typename T>
struct sorter
{
    struct chunk_to_sort
    {
        std::list<T> data;
        std::promise<std::list<T> > promise;
    };
    thread_safe_stack<chunk_to_sort> chunks;
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    unsigned const max_thread_count;
    std::atomic<bool> end_of_data;
    sorter():
        max_thread_count(std::thread::hardware_concurrency()-1),
        end_of_data(false)
    {}
    ~sorter()
    {
        end_of_data=true;
        for(unsigned i=0;i<threads.size();++i)
        {
            threads[i].join();
        }
    }
    void try_sort_chunk()
    {
        boost::shared_ptr<chunk_to_sort > chunk=chunks.pop();
        if(chunk)
        {
            sort_chunk(chunk);
        }
    }
    std::list<T> do_sort(std::list<T>& chunk_data)
    {
        if(chunk_data.empty())
        {
            return chunk_data;
        }
        std::list<T> result;
        result.splice(result.begin(),chunk_data,chunk_data.begin());
        T const& partition_val=*result.begin();
        typename std::list<T>::iterator divide_point=
            std::partition(chunk_data.begin(),chunk_data.end(),
                           [&](T const& val){return val<partition_val;});
        chunk_to_sort new_lower_chunk;
        new_lower_chunk.data.splice(new_lower_chunk.data.end(),
                                    chunk_data,chunk_data.begin(),
                                    divide_point);
        std::future<std::list<T> > new_lower=
            new_lower_chunk.promise.get_future();
        chunks.push(std::move(new_lower_chunk));
        if(threads.size()<max_thread_count)
        {
            threads.push_back(std::thread(&sorter<T>::sort_thread,this));
        }
        std::list<T> new_higher(do_sort(chunk_data));
        result.splice(result.end(),new_higher);
        while(new_lower.wait_for(std::chrono::seconds(0)) !=
              std::future_status::ready)
        {
            try_sort_chunk();
        }
        result.splice(result.begin(),new_lower.get());
        return result;
    }
    void sort_chunk(boost::shared_ptr<chunk_to_sort > const& chunk)
    {
        chunk->promise.set_value(do_sort(chunk->data));
    }
    void sort_thread()
    {
        while(!end_of_data)
        {
            try_sort_chunk();
            std::this_thread::yield();
        }
    }
};
template<typename T>
std::list<T> parallel_quick_sort(std::list<T> input)
{
    if(input.empty())
    {
        return input;
    }
    sorter<T> s;
    return s.do_sort(input);
}

Listing 8.2 · The naïve parallel accumulate

Deliberately not exception-safe: an exception escaping a worker calls terminate, while an exception in the launching thread can destroy joinable thread objects. The printed final accumulate_block() lacks template arguments; use accumulate_block<Iterator,T>(). Requires headers and a valid multipass range. Chunk regrouping assumes an appropriate additive identity and associative operation; floating-point results can differ from sequential accumulation.

Listing 8.2 · Book pp. 244
template<typename Iterator,typename T>
struct accumulate_block
{
    void operator()(Iterator first,Iterator last,T& result)
    {
        result=std::accumulate(first,last,result);
    }
};
template<typename Iterator,typename T>
T parallel_accumulate(Iterator first,Iterator last,T init)
{
    unsigned long const length=std::distance(first,last);
    if(!length)
        return init;
    unsigned long const min_per_thread=25;
    unsigned long const max_threads=
        (length+min_per_thread-1)/min_per_thread;
    unsigned long const hardware_threads=
        std::thread::hardware_concurrency();
    unsigned long const num_threads=
        std::min(hardware_threads!=0?hardware_threads:2,max_threads);
    unsigned long const block_size=length/num_threads;
    std::vector<T> results(num_threads);
    std::vector<std::thread>  threads(num_threads-1);
    Iterator block_start=first;
    for(unsigned long i=0;i<(num_threads-1);++i)
    {
        Iterator block_end=block_start;
        std::advance(block_end,block_size);
        threads[i]=std::thread(
            accumulate_block<Iterator,T>(),
            block_start,block_end,std::ref(results[i]));
        block_start=block_end;
    }
    accumulate_block()(block_start,last,results[num_threads-1]);
    std::for_each(threads.begin(),threads.end(),
        std::mem_fn(&std::thread::join));
    return std::accumulate(results.begin(),results.end(),init);
}

Listing 8.3 · Packaged tasks capture worker exceptions

An intermediate version, not yet exception-safe around thread ownership. Explicitly name accumulate_block<Iterator,T>() in the final-block call. The packaged_task declaration using parenthesized accumulate_block<Iterator,T>() is a most-vexing-parse candidate; use braces for task construction. Capturing a worker exception is not the same as joining every launched thread during unwinding.

Listing 8.3 · Book pp. 245–246
template<typename Iterator,typename T>
struct accumulate_block
{
    T operator()(Iterator first,Iterator last)
    {
        return std::accumulate(first,last,T());
    }
};
template<typename Iterator,typename T>
T parallel_accumulate(Iterator first,Iterator last,T init)
{
    unsigned long const length=std::distance(first,last);
    if(!length)
        return init;
    unsigned long const min_per_thread=25;
    unsigned long const max_threads=
        (length+min_per_thread-1)/min_per_thread;
    unsigned long const hardware_threads=
        std::thread::hardware_concurrency();
    unsigned long const num_threads=
        std::min(hardware_threads!=0?hardware_threads:2,max_threads);
    unsigned long const block_size=length/num_threads;
    std::vector<std::future<T> > futures(num_threads-1);
    std::vector<std::thread> threads(num_threads-1);
    Iterator block_start=first;
    for(unsigned long i=0;i<(num_threads-1);++i)
    {
        Iterator block_end=block_start;
        std::advance(block_end,block_size);
        std::packaged_task<T(Iterator,Iterator)> task(
            accumulate_block<Iterator,T>());
        futures[i]=task.get_future();
        threads[i]=std::thread(std::move(task),block_start,block_end);
        block_start=block_end;
    }
    T last_result=accumulate_block()(block_start,last);
    std::for_each(threads.begin(),threads.end(),
        std::mem_fn(&std::thread::join));
    T result=init;
    for(unsigned long i=0;i<(num_threads-1);++i)
    {
        result+=futures[i].get();
    }
    result += last_result;
    return result;
}

Listing 8.4 · RAII joins the threads on every exit

Use the unnumbered join_threads helper and the accumulate_block from Listing 8.3. Correct the final-block functor to accumulate_block<Iterator,T>() and use braces for the packaged_task construction to avoid the most vexing parse. Futures retrieve values/exceptions; the joiner handles both normal exit and unwinding, and must outlive no object still accessed by workers. This provides cleanup, not rollback of arbitrary user side effects.

Listing 8.4 · Book pp. 248–249
template<typename Iterator,typename T>
T parallel_accumulate(Iterator first,Iterator last,T init)
{
    unsigned long const length=std::distance(first,last);
    if(!length)
        return init;
    unsigned long const min_per_thread=25;
    unsigned long const max_threads=
        (length+min_per_thread-1)/min_per_thread;
    unsigned long const hardware_threads=
        std::thread::hardware_concurrency();
    unsigned long const num_threads=
        std::min(hardware_threads!=0?hardware_threads:2,max_threads);
    unsigned long const block_size=length/num_threads;
    std::vector<std::future<T> > futures(num_threads-1);
    std::vector<std::thread> threads(num_threads-1);
    join_threads joiner(threads);
    Iterator block_start=first;
    for(unsigned long i=0;i<(num_threads-1);++i)
    {
        Iterator block_end=block_start;
        std::advance(block_end,block_size);
        std::packaged_task<T(Iterator,Iterator)> task(
            accumulate_block<Iterator,T>());
        futures[i]=task.get_future();
        threads[i]=std::thread(std::move(task),block_start,block_end);
        block_start=block_end;
    }
    T last_result=accumulate_block()(block_start,last);
    T result=init;
    for(unsigned long i=0;i<(num_threads-1);++i)
    {
        result+=futures[i].get();
    }
    result += last_result;
    return result;
}

Listing 8.5 · Recursive accumulate using async

Default std::async may execute asynchronously or defer until a waiting call; it does not promise a bounded pool or prevent oversubscription. A future associated with an async-launched task can wait on last release, including during unwinding; this is not a general property of every future. Requires a valid multipass range and suitable additive identity/associativity.

Listing 8.5 · Book pp. 249–250
template<typename Iterator,typename T>
T parallel_accumulate(Iterator first,Iterator last,T init)
{
    unsigned long const length=std::distance(first,last);
    unsigned long const max_chunk_size=25;
    if(length<=max_chunk_size)
    {
        return std::accumulate(first,last,init);
    }
    else
    {
    Iterator mid_point=first;
        std::advance(mid_point,length/2);
        std::future<T> first_half_result=
            std::async(parallel_accumulate<Iterator,T>,
                       first,mid_point,init);
        T second_half_result=parallel_accumulate(mid_point,last,T());
        return first_half_result.get()+second_half_result;
    }
}

Listing 8.6 · GUI and worker separation

An application outline with placeholder event APIs, not compilable standalone GUI code. Guard the task state: assigning a new thread while the previous one is joinable terminates; stop/completion handlers must not join a nonjoinable thread; quit must cancel/join safely. A GUI-thread join can freeze the interface until a worker cooperates. Also separate the task_complete event identifier from the predicate name in a real API, and handle worker exceptions and stale completion events.

Listing 8.6 · Book pp. 253–254
std::thread task_thread;
std::atomic<bool> task_cancelled(false);
void gui_thread()
{
    while(true)
    {
        event_data event=get_event();
        if(event.type==quit)
            break;
        process(event);
    }
}
void task()
{
    while(!task_complete() && !task_cancelled)
    {
        do_next_operation();
    }
    if(task_cancelled)
    {
        perform_cleanup();
    }
    else
    {
        post_gui_event(task_complete);
    }
}
void process(event_data const& event)
{
    switch(event.type)
    {
    case start_task:
        task_cancelled=false;
        task_thread=std::thread(task);
        break;
    case stop_task:
        task_cancelled=true;
        task_thread.join();
        break;
    case task_complete:
        task_thread.join();
        display_results();
        break;
    default:
        //...
    }
}

Listing 8.7 · Block-based parallel for_each

Requires join_threads and standard headers. Calls on different elements may overlap and occur out of order. Copies of the callable may still share captured objects; those accesses need independent synchronization. Non-overlapping indices do not guarantee independent storage (for example vector<bool> proxy bits). No rollback is provided if a task throws.

Listing 8.7 · Book pp. 255–256
template<typename Iterator,typename Func>
void parallel_for_each(Iterator first,Iterator last,Func f)
{
    unsigned long const length=std::distance(first,last);
    if(!length)
        return;
    unsigned long const min_per_thread=25;
    unsigned long const max_threads=
        (length+min_per_thread-1)/min_per_thread;
    unsigned long const hardware_threads=
        std::thread::hardware_concurrency();
    unsigned long const num_threads=
        std::min(hardware_threads!=0?hardware_threads:2,max_threads);
    unsigned long const block_size=length/num_threads;
    std::vector<std::future<void> > futures(num_threads-1);
    std::vector<std::thread> threads(num_threads-1);
    join_threads joiner(threads);
    Iterator block_start=first;
    for(unsigned long i=0;i<(num_threads-1);++i)
    {
        Iterator block_end=block_start;
        std::advance(block_end,block_size);
        std::packaged_task<void(void)> task(
            [=]()
            {
                std::for_each(block_start,block_end,f);
            });
        futures[i]=task.get_future();
        threads[i]=std::thread(std::move(task));
        block_start=block_end;
    }
    std::for_each(block_start,last,f);
    for(unsigned long i=0;i<(num_threads-1);++i)
    {
        futures[i].get();
    }
}

Listing 8.8 · Recursive async for_each

Uses first+length/2, so the printed version requires random-access iterators. Default async policy does not guarantee parallel execution, a thread limit, or a pool. Element operations and captured state must be safe for concurrent invocation. The caller waits for async work before referenced range storage can be released.

Listing 8.8 · Book pp. 257
template<typename Iterator,typename Func>
void parallel_for_each(Iterator first,Iterator last,Func f)
{
    unsigned long const length=std::distance(first,last);
    if(!length)
        return;
    unsigned long const min_per_thread=25;
    if(length<(2*min_per_thread))
    {
        std::for_each(first,last,f);
    }
    else
    {
        Iterator const mid_point=first+length/2;
        std::future<void> first_half=
            std::async(&parallel_for_each<Iterator,Func>,
                       first,mid_point,f);
        parallel_for_each(mid_point,last,f);
        first_half.get();
    }
}

Listing 8.9 · Parallel find with a promise and stop flag

Requires join_threads. Returns a winning matching iterator, not necessarily the first in sequence. Concurrent promise setters compete; the promise serializes its state and losing setters throw future_error, which this sketch catches. The flag requests cooperative stopping, while the promise transports the result or exception. Join everyone before inspecting the no-match state so an absent item does not leave get() waiting forever.

Listing 8.9 · Book pp. 258–260
template<typename Iterator,typename MatchType>
Iterator parallel_find(Iterator first,Iterator last,MatchType match)
{
    struct find_element
    {
        void operator()(Iterator begin,Iterator end,
                        MatchType match,
                        std::promise<Iterator>* result,
                        std::atomic<bool>* done_flag)
        {
            try
            {
                for(;(begin!=end) && !done_flag->load();++begin)
                {
                    if(*begin==match)
                    {
                        result->set_value(begin);
                        done_flag->store(true);
                        return;
                    }
                }
            }
            catch(...)
            {
                try
                {
                    result->set_exception(std::current_exception());
                    done_flag->store(true);
                }
                catch(...)
                {}
            }
        }
    };
    unsigned long const length=std::distance(first,last);
    if(!length)
        return last;
    unsigned long const min_per_thread=25;
    unsigned long const max_threads=
        (length+min_per_thread-1)/min_per_thread;
    unsigned long const hardware_threads=
        std::thread::hardware_concurrency();
    unsigned long const num_threads=
        std::min(hardware_threads!=0?hardware_threads:2,max_threads);
    unsigned long const block_size=length/num_threads;
    std::promise<Iterator> result;
    std::atomic<bool> done_flag(false);
    std::vector<std::thread> threads(num_threads-1);
    {
        join_threads joiner(threads);
        Iterator block_start=first;
        for(unsigned long i=0;i<(num_threads-1);++i)
        {
            Iterator block_end=block_start;
            std::advance(block_end,block_size);
            threads[i]=std::thread(find_element(),
                                   block_start,block_end,match,
                                   &result,&done_flag);
            block_start=block_end;
        }
        find_element()(block_start,last,match,&result,&done_flag);
    }
    if(!done_flag.load())
    {
        return last;
    }
    return result.get_future().get();
}

Listing 8.10 · Recursive async find

Requires random-access iterators. The shared flag stops unnecessary searches; it does not establish earliest-match semantics. Default async permits deferred execution and is not a bounded scheduling guarantee. Only exceptions actually retrieved by get() are rethrown; an async branch’s exception can be unobserved if another branch returns a match without calling get(). Decide that policy explicitly.

Listing 8.10 · Book pp. 261–262
template<typename Iterator,typename MatchType>
Iterator parallel_find_impl(Iterator first,Iterator last,MatchType match,
                            std::atomic<bool>& done)
{
    try
    {
        unsigned long const length=std::distance(first,last);
        unsigned long const min_per_thread=25;
        if(length<(2*min_per_thread))
        {
            for(;(first!=last) && !done.load();++first)
            {
                if(*first==match)
                {
                    done=true;
                    return first;
                }
            }
            return last;
        }
        else
        {
            Iterator const mid_point=first+(length/2);
            std::future<Iterator> async_result=
                std::async(&parallel_find_impl<Iterator,MatchType>,
                           mid_point,last,match,std::ref(done));
            Iterator const direct_result=
                    parallel_find_impl(first,mid_point,match,done);
            return (direct_result==mid_point)?
                async_result.get():direct_result;
        }
    }
    catch(...)
    {
        done=true;
        throw;
    }
}
template<typename Iterator,typename MatchType>
Iterator parallel_find(Iterator first,Iterator last,MatchType match)
{
    std::atomic<bool> done(false);
    return parallel_find_impl(first,last,match,done);
}

Listing 8.11 · Block-based partial sums

Printed corrections required: use iterator_traits<Iterator>::value_type for general iterators; return; rather than return last; in this void function; and value_type addend=previous_end_value->get(), not a non-const lvalue reference to a returned temporary. Requires join_threads. More seriously, it publishes the endpoint before updating the rest of its chunk: a later throwing adjustment can enter catch and attempt set_exception on an already satisfied promise, potentially terminating a worker. The range may be partially modified; this is not a general exception-safe implementation for arbitrary throwing value types.

Listing 8.11 · Book pp. 264–265
template<typename Iterator>
void parallel_partial_sum(Iterator first,Iterator last)
{
    typedef typename Iterator::value_type value_type;

    struct process_chunk
    {
        void operator()(Iterator begin,Iterator last,
                        std::future<value_type>* previous_end_value,
                        std::promise<value_type>* end_value)
        {
            try
            {
                Iterator end=last;
                ++end;
                std::partial_sum(begin,end,begin);
                if(previous_end_value)
                {
                    value_type& addend=previous_end_value->get();
                    *last+=addend;
                    if(end_value)
                    {
                        end_value->set_value(*last);
                    }
                    std::for_each(begin,last,[addend](value_type& item)
                                  {
                                      item+=addend;
                                  });
                }
                else if(end_value)
                {
                    end_value->set_value(*last);
                }
            }
            catch(...)
            {
                if(end_value)
                {
                    end_value->set_exception(std::current_exception());
                }
                else
                {
                    throw;
                }
            }
        }
    };
    unsigned long const length=std::distance(first,last);
    if(!length)
        return last;
    unsigned long const min_per_thread=25;
    unsigned long const max_threads=
        (length+min_per_thread-1)/min_per_thread;
    unsigned long const hardware_threads=
        std::thread::hardware_concurrency();
    unsigned long const num_threads=
        std::min(hardware_threads!=0?hardware_threads:2,max_threads);
    unsigned long const block_size=length/num_threads;
    typedef typename Iterator::value_type value_type;
    std::vector<std::thread> threads(num_threads-1);
    std::vector<std::promise<value_type> >
         end_values(num_threads-1);
    std::vector<std::future<value_type> >
         previous_end_values;
    previous_end_values.reserve(num_threads-1);
    join_threads joiner(threads);
    Iterator block_start=first;
    for(unsigned long i=0;i<(num_threads-1);++i)
    {
        Iterator block_last=block_start;
        std::advance(block_last,block_size-1);
        threads[i]=std::thread(process_chunk(),
                               block_start,block_last,
                               (i!=0)?&previous_end_values[i-1]:0,
                               &end_values[i]);
        block_start=block_last;
        ++block_start;
        previous_end_values.push_back(end_values[i].get_future());
    }
    Iterator final_element=block_start;
    std::advance(final_element,std::distance(block_start,last)-1);
    process_chunk()(block_start,final_element,
                    (num_threads>1)?&previous_end_values.back():0,
                    0);
}

Listing 8.12 · A reusable spin barrier

Requires atomic/thread headers and a nonzero participant count. Exactly the registered cohort must arrive once in every phase. A generation distinguishes successive rounds; resetting spaces alone would confuse fast re-entry with the old phase. yield() is a scheduling hint, not a blocking wait or a guarantee of fairness. If a participant never arrives, the others can wait forever. C++20 offers std::barrier for supported use cases.

Listing 8.12 · Book pp. 267–268
class barrier
{
    unsigned const count;
    std::atomic<unsigned> spaces;
    std::atomic<unsigned> generation;
public:
    explicit barrier(unsigned count_):
        count(count_),spaces(count),generation(0)
    {}
    void wait()
    {
        unsigned const my_generation=generation;
        if(!--spaces)
        {
            spaces=count;
            ++generation;
        }
        else
        {
            while(generation==my_generation)
                std::this_thread::yield();
        }
    }
};

Listing 8.13 · Pairwise doubling scan with a dropping barrier

Requires join_threads and random-access iterators; use iterator_traits to support raw pointers. This deliberately launches roughly one thread per element and is not scalable CPU-thread-pool code. It is not exception-safe: a throwing worker may terminate the process; a launch failure or an exception on the calling thread can strand other threads at the barrier and make RAII joining hang. Merely storing an exception does not release missing participants—failure/cancellation must be coordinated with the phase protocol. Also audit unsigned stride/count ranges.

Listing 8.13 · Book pp. 269–271
struct barrier
{
    std::atomic<unsigned> count;
    std::atomic<unsigned> spaces;
    std::atomic<unsigned> generation;
    barrier(unsigned count_):
        count(count_),spaces(count_),generation(0)
    {}
    void wait()
    {
        unsigned const gen=generation.load();
        if(!--spaces)
        {
            spaces=count.load();
            ++generation;
        }
        else
        {
            while(generation.load()==gen)
            {
                std::this_thread::yield();
            }
        }
    }
    void done_waiting()
    {
        --count;
        if(!--spaces)
        {
            spaces=count.load();
            ++generation;
        }
    }
};
template<typename Iterator>
void parallel_partial_sum(Iterator first,Iterator last)
{
    typedef typename Iterator::value_type value_type;
    struct process_element
    {
        void operator()(Iterator first,Iterator last,
                        std::vector<value_type>& buffer,
                        unsigned i,barrier& b)
        {
            value_type& ith_element=*(first+i);
            bool update_source=false;

            for(unsigned step=0,stride=1;stride<=i;++step,stride*=2)
            {
                value_type const& source=(step%2)?
                    buffer[i]:ith_element;
                value_type& dest=(step%2)?
                    ith_element:buffer[i];
                value_type const& addend=(step%2)?
                    buffer[i-stride]:*(first+i-stride);
                dest=source+addend;
                update_source=!(step%2);
                b.wait();
            }
            if(update_source)
            {
                ith_element=buffer[i];
            }
            b.done_waiting();
        }
    };
    unsigned long const length=std::distance(first,last);
    if(length<=1)
        return;
    std::vector<value_type> buffer(length);
    barrier b(length);
    std::vector<std::thread> threads(length-1);
    join_threads joiner(threads);
    Iterator block_start=first;
    for(unsigned long i=0;i<(length-1);++i)
    {
        threads[i]=std::thread(process_element(),first,last,
                               std::ref(buffer),i,std::ref(b));
    }
    process_element()(first,last,buffer,length-1,b);
}

Additional unnumbered examples

All ten standalone source fragments are included, including the reusable join helper and the incremental barrier edits.

A contended relaxed atomic counter

do_something() is a placeholder. Relaxed ordering removes unrelated synchronization obligations, not the single modification order or physical contention on the shared read-modify-write location.

Book p. 235 · unnumbered example
std::atomic<unsigned long> counter(0);
void processing_loop()
{
    while(counter.fetch_add(1,std::memory_order_relaxed)<100000000)
    {
        do_something();
    }
}

Mutex contention in a loop

my_data and done_processing are application placeholders. Both the protected work and the synchronization object can become bottlenecks. The amount of spinning versus kernel blocking depends on the mutex implementation.

Book p. 236 · unnumbered example
std::mutex m;
my_data data;
void processing_loop_with_mutex()
{
    while(true)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m);
        if(done_processing(data)) break;
    }
}

Padding between a mutex and its data

A diagnostic experiment, not a recommended object layout. Huge padding changes cache capacity, allocation, alignment, and other behavior; an improvement is evidence worth investigating, not conclusive proof of false sharing.

Book p. 243 · unnumbered example
struct protected_data
{
    std::mutex m;
    char padding[65536];
    my_data data_to_protect;
};

Padding between array elements

data_item1 and data_item2 are placeholders. A 64 KiB gap has a substantial memory cost. Prefer measured, platform-appropriate alignment/layout changes; C++17 offers hardware_destructive_interference_size where supported.

Book p. 243 · unnumbered example
struct my_data
{
    data_item1 d1;
    data_item2 d2;
    char padding[65536];
};
my_data some_array[256];

Manual catch, join, and rethrow

An abbreviated replacement block, not standalone code. Correct num_thread to num_threads, thread[i] to threads[i], and supply accumulate_block<Iterator,T>() for the final block. RAII removes the duplicated join loop.

Book p. 247 · unnumbered example
try
{
    for(unsigned long i=0;i<(num_threads-1);++i)
    {
        // ... as before
    }
    T last_result=accumulate_block()(block_start,last);
    std::for_each(threads.begin(),threads.end(),
        std::mem_fn(&std::thread::join));
}
catch(...)
{
    for(unsigned long i=0;i<(num_thread-1);++i)
    {
        if(threads[i].joinable())
            thread[i].join();
    }
    throw;
}

The reusable join_threads helper

Declare the joiner after the thread vector and after other resources workers reference, so it is destroyed before those resources. Never use it to join the current thread; a destructor must not allow join errors to escape. Joining does not itself cancel a worker or break a dependency deadlock.

Book p. 248 · unnumbered example
class join_threads
{
    std::vector<std::thread>& threads;
public:
    explicit join_threads(std::vector<std::thread>& threads_):
        threads(threads_)
    {}
    ~join_threads()
    {
        for(unsigned long i=0;i<threads.size();++i)
        {
            if(threads[i].joinable())
                threads[i].join();
        }
    }
};

A minimal event loop

get_event and process stand for a framework-specific event API. Long-running processing here delays every subsequent event; background work still needs safe communication and GUI-thread affinity.

Book p. 253 · unnumbered example
while(true)
{
    event_data event=get_event();
    if(event.type==quit)
        break;
    process(event);
}

Allowing a barrier cohort to shrink

Replace the original non-atomic count member before using the drop operation. This one-line declaration is a class edit, not a separate complete object definition.

Book p. 268 · unnumbered example
std::atomic<unsigned> count;

Resetting spaces from an atomic count

Replacement statement for the barrier’s last-arrival path. Atomic objects cannot simply be copied; load the current count value.

Book p. 268 · unnumbered example
spaces=count.load();

Dropping out of future phases

Class-member fragment for the modified barrier. Dropping both the participant count and the current phase’s remaining arrivals prevents the cohort from waiting for an arrival that will never come. This is a prescribed protocol, not arbitrary cancellation from any phase.

Book p. 269 · unnumbered example
void done_waiting()
{
    --count;
    if(!--spaces)
    {
        spaces=count.load();
        ++generation;
    }
}
8.6 / Check your understandingp. 272

Design for useful work—and orderly failure.

When is a pipeline better than partitioning the data?

When stages are natural responsibilities, input arrives over time, or steady completion cadence matters. It can have worse startup and finite-batch completion time; the slowest stage limits throughput.

Does relaxed ordering remove contention?

No. A relaxed RMW still updates one shared object in its modification order and can cause cache-line contention. Distributing counters and reducing less often may matter more than weakening ordering.

Can race-free code suffer false sharing?

Yes. Separate objects may occupy the same cache line. Competing writes then generate coherence traffic without violating the C++ object-level access rules.

Why do we need futures and an RAII joiner?

A future can transport a worker’s exception; the joiner preserves thread ownership during normal return and unwinding. Neither mechanism by itself provides rollback, cancellation, or freedom from dependency deadlock.

Does parallel_find preserve std::find’s first-match contract?

Not in these implementations. A later match can win the concurrent search. If earliest position matters, use a different result/termination protocol and prove it separately.

Why is capturing a barrier worker’s exception insufficient?

The other participants may still owe or await arrivals. Recovery must coordinate the participant count and phase transitions, not merely store an error and abandon the barrier.

Chapter in one sentence

Partition work to fit the goal, arrange memory to fit ownership, bound execution resources, and make failure paths as deliberate as the fast path.

Chapter 09 / Illustrated summary

Advanced
thread management.

Separate tasks from execution resources—and separate asking a thread to stop from knowing that it has finished.

PRINTED PAGES 273–299PDF PAGES 296–32213 LISTINGS · 7 SUPPORTING SNIPPETS
The central idea

A pool owns worker threads, futures describe task completion, and interruption requests cooperation. None of these automatically solves dependencies, lifetime, or shutdown.

9.1.1 / A fixed pool of workerspp. 274–276

Submit work, not a new thread.

The car-pool analogy separates a reusable resource from the many jobs needing it. A thread pool owns a limited set of workers. submit queues a callable; a worker removes a task, invokes it, and looks for more. Many tasks can share the same execution resources over time.

Listing 9.1 starts workers in the constructor, polls a thread-safe queue, and yields when no task is found. It queues copyable std::function<void()> values, offers no direct completion handle, and relies on application code for result/error synchronization.

Ownership extends through construction failure

If starting worker N throws, previously started workers must be signaled to stop and joined. The done flag and work queue are declared before the thread vector, and the joiner after it, so reverse destruction joins workers before destroying their state.

Also avoid creating an unowned temporary thread during a potentially throwing vector insertion. Establish storage and ownership before worker launch. Supply a nonzero fallback when hardware_concurrency() reports zero, and do not interpret that hint as a reservation of CPUs.

Define what shutdown means

The printed destructor sets done and joins: running tasks finish, but queued tasks may be abandoned. It is not a drain-until-empty contract. A production API needs policies for accepting/rejecting new submissions, bounded queue capacity/backpressure, active tasks, abandoned futures, and whether cancellation is requested.

A yield loop is still polling; yield is not a promise to sleep or a fairness guarantee. A blocking work queue can reduce idle CPU usage, but must wake correctly for both new work and shutdown. Uncaught exceptions escaping a raw task entry still terminate the process.
9.1.2 / Waitable taskspp. 276–280

The future belongs to the task, not the worker.

Wrap a nullary callable in packaged_task<R()>, get its future, then move the task into the queue. The worker can execute it later; get() waits for the result and rethrows a captured callable exception. A void future still carries completion and errors.

packaged_task is move-only, but C++11 std::function requires a copyable target. Listing 9.2 introduces function_wrapper: an owning type-erased callable using a unique_ptr to a virtual call interface. It can move through a queue without copying the packaged task. Modern C++23 has std::move_only_function for supported use cases; the book’s wrapper remains a small teaching example, not its equivalent full interface.

Independent blocks are the easy case

Listing 9.3 divides accumulation into fixed-size tasks, keeps their futures, computes the last block locally, and combines results. The number of tasks need not equal the number of workers. Too-small tasks spend their time allocating, enqueueing, synchronizing, and delivering results rather than doing useful work.

The printed submission is missing the range arguments; the pool expects a no-argument callable, so bind or capture block_start and block_end. Preserve range storage until all running tasks using it have finished. Queue destruction abandons unexecuted packaged tasks and readies their futures with broken_promise; it does not complete their intended work.

A future from this pool does not automatically join a worker when destroyed. Pool lifetime, task lifetime, and borrowed-state lifetime must be coordinated explicitly. Replacing std::async with this submit function changes those ownership semantics.

9.1.3 / Dependent taskspp. 280–282

All workers can wait while work is still queued.

Suppose each running task submits a child and then blocks on the child’s future. If every worker does this, the children remain queued with no worker available to execute them. A fixed-size pool has created a starvation deadlock even when the task graph has no cycle.

Listings 9.4–9.5 expose run_pending_task and let a waiting Quicksort caller execute queued work until its required future becomes ready. This turns dependency waiting into useful execution. It is a strategy for this class of dependency—not a proof that every task graph or resource wait is safe.

Interactive study aid / Two workers, two dependencies

What happens while the parents wait?

A deterministic symbolic schedule. Child C1 is needed by parent P1, and C2 by P2. Children do not wait for their parents and need no locks. No real C++ threads are launched.

Helping may run unrelated tasks reentrantly. Do not hold a mutex or depend on thread-local invariants that nested work can violate. Cyclic dependencies and uninterruptible external waits remain possible.

Be careful what a “wait” is allowed to execute

A helping caller can run arbitrary queued tasks on its own stack. That affects lock ordering, reentrancy, task-local assumptions, priority, stack depth, and fairness. A robust executor can offer dependency-aware waits or continuations rather than asking each algorithm to write a polling loop.

9.1.4–9.1.5 / Local queues & work stealingpp. 283–288

Locality first. Balance when necessary.

A single shared queue is a common write hotspot. Listing 9.6 gives each worker a private queue for newly spawned tasks, falling back to a shared queue for work submitted from outside the pool. This reduces shared queue traffic but can hide a large recursive task tree on one worker while the others run out of work.

Work stealing makes those local queues visible to other workers. The owner normally pushes and pops at the front; an idle thief takes an older item from the back. Local LIFO execution can favor recently touched data and depth-first task completion, while older tasks often represent independent branches worth sharing.

Listing 9.7 uses a mutex-protected deque. Both ends are serialized by that mutex; opposite ends are a scheduling/locality choice here, not lock-free concurrent access. Tasks are moved out under the lock and invoked after it is released.

The work-selection order

  1. Try the current worker’s local deque.
  2. Try the shared incoming-work queue.
  3. Probe other workers’ deques, offsetting the victim order by worker index.
  4. If no task is found, yield in the printed design; a production pool may park and use a wakeup protocol.

Work stealing balances available runnable tasks. It does not wake workers blocked on ordinary futures or I/O, remove graph cycles, or guarantee fairness. Local-first execution and a deterministic stealing order can starve some tasks or concentrate contention; measure and define the scheduler’s goals.

Important source limitations: Listing 9.8 starts workers while still modifying the vector of queues that those workers read. Build the entire queue collection before starting workers. The static thread_local queue pointer also needs pool-instance identity: otherwise a worker submitting to a different pool can send work to its current pool’s local queue. The listing’s missing TLS definitions, zero-worker behavior, exception paths, and shutdown rules also require completion.
9.2.1–9.2.2 / Cooperative interruptionpp. 289–291

“Please stop” is not “you have stopped.”

C++11 has no standard forced interruption facility. The chapter builds an interruptible_thread interface around std::thread and a flag. A request sets the flag; cooperating code checks an interruption point and throws thread_interrupted where ordinary stack unwinding can preserve its invariants.

The constructor uses a promise/future handshake to publish the address of the new thread’s thread_local flag before returning. That synchronizes publication, but does not extend the flag’s lifetime: if the thread exits, a later interrupt can dereference freed TLS state. A complete design needs synchronized shared ownership or another proven lifetime protocol, not just an unchecked raw pointer.

Choose safe interruption points

Between independent items is often appropriate. Throwing midway through an unprotected invariant update is not. RAII can release locks and resources while unwinding, but application state still needs its documented exception guarantee.

Cancellation remains cooperative: an atomic flag cannot force an uninterruptible system call to return, release a mutex held elsewhere, or make a long item finish sooner. A stop request does not itself join a thread or make its output safe to read.

Modern context: C++20 std::jthread and stop_token offer standard cooperative stop-state ownership and request mechanisms. They do not asynchronously kill threads, insert interruption points into arbitrary code, or automatically cancel every blocking API. The book’s exception-based mechanism is a historical teaching design, not the semantics of stop_token.
9.2.3–9.2.5 / Interruptible waitspp. 291–297

A notification can arrive before anyone is waiting.

The broken condition-variable attempt

Listing 9.10 checks the stop flag, registers a condition variable, waits, unregisters, then checks again. A request between the last check and wait can send a notification that has no waiter. Notifications are not stored, so the thread may sleep indefinitely. An exception also skips manual unregistration.

Timed waits plus RAII registration

Listing 9.11 unregisters with a destructor and uses short timed waits, ensuring a missed stop notification can be detected on a later timeout. The predicate overload keeps checking both cancellation and the application condition under the caller’s lock. This trades periodic wakeups for a simpler protocol.

The printed flag must be initialized false in C++11. A nominal 1 ms polling interval is not a hard response bound or a guaranteed average of 0.5 ms: scheduling, timer granularity, mutex reacquisition, work already underway, and cleanup can dominate.

Coordinate the unlock-and-wait boundary

condition_variable_any accepts a custom lock. Listing 9.12 combines the caller’s lock with the interruption-state mutex so notification registration remains protected through the transition into waiting. The wait releases both through the composite unlock; reacquisition uses std::lock to avoid a simple lock-order inversion.

The registration is cleared while protected when the custom lock is destroyed. This closes the demonstrated notification gap, but the application still needs predicate loops for spurious wakes and a full lifetime/exception analysis of the custom locking protocol.

Other waits need their own cancellation semantics

The future-polling fragment has syntax/API errors and must also account for deferred futures: wait_for on a deferred task does not start it. Decide whether to execute it, reject it, or use a different API; calling get may execute an uninterruptible task. Abandoning a wait does not cancel the task producing the result, and an async future’s last release may still block.

Likewise, ordinary mutex acquisition is not made cancelable by a flag. Timed-lock retries or application-specific wakeups can be used where available, but cancellation must not violate lock ownership or data invariants.

9.2.6–9.2.7 / Handling stop & shutting downpp. 297–299

Request everyone. Then join everyone.

Handle thread_interrupted like any other exception, or catch it in the launch wrapper so it ends only that thread rather than escaping to std::thread and terminating the process. Unrelated exceptions still need an explicit policy.

The shown flag is sticky: catching interruption does not clear it. Continuing to another interruption point will throw again even without a second request. Reusing the same mechanism for multiple independent tasks needs a separately designed reset, masking, or per-task stop-state protocol.

In the filesystem indexer outline, background threads check for interruption between changes and update work. Shutdown first requests all workers to stop, then joins all of them. This lets cleanup overlap instead of delaying each request until the previous worker has exited.

Three checks before calling join

  1. Can the worker actually leave its current wait? A blocking filesystem API needs its own wakeup or cancellation mechanism.
  2. Am I holding a lock or resource the worker needs to finish? Joining while holding config_mutex can deadlock if the worker needs that mutex.
  3. Is every thread and stop state still owned correctly, including partial startup failure, detach, repeated requests, and natural early exit?

A complete shutdown protocol also prevents new submissions and preserves referenced queues/configuration until all active accesses have ended. Thread termination, cancellation request, and successful application-level completion are distinct events.

Listing 9.1 · The simplest thread pool

Requires join_threads from Chapter 8 and a compatible thread_safe_queue with nonblocking try_pop. A zero hardware_concurrency hint creates no workers; provide a nonzero policy. Destruction stops worker loops, joins active workers, and abandons queued tasks rather than draining them. Uncaught task exceptions terminate the process. Starting a temporary thread inside vector::push_back is unsafe if insertion throws: reserve storage before launching and use exception-safe ownership. Do not destroy the pool on one of its own workers or race destruction with submission.

Listing 9.1 · Book pp. 275
class thread_pool
{
    std::atomic_bool done;
    thread_safe_queue<std::function<void()> > work_queue;
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    join_threads joiner;
    void worker_thread()
    {
        while(!done)
        {
            std::function<void()> task;
            if(work_queue.try_pop(task))
            {
                task();
            }
            else
            {
                std::this_thread::yield();
            }
        }
    }
public:
    thread_pool():
        done(false),joiner(threads)
    {
        unsigned const thread_count=std::thread::hardware_concurrency();
        try
        {
            for(unsigned i=0;i<thread_count;++i)
            {
                threads.push_back(
                    std::thread(&thread_pool::worker_thread,this));
            }
        }
        catch(...)
        {
            done=true;
            throw;
        }
    }
    ~thread_pool()
    {
        done=true;
    }
    template<typename FunctionType>
    void submit(FunctionType f)
    {
        work_queue.push(std::function<void()>(f));
    }
};

Listing 9.2 · Move-only tasks and result futures

A replacement wrapper plus partial pool class; merge omitted members/constructor with the earlier version instead of concatenating definitions. The wrapper is intended here for rvalue tasks: its template uses std::move rather than a general decay/forward design and is not a robust arbitrary-callable wrapper. Never invoke an empty or moved-from wrapper. packaged_task captures callable exceptions, but queue/allocation failures still need handling. Destroying queued, unexecuted packaged tasks makes their futures report broken_promise; it does not run them. std::result_of is historical C++11 syntax (removed in C++20); modern code generally uses invoke_result.

Listing 9.2 · Book pp. 277–278
class function_wrapper
{
    struct impl_base {
        virtual void call()=0;
        virtual ~impl_base() {}
    };
    std::unique_ptr<impl_base> impl;
    template<typename F>
    struct impl_type: impl_base
    {
        F f;
        impl_type(F&& f_): f(std::move(f_)) {}
        void call() { f(); }
    };
public:
    template<typename F>
    function_wrapper(F&& f):
        impl(new impl_type<F>(std::move(f)))
    {}
    void operator()() { impl->call(); }
    function_wrapper() = default;
    function_wrapper(function_wrapper&& other):
        impl(std::move(other.impl))
    {}
    function_wrapper& operator=(function_wrapper&& other)
    {
        impl=std::move(other.impl);
        return *this;
    }
    function_wrapper(const function_wrapper&)=delete;
    function_wrapper(function_wrapper&)=delete;
    function_wrapper& operator=(const function_wrapper&)=delete;
};
class thread_pool
{
    thread_safe_queue<function_wrapper> work_queue;
    void worker_thread()
    {
        while(!done)
        {
            function_wrapper task;
            if(work_queue.try_pop(task))
            {
                task();
            }
            else
            {
                std::this_thread::yield();
            }
        }
    }
public:
    template<typename FunctionType>
    std::future<typename std::result_of<FunctionType()>::type>
        submit(FunctionType f)
    {
        typedef typename std::result_of<FunctionType()>::type
            result_type;
        std::packaged_task<result_type()> task(std::move(f));
        std::future<result_type> res(task.get_future());
        work_queue.push(std::move(task));
        return res;
    }
    // rest as before
};

Listing 9.3 · Accumulation using waitable tasks

Requires the nullary-task pool and accumulate_block from Chapter 8. The printed submission omits the block boundaries: submit a zero-argument bound callable, such as std::bind(accumulate_block<Iterator,T>(),block_start,block_end). Select a grain size based on measurements; 25 is a teaching constant. Requires multipass iterators and suitable arithmetic identity/associativity; regrouped floating-point sums can differ. Pool shutdown must finish all running tasks before borrowed range state expires.

Listing 9.3 · Book pp. 279
template<typename Iterator,typename T>
T parallel_accumulate(Iterator first,Iterator last,T init)
{
    unsigned long const length=std::distance(first,last);
    if(!length)
        return init;
    unsigned long const block_size=25;
    unsigned long const num_blocks=(length+block_size-1)/block_size;
    std::vector<std::future<T> > futures(num_blocks-1);
    thread_pool pool;
    Iterator block_start=first;
    for(unsigned long i=0;i<(num_blocks-1);++i)
    {
        Iterator block_end=block_start;
        std::advance(block_end,block_size);
        futures[i]=pool.submit(accumulate_block<Iterator,T>());
        block_start=block_end;
    }
    T last_result=accumulate_block<Iterator,T>()(block_start,last);
    T result=init;
    for(unsigned long i=0;i<(num_blocks-1);++i)
    {
        result+=futures[i].get();
    }
    result += last_result;
    return result;
}

Listing 9.4 · Executing one pending task

Add a matching public declaration to the waitable pool. A caller may execute arbitrary queued work, not only its own dependency. Helping does not solve cycles, waits on external resources, or locks held across nested execution. Worker exception/lifetime policy still applies.

Listing 9.4 · Book pp. 281
void thread_pool::run_pending_task()
{
    function_wrapper task;
    if(work_queue.try_pop(task))
    {
        task();
    }
    else
    {
        std::this_thread::yield();
    }
}

Listing 9.5 · Quicksort that helps while waiting

Requires the waitable pool with run_pending_task. The printed !new_lower.wait_for(...) == timeout is invalid for the scoped future_status enumeration. Replace the entire test with new_lower.wait_for(std::chrono::seconds(0)) != std::future_status::ready. This is an algorithm-specific wait loop, not a general deadlock proof. Reentrant tasks, exceptions, task graph cycles, adversarial partitions, and pool shutdown all need review.

Listing 9.5 · Book pp. 281–282
template<typename T>
struct sorter
{
    thread_pool pool;

    std::list<T> do_sort(std::list<T>& chunk_data)
    {
        if(chunk_data.empty())
        {
            return chunk_data;
        }
        std::list<T> result;
        result.splice(result.begin(),chunk_data,chunk_data.begin());
        T const& partition_val=*result.begin();
        typename std::list<T>::iterator divide_point=
            std::partition(chunk_data.begin(),chunk_data.end(),
                           [&](T const& val){return val<partition_val;});
        std::list<T> new_lower_chunk;
        new_lower_chunk.splice(new_lower_chunk.end(),
                               chunk_data,chunk_data.begin(),
                               divide_point);
        std::future<std::list<T> > new_lower=
            pool.submit(std::bind(&sorter::do_sort,this,
                                  std::move(new_lower_chunk)));
        std::list<T> new_higher(do_sort(chunk_data));
        result.splice(result.end(),new_higher);
        while(!new_lower.wait_for(std::chrono::seconds(0)) ==
            std::future_status::timeout)
        {
            pool.run_pending_task();
        }
        result.splice(result.begin(),new_lower.get());
        return result;
    }
};
template<typename T>
std::list<T> parallel_quick_sort(std::list<T> input)
{
    if(input.empty())
    {
        return input;
    }
    sorter<T> s;
    return s.do_sort(input);
}

Listing 9.6 · Thread-local work queues

Partial replacement pool; provide remaining members, construction/shutdown, and an out-of-class definition for the static thread_local queue in C++11. The plain local queue is safe only while exclusively accessed by its owner. A class-static TLS queue identifies a thread, not a pool instance: nested/multiple pools can misroute tasks. Bind local state to the owning pool. Use std::move(f) when constructing packaged_task to support move-only callables.

Listing 9.6 · Book pp. 283–284
class thread_pool
{
    thread_safe_queue<function_wrapper> pool_work_queue;
    typedef std::queue<function_wrapper> local_queue_type;
    static thread_local std::unique_ptr<local_queue_type>
        local_work_queue;
    void worker_thread()
    {
        local_work_queue.reset(new local_queue_type);

        while(!done)
        {
            run_pending_task();
        }
    }
public:
    template<typename FunctionType>
    std::future<typename std::result_of<FunctionType()>::type>
        submit(FunctionType f)
    {
        typedef typename std::result_of<FunctionType()>::type result_type;
        std::packaged_task<result_type()> task(f);
        std::future<result_type> res(task.get_future());
        if(local_work_queue)
        {
            local_work_queue->push(std::move(task));
        }
        else
        {
            pool_work_queue.push(std::move(task));
        }
        return res;
    }
    void run_pending_task()
    {
        function_wrapper task;
        if(local_work_queue && !local_work_queue->empty())
        {
            task=std::move(local_work_queue->front());
            local_work_queue->pop();
            task();
        }
        else if(pool_work_queue.try_pop(task))
        {
            task();
        }
        else
        {
            std::this_thread::yield();
        }
    }
    // rest as before
};

Listing 9.7 · A synchronized work-stealing deque

Requires function_wrapper. The owner pushes/pops at the front (LIFO); thieves remove older tasks from the back. One mutex protects the entire deque, including both ends. This is lock-based, and opposite-end access does not remove that serialization. A successful pop/steal transfers ownership; invoke the task after releasing the queue mutex.

Listing 9.7 · Book pp. 285–286
class work_stealing_queue
{
private:
    typedef function_wrapper data_type;
    std::deque<data_type> the_queue;
    mutable std::mutex the_mutex;
public:
    work_stealing_queue()
    {}
    work_stealing_queue(const work_stealing_queue& other)=delete;
    work_stealing_queue& operator=(
        const work_stealing_queue& other)=delete;
    void push(data_type data)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(the_mutex);
        the_queue.push_front(std::move(data));
    }
    bool empty() const
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(the_mutex);
        return the_queue.empty();
    }
    bool try_pop(data_type& res)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(the_mutex);
        if(the_queue.empty())
        {
            return false;
        }
        res=std::move(the_queue.front());
        the_queue.pop_front();
        return true;
    }
    bool try_steal(data_type& res)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(the_mutex);
        if(the_queue.empty())
        {
            return false;
        }
        res=std::move(the_queue.back());
        the_queue.pop_back();
        return true;
    }
};

Listing 9.8 · A work-stealing pool

Historical teaching implementation with a startup race: workers read queues and queues.size() while the constructor is still modifying that vector. Fully construct the queue collection before launching any worker; reserving capacity alone does not remove concurrent size/access races. Also provide the two static thread_local definitions, a nonzero worker count, instance-aware TLS, move-only submission, safe thread insertion, and an explicit shutdown policy. This transcription is not a verified production pool.

Listing 9.8 · Book pp. 286–288
class thread_pool
{
    typedef function_wrapper task_type;
    std::atomic_bool done;
    thread_safe_queue<task_type> pool_work_queue;
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<work_stealing_queue> > queues;
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    join_threads joiner;
    static thread_local work_stealing_queue* local_work_queue;
    static thread_local unsigned my_index;
    void worker_thread(unsigned my_index_)
    {
        my_index=my_index_;
        local_work_queue=queues[my_index].get();
        while(!done)
        {
            run_pending_task();
        }
    }
    bool pop_task_from_local_queue(task_type& task)
    {
        return local_work_queue && local_work_queue->try_pop(task);
    }
    bool pop_task_from_pool_queue(task_type& task)
    {
        return pool_work_queue.try_pop(task);
    }
    bool pop_task_from_other_thread_queue(task_type& task)
    {
        for(unsigned i=0;i<queues.size();++i)
        {
            unsigned const index=(my_index+i+1)%queues.size();
            if(queues[index]->try_steal(task))
            {
                return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }
public:
    thread_pool():
        done(false),joiner(threads)
    {
        unsigned const thread_count=std::thread::hardware_concurrency();
        try
        {
            for(unsigned i=0;i<thread_count;++i)
            {
                queues.push_back(std::unique_ptr<work_stealing_queue>(
                                     new work_stealing_queue));
                threads.push_back(
                    std::thread(&thread_pool::worker_thread,this,i));
            }
        }
        catch(...)
        {
            done=true;
            throw;
        }
    }
    ~thread_pool()
    {
        done=true;
    }
    template<typename FunctionType>
    std::future<typename std::result_of<FunctionType()>::type> submit(
        FunctionType f)
    {
        typedef typename std::result_of<FunctionType()>::type result_type;
        std::packaged_task<result_type()> task(f);
        std::future<result_type> res(task.get_future());
        if(local_work_queue)
        {
            local_work_queue->push(std::move(task));
        }
        else
        {
            pool_work_queue.push(std::move(task));
        }
        return res;
    }
    void run_pending_task()
    {
        task_type task;
        if(pop_task_from_local_queue(task) ||
           pop_task_from_pool_queue(task) ||
           pop_task_from_other_thread_queue(task))
        {
            task();
        }
        else
        {
            std::this_thread::yield();
        }
    }
};

Listing 9.9 · Launching an interruptible thread

Incomplete interface and lifetime sketch. The promise publishes the worker TLS flag address before the constructor returns, but the worker may already have exited, leaving a dangling pointer. An unsynchronized “clear the pointer” is not enough; use a properly synchronized shared-lifetime stop state. Supply join/detach/move/destructor semantics and exception handling. The later wrapper catches interruption, not arbitrary failures.

Listing 9.9 · Book pp. 290
class interrupt_flag
{
public:
    void set();
    bool is_set() const;
};
thread_local interrupt_flag this_thread_interrupt_flag;
class interruptible_thread
{
    std::thread internal_thread;
    interrupt_flag* flag;
public:
    template<typename FunctionType>
    interruptible_thread(FunctionType f)
    {
        std::promise<interrupt_flag*> p;
        internal_thread=std::thread([f,&p]{
                p.set_value(&this_thread_interrupt_flag);
                f();
            });
        flag=p.get_future().get();
    }
    void interrupt()
    {
        if(flag)
        {
            flag->set();
        }
    }
};

Listing 9.10 · The deliberately broken condition-variable wait

Intentionally broken. A stop notification between the last check and actual wait can be lost, leaving the thread asleep forever. If wait exits exceptionally, the raw registration also remains stale. RAII fixes registration cleanup but does not close the notification gap by itself.

Listing 9.10 · Book pp. 292
void interruptible_wait(std::condition_variable& cv,
                        std::unique_lock<std::mutex>& lk)
{
    interruption_point();
    this_thread_interrupt_flag.set_condition_variable(cv);
    cv.wait(lk);
    this_thread_interrupt_flag.clear_condition_variable();
    interruption_point();
}

Listing 9.11 · Timed condition-variable interruption

Initialize flag(false) explicitly for C++11 objects; the printed constructor initializes only thread_cond. Supply the TLS declaration before references to it (for example an extern thread_local declaration after a forward declaration of interrupt_flag), and provide interruption_point/thread_interrupted. The RAII guard unregisters on exit; periodic waits recover from a missed stop notification. A 1 ms timeout is not a maximum real response latency: scheduling, mutex reacquisition, user work, and cleanup can delay progress.

Listing 9.11 · Book pp. 293–294
class interrupt_flag
{
    std::atomic<bool> flag;
    std::condition_variable* thread_cond;
    std::mutex set_clear_mutex;
public:
    interrupt_flag():
        thread_cond(0)
    {}
    void set()
    {
        flag.store(true,std::memory_order_relaxed);
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(set_clear_mutex);
        if(thread_cond)
        {
            thread_cond->notify_all();
        }
    }
    bool is_set() const
    {
        return flag.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
    }
    void set_condition_variable(std::condition_variable& cv)
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(set_clear_mutex);
        thread_cond=&cv;
    }
    void clear_condition_variable()
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(set_clear_mutex);
        thread_cond=0;
    }
    struct clear_cv_on_destruct
    {
        ~clear_cv_on_destruct()
        {
            this_thread_interrupt_flag.clear_condition_variable();
        }
    };
};
void interruptible_wait(std::condition_variable& cv,
                        std::unique_lock<std::mutex>& lk)
{
    interruption_point();
    this_thread_interrupt_flag.set_condition_variable(cv);
    interrupt_flag::clear_cv_on_destruct guard;
    interruption_point();
    cv.wait_for(lk,std::chrono::milliseconds(1));
    interruption_point();
}

Listing 9.12 · Condition_variable_any and a composite lock

Partial interrupt_flag replacement. Initialize flag(false), supply the omitted members and TLS declarations, and enter with the caller lock already held. The composite lock coordinates notification registration with the atomic unlock-and-wait phase; reacquisition uses std::lock for the internal mutex plus caller lock. The internal registration is cleared while protected. Spurious wakeups still require an application predicate loop. Nested waits, lock exceptions, lifetime, and callback reentrancy need a full audit.

Listing 9.12 · Book pp. 294–296
class interrupt_flag
{
    std::atomic<bool> flag;
    std::condition_variable* thread_cond;
    std::condition_variable_any* thread_cond_any;
    std::mutex set_clear_mutex;
public:
    interrupt_flag():
        thread_cond(0),thread_cond_any(0)
    {}
    void set()
    {
        flag.store(true,std::memory_order_relaxed);
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(set_clear_mutex);
        if(thread_cond)
        {
            thread_cond->notify_all();
        }
        else if(thread_cond_any)
        {
            thread_cond_any->notify_all();
        }
    }
    template<typename Lockable>
    void wait(std::condition_variable_any& cv,Lockable& lk)
    {
        struct custom_lock
        {
            interrupt_flag* self;
            Lockable& lk;
            custom_lock(interrupt_flag* self_,
                        std::condition_variable_any& cond,
                        Lockable& lk_):
                self(self_),lk(lk_)
            {
                self->set_clear_mutex.lock();
                self->thread_cond_any=&cond;
            }
            void unlock()
            {
                lk.unlock();
                self->set_clear_mutex.unlock();
            }
            void lock()
            {
                std::lock(self->set_clear_mutex,lk);
            }
            ~custom_lock()
            {
                self->thread_cond_any=0;
                self->set_clear_mutex.unlock();
            }
        };
        custom_lock cl(this,cv,lk);
        interruption_point();
        cv.wait(cl);
        interruption_point();
    }
    // rest as before
};
template<typename Lockable>
void interruptible_wait(std::condition_variable_any& cv,
                        Lockable& lk)
{
    this_thread_interrupt_flag.wait(cv,lk);
}

Listing 9.13 · Stopping filesystem background workers

An application outline with placeholder filesystem/GUI APIs. The shown one-callable interruptible_thread constructor does not accept (function,disk_id); bind the argument or supply a suitable forwarding constructor. vector storage needs move support and startup-failure cleanup. Request stop on every worker before joining any, but do not hold config_mutex while joining if a worker might need it. A blocking get_fs_changes must itself support wakeup/cancellation or a bounded polling policy—an interruption point before it cannot interrupt that blocking call.

Listing 9.13 · Book pp. 298–299
std::mutex config_mutex;
std::vector<interruptible_thread> background_threads;
void background_thread(int disk_id)
{
    while(true)
    {
        interruption_point();
        fs_change fsc=get_fs_changes(disk_id);
        if(fsc.has_changes())
        {
            update_index(fsc);
        }
    }
}
void start_background_processing()
{
    background_threads.push_back(
        interruptible_thread(background_thread,disk_1));
    background_threads.push_back(
        interruptible_thread(background_thread,disk_2));
}
int main()
{
    start_background_processing();
    process_gui_until_exit();
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(config_mutex);
    for(unsigned i=0;i<background_threads.size();++i)
    {
        background_threads[i].interrupt();
    }
    for(unsigned i=0;i<background_threads.size();++i)
    {
        background_threads[i].join();
    }
}

Additional unnumbered examples

All seven standalone supporting fragments are included below. The join_threads dependency remains embedded in Chapter 8, and pool queue implementations are discussed in Chapter 6; choose a compatible queue rather than assuming every earlier revision is interchangeable.

The interruptible-thread interface

Interface sketch only. Join, detach, destruction, move operations, and stop-state ownership must be designed together; std::thread itself has no interrupt() member.

Book p. 289 · unnumbered example
class interruptible_thread
{
public:
    template<typename FunctionType>
    interruptible_thread(FunctionType f);
    void join();
    void detach();
    bool joinable() const;
    void interrupt();
};

An explicit interruption point

Requires the current thread’s flag and a user-defined thread_interrupted exception type. A stop request is acted on only when cooperating code checks it. Call only where stack unwinding preserves invariants.

Book p. 291 · unnumbered example
void interruption_point()
{
    if(this_thread_interrupt_flag.is_set())
    {
        throw thread_interrupted();
    }
}

Checking between items

done and process_next_item are application placeholders. A long or uninterruptible item makes the interval between checks long regardless of how quickly the flag was set.

Book p. 291 · unnumbered example
void foo()
{
    while(!done)
    {
        interruption_point();
        process_next_item();
    }
}

A timed predicate wait

Overload for the initialized flag/registration machinery from Listing 9.11. The predicate is evaluated with the caller mutex held. A cancellation may race a true predicate; define which outcome your application wants. Polling adds wakeups and no hard deadline guarantee.

Book p. 294 · unnumbered example
template<typename Predicate>
void interruptible_wait(std::condition_variable& cv,
                        std::unique_lock<std::mutex>& lk,
                        Predicate pred)
{
    interruption_point();
    this_thread_interrupt_flag.set_condition_variable(cv);
    interrupt_flag::clear_cv_on_destruct guard;
    while(!this_thread_interrupt_flag.is_set() && !pred())
    {
        cv.wait_for(lk,std::chrono::milliseconds(1));
    }
    interruption_point();
}

Polling a future for interruption

The printed uf.wait_for(lk,std::chrono::milliseconds(1)==... is malformed: use uf.wait_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(1)) == std::future_status::ready. No lock argument belongs here. Handle future_status::deferred explicitly: repeatedly polling a deferred future never executes its task. This helper only waits, not get(), and stopping the wait does not cancel the producer. Releasing an async future may still wait for its task.

Book p. 296 · unnumbered example
template<typename T>
void interruptible_wait(std::future<T>& uf)
{
   while(!this_thread_interrupt_flag.is_set())
   {
       if(uf.wait_for(lk,std::chrono::milliseconds(1)==
           std::future_status::ready)
           break;
   }
   interruption_point();
}

Handling interruption as an exception

A partial try/catch block with application placeholders. An exception is a control-flow request, not forced thread termination. The flag remains set in this design, so future interruption points keep throwing unless a separately designed reset/disable policy exists.

Book p. 297 · unnumbered example
try
{
    do_something();
}
catch(thread_interrupted&)
{
    handle_interruption();
}

Catching interruption at the thread boundary

Replacement launch expression, not a standalone thread class. Catch thread_interrupted before it escapes the std::thread entry function. Other unhandled exceptions still terminate the process. This does not fix the TLS pointer lifetime or missing thread ownership operations in Listing 9.9.

Book p. 297–298 · unnumbered example
internal_thread=std::thread([f,&p]{
        p.set_value(&this_thread_interrupt_flag);
        try
        {
            f();
        }
        catch(thread_interrupted const&)
        {}
    });
9.3 / Check your understandingp. 299

Own resources. Schedule dependencies. Cooperate on stop.

Why can a pool deadlock on an acyclic task graph?

All workers can be blocked in parent tasks waiting for queued children. The graph need not contain a cycle; the missing resource is an available worker. Helping or a nonblocking dependency strategy can address this pattern.

Why not store packaged_task in C++11 std::function?

packaged_task is move-only, while that std::function interface requires a copyable target. The book uses an owning move-only type-erased wrapper instead.

Does setting done drain the task queue?

Not in the printed pools. Workers finish current work and stop checking for more; queued tasks can be abandoned. Define draining, cancellation, future completion, and submission rejection explicitly.

What does work stealing solve—and not solve?

It makes runnable tasks hidden on another worker’s queue available to an idle worker. It does not automatically break dependency cycles, unblock I/O, or release workers already asleep on ordinary futures.

Why is notify_all plus a stop flag insufficient?

If notification occurs before the wait begins, no notification is saved for the future waiter. The stop-check and wait transition need a coordinated protocol, or a timeout-based retry strategy.

Why does the constructor handshake not fix flag lifetime?

It publishes a TLS address safely, but the worker can exit and destroy that TLS object before a later interrupt call. Publication and lifetime are separate proof obligations.

Why request all stops before joining any worker?

It lets all workers reach safe interruption points and clean up concurrently. A join is a completion wait, not a stop request, and should not hold a lock required by a worker.

Chapter in one sentence

A useful executor and a safe stop protocol must account for who owns each thread, who can execute each dependency, and how every participant reaches a finished state.
