Chapter 10 / Illustrated summary

Testing & debugging
multithreaded applications.

A passing run is evidence about one execution—not a proof about every schedule. Build small tests, control the conditions, and state precisely what your evidence covers.

PRINTED PAGES 300–314PDF PAGES 323–3371 LISTING · NO NUMBERED FIGURES
The central idea

Test the harness as carefully as the concurrent component. Review invariants, explore adversarial schedules, preserve lifetime on failures, and measure performance separately from correctness.

10.1 / Classes of concurrency bugspp. 301–303

A hang and a bad result need different investigations.

Unwanted blocking

A required operation cannot proceed: threads may form a deadlock, all workers may wait for queued dependencies, or a thread may wait indefinitely for external input that never arrives.

Livelock & starvation

Threads may keep retrying or reacting without useful completion. Distinguish system-wide lack of progress from one thread starving while others complete. High CPU usage is a clue, not proof of livelock.

Data races

Conflicting accesses to the same memory location, at least one non-atomic, without the required happens-before ordering produce undefined behavior. Atomicity of one flag does not automatically protect nearby ordinary data.

Logical races & lifetime

Individually synchronized operations can still violate a larger invariant. A thread can also outlive its borrowed data, access a reclaimed node, or skip required cleanup when an exception changes the control flow.

A race condition is broader than a data race: the order of otherwise legal operations can determine an incorrect outcome. Which worker gets a task is often intentionally nondeterministic; duplicate removal, stale observations, broken temporal ordering, or a lost update are not.

The chapter groups spin-based no-progress behavior under livelock. More precisely, a spin wait can participate in a deadlock too; the defining question is what progress or dependency protocol fails, not whether the CPU is busy.

Symptoms can occur far from the cause

A corrupted pointer may fail much later in unrelated code. For a hang, capture all thread stacks, ownership and wait relationships, pool queue state, and pending external operations. For corruption, trace object ownership and earlier conflicting accesses rather than assuming the crashing line caused the damage.

10.2.1 / Review as a concurrency toolpp. 303–305

Explain why every shared access is safe.

A quick style review is not a concurrency review. Give an independent reviewer enough time to reconstruct the synchronization argument. Explaining the code line by line—even in written notes or to a rubber duck—can expose assumptions hidden by familiarity.

  1. Inventory shared state. Which objects, aliases, references, callbacks, globals, and library-internal state can more than one thread access?
  2. Name the protection. Which mutex, ownership transfer, atomic operation, or happens-before relation permits each access?
  3. Place the other threads. What can they be doing at this point? Which locks can they hold, and which order do they acquire them in?
  4. Prove required ordering. If one action must occur before another, what actually enforces that requirement?
  5. Revalidate observations. Is a previously loaded value still current? Is its object still alive? Did releasing and reacquiring a lock invalidate the assumption?
  6. Assume an adversary. Suppose another thread changes or destroys this data right here. What prevents that execution?
  7. Walk exceptional exits. Can an exception skip a join, leave a waiter asleep, retain a stale registration, or expose partially updated state?

Holding one mutex is not proof that every access is protected: if an object changes protection domains, demonstrate the handoff between them. Escaped references and public state deserve particular scrutiny.

Thread-safe methods need not compose

Calling empty(), top(), and pop() as separately locked operations can leave a gap in which another thread changes the structure. Review the whole logical transaction. A combined operation under one protection boundary can be safer than adding more checks around the split interface.

10.2.2–10.2.3 / Scenarios & testabilitypp. 305–308

Test the smallest meaningful concurrent boundary.

Exercise the queue directly before relying on an end-to-end application test to diagnose its push/pop behavior. Start with a sequential baseline, then vary the number and roles of threads, initial state, available processors, and target architecture.

A failure with only one thread establishes an ordinary bug worth fixing, but a pass in that configuration does not establish concurrent correctness. Likewise, a failure disappearing on one core is a clue—not proof of a race or a specific memory-ordering fault. Time-sliced threads can interleave incorrectly on a single core, and data races remain undefined behavior regardless of the core count.

A queue scenario matrix

Initial stateActorsWhat to verify
EmptyOne push, one popBlocking pop returns the inserted value; after both complete, the queue is empty.
Empty or populatedMultiple producersNo loss or duplication; every successfully inserted value is accounted for.
Empty or insufficient itemsMultiple consumersDefined empty/blocking behavior; no double removal; a safe way to finish waiting consumers.
Full, if boundedMultiple producers, with/without consumersCapacity and backpressure semantics; cancellation or closure releases blocked callers correctly.
Empty, partially full, or fullMultiple producers and consumersAccounting and ordering guarantees, safety under overlap, and eventual completion under stated assumptions.

“Full” is meaningful only for a bounded queue. Match the test to the API’s actual contract. A nonblocking pop racing one push can legally find no item, leaving one queued afterward, or consume the item and leave the queue empty. Do not assert only one outcome unless synchronization forces that ordering.

Separate state transformations from communication

Keep responsibilities clear and functions small. Test pure transformations and per-thread state transitions with ordinary single-threaded inputs. Test routing, synchronization, ownership transfer, and shared-state updates separately with deliberately simple payload logic.

Provide control over external dependencies, clocks, inputs, and test hooks where appropriate. Avoid adding global synchronization that serializes the very operation being tested. Library calls may hide shared state, so include their thread-safety contracts in the review.

10.2.4 / How to expose bad schedulespp. 308–310

Combine methods; no single green check is enough.

Stress testing

Repeat small tests with varied thread counts, contention, workloads, and environments. Useful for finding failures, but repeated passes are weak evidence when the harness or hardware never permits the problematic execution.

Systematic exploration

Explore permitted schedules and memory behaviors with a suitable simulator/model checker. State-space explosion favors small components. A result is exhaustive only within the supported model, inputs, bounds, and properties actually checked.

Instrumented execution

Detect observed races, invalid lock usage, missing protection, or potential lock-order cycles. Tool coverage and the exercised paths matter. Instrumentation changes timing, so absence of a report is not proof of correctness.

Controlled scheduling

Use gates and explicit hooks to place threads near a critical boundary, then deliberately explore legal orderings. A start gate removes startup skew but does not force instruction-level overlap or enumerate all schedules.

The chapter describes specialized checking libraries and simulation tools conceptually. As a modern addition, ThreadSanitizer can detect many dynamically observed data races, while AddressSanitizer can help expose memory errors in separate suitable builds. Neither establishes linearizability, freedom from all deadlocks, or correctness of arbitrary weak-memory algorithms. Use tool-specific build/runtime guidance rather than assuming sanitizers are interchangeable or universally combinable.

Architectures differ in ordering, coherence, and instruction mapping; compiler transformations matter too. A program that appears sound on x86 can still violate the C++ memory model. The book’s instruction-mapping examples are historical, not a portable rule about every atomic load today.

The source’s “guaranteed” exhaustive-testing language is conditional: the implementation must be modeled faithfully, the relevant executions must be explored, and the property must be checked. A sequentially consistent interleaving model alone does not cover all relaxed-atomic behaviors or undefined ordinary accesses.
Interactive study aid / A tiny schedule explorerOriginal illustration

Six schedules, one lost-update bug.

Two workers each increment a counter starting at zero. In the split version, each worker does an atomic load followed by an atomic store of its saved value plus one. Every access is atomic, so this example has no data race—but the compound increment is not indivisible.

This enumerates a finite sequentially consistent symbolic model, not real browser threads, ordinary unsynchronized C++ increments, or the entire C++ memory model. The six split schedules preserve each worker’s load-before-store order. fetch_add is modeled as one indivisible update.

Both serialized split schedules end at 2. The other four end at 1 because both workers save zero before either store. A harness that permits only serialized execution can run forever without exposing this logical race. Changing the shared counter to an atomic is not enough; choose the atomic operation that matches the invariant.

10.2.5 / Structuring the testpp. 311–313

Arrange. Signal ready. Release. Observe.

  1. General setup: construct the shared queue and synchronization objects.
  2. Per-thread setup: prepare each worker’s input, then publish that it has reached the start boundary.
  3. Concurrent work: both workers wait on copies of one shared go future; the controller releases them only after both report ready.
  4. Completion and assertions: retrieve all task results, then check the component’s final state.

Listing 10.1 uses explicit launch::async so a default-policy deferred task cannot leave the controller waiting forever for its ready signal. Result futures are declared outside the try block so an exceptional exit can release the go gate before last-release waits for async tasks occur.

A ready signal proves a worker reached the boundary; it does not prove both workers are already asleep in wait() or will execute the queue calls simultaneously. That is fine for this gate: shared-future readiness is persistent, unlike a bare condition-variable notification.

The harness also needs failure semantics

The catch block calls go.set_value() unconditionally, even if the normal path already released it. If a later get() throws, the second set_value() throws promise_already_satisfied and can mask the original failure. Track whether the gate was released or use an idempotent gate abstraction.

Releasing the start gate does not unblock a consumer if a producer fails before producing an item. Async-future cleanup may then wait indefinitely. A robust negative test needs queue close/cancel semantics, failure injection designed around that contract, or an external process watchdog—not just a catch block or wait_for followed by destruction of a still-running async future.

Do not put the essential pop_done.get() inside assert in a test intended to run with NDEBUG: the entire expression disappears. Retrieve the result unconditionally, then check it with a test assertion mechanism enabled in the test build. Separately retrieve all task outcomes when diagnosing multiple failures.

The start barrier itself creates ordering and affects which executions are reachable. It is useful for startup coordination but not a substitute for targeted internal hooks, a reference model, or a linearizability argument. Test your assertion and timeout paths, not only the successful path.
Source notebook / Listing 10.1p. 312

The chapter’s source example, embedded.

This is the chapter’s only numbered code listing. It has no additional standalone code snippets, numbered figures, or numbered tables. The review matrix and schedule explorer above are original study aids, not reproduced book figures. PDF transcription normalizes whitespace and omits callout markers; the printed code and its limitations are retained.

Listing 10.1 · Concurrent push and pop on an empty queue

Requires headers for future/assert and a threadsafe_queue<int> whose pop() blocks and returns int by value. Earlier queue versions do not all have this exact API; use an explicit adapter if needed. The test assumes a functioning nonthrowing int enqueue/dequeue path. Fix the double-release exception path and assertion side effect for a reusable harness; design an explicit abort protocol for worker failures. This printed example does not guarantee instruction-level overlap or a bounded finish time.

Listing 10.1 · Book p. 312
void test_concurrent_push_and_pop_on_empty_queue()
{
    threadsafe_queue<int> q;
    std::promise<void> go,push_ready,pop_ready;
    std::shared_future<void> ready(go.get_future());
    std::future<void> push_done;
    std::future<int> pop_done;
    try
    {
        push_done=std::async(std::launch::async,
                             [&q,ready,&push_ready]()
                             {
                                 push_ready.set_value();
                                 ready.wait();
                                 q.push(42);
                             }
            );
        pop_done=std::async(std::launch::async,
                            [&q,ready,&pop_ready]()
                            {
                                pop_ready.set_value();
                                ready.wait();
                                return q.pop();
                            }
            );
        push_ready.get_future().wait();
        pop_ready.get_future().wait();
        go.set_value();
        push_done.get();
        assert(pop_done.get()==42);
        assert(q.empty());
    }
    catch(...)
    {
        go.set_value();
        throw;
    }
}
10.2.6 / Performance testingp. 314

Draw the scaling curve, not one impressive number.

Measure the goal: elapsed time, throughput, latency distribution, responsiveness, or resource consumption. Compare with a correct sequential baseline and a one-worker configuration; increasing worker count is not itself a success metric.

Vary the workload and processor configuration, from one worker/core up to the largest relevant system you can test. Record how serial work, contention, scheduling, and memory behavior change the curve. Revisit Chapter 8’s Amdahl model to understand an ideal ceiling, not to manufacture an expected benchmark result.

A practical measurement checklist

  1. Record hardware, compiler flags, build mode, worker count, dataset, CPU constraints, and relevant background load.
  2. Use a monotonic elapsed-time clock, representative workloads, and repeated trials; separate setup/warm-up from the region being studied when appropriate.
  3. Retain observable results so optimization cannot erase the measured work. Validate correctness outside or alongside the timed region.
  4. Report variability and latency tails, not only the fastest run or a mean.
  5. Measure optimized builds separately from race-detection/instrumented builds; tooling overhead changes timing and contention.
  6. Distinguish fixed-workload speedup from growing-workload throughput. Compare like-for-like and explain where scaling stops.

The chapter motivates measuring across configurations; the detailed measurement checklist here is an original extension. Do not interpret the example aspiration of “24 times faster on 24 cores” as a guarantee for a real workload.

10.3 / Check your understandingp. 314

State what was tested—and what was not.

Does a billion passing stress-test runs prove correctness?

No. The harness, platform, input, or scheduling pattern may never allow the bad execution. Repetition is useful evidence only with a clear account of coverage and limitations.

Can all accesses be atomic and the algorithm still be wrong?

Yes. Separate atomic load/store increments can overwrite each other without a data race. Correctness depends on the compound operation and invariant, not just individual accesses.

What does the shared start gate guarantee?

Each worker can reach the test boundary before the controller releases it, and no test operation passes the gate early. It does not guarantee simultaneous execution, internal overlap, or schedule exhaustiveness.

Why can the printed catch block hide the real exception?

After the gate was released normally, a second set_value() throws promise_already_satisfied. That replaces the exception the harness was trying to rethrow.

Why is a future timeout not necessarily a safe escape hatch?

A timed wait returning does not stop its task. Last-release cleanup of an async-launched task’s future can still wait, and destroying borrowed state while work runs is unsafe. Provide cancellation/closure or isolate the test behind a process watchdog.

What does exhaustive mean for a model checker?

Exhaustive within its supported semantics, modeled environment, bounds, inputs, and checked properties—not a universal proof about all program behavior or all real executions.

How do correctness and performance tests differ?

Correctness tests deliberately expose failures and check contracts. Performance tests measure representative optimized workloads under recorded conditions. Instrumentation can change the performance profile, so keep the conclusions separate.

Chapter in one sentence

Small adversarial tests, explicit synchronization arguments, controlled environments, and honest coverage claims are stronger than a large pile of unexplained passing runs.

Appendix A / Language reference

C++11 language
features in context.

The ownership, callable, and lifetime vocabulary behind the thread library: moves, captures, constant initialization, parameter packs, deduction, and per-thread state.

PRINTED PAGES 315–339PDF PAGES 338–3624 LISTINGS · NO NUMBERED FIGURES
Where we are in the book

Chapter 10 completes the numbered chapters. Appendix A supplies the C++11 language background used throughout them; it is not Chapter 11. Read the examples in their original standard-version context.

A.1 / Rvalue references & movespp. 315–319

A move is an ownership decision, not a spelling trick.

An lvalue reference normally aliases an existing object. A const lvalue reference can also bind a temporary. An ordinary non-template T&& can bind an appropriate rvalue, permitting overloads that consume or modify a resource instead of copying it.

The historical “left/right side of assignment” explanation is only a mnemonic. Modern value categories describe expression identity and permitted resource reuse more precisely; a named rvalue-reference variable is an lvalue expression when used by name.

std::move does not itself move anything

It casts its argument to an rvalue-reference expression, enabling a suitable move overload. The selected constructor or assignment performs the transfer. A const source usually cannot bind to a consuming non-const move overload and may be copied instead.

Listing A.1 contrasts allocating/copying a large buffer with stealing its pointer and clearing the source. Its raw owner is incomplete and unsafe for some uses, including copying uninitialized elements or the null moved-from state. Prefer standard ownership types or define every relevant invariant and operation deliberately.

thread, unique_lock, future, promise, packaged_task, and unique_ptr transfer resources without copying them. Moving a std::thread transfers join responsibility; it does not stop the running thread. A moved-from library object remains valid subject to its documented contract, but its contents are not universally guaranteed empty. Use only operations whose preconditions it satisfies.

Deduced T&& is different

When T is a deduced cv-unqualified function-template parameter in this form, T&& is a forwarding reference: an lvalue argument deduces T as an lvalue reference, and reference collapsing yields an lvalue reference. Rvalues deduce a non-reference T. This special rule does not apply to every spelling containing &&.

Inside that function the named parameter is still an lvalue. std::forward<T>(t) preserves the caller’s category when forwarding; unconditional std::move(t) would instead offer to consume lvalue arguments too. Forwarding across a call does not itself extend lifetime or promise reference storage inside std::thread, which normally stores decayed argument values unless a reference wrapper is used.

A.2–A.3 / Deleted & defaulted functionspp. 319–323

Make the resource contract visible to the compiler.

= delete explicitly forbids a selected function, including copies or an unwanted overload. A deleted overload still participates in overload resolution; if it wins, the call is ill-formed. This is stronger and clearer than the old private-but-undefined copy idiom.

= default asks for the compiler-defined special-member implementation where allowed. It can document intent, change accessibility, restore a constructor suppressed by another declaration, or request appropriate memberwise moves. It can still be defined as deleted when members make the operation impossible.

Declaring copy/move operations or a destructor affects which other special members are implicitly generated. The move-only Listing A.2 therefore needs an explicitly supplied default constructor before its printed default construction is valid. A correct resource type also needs a destruction, assignment, exception, and moved-from-state policy.

Defaulted does not mean zero-initialized or trivial

For the shown simple type with an in-class non-user-provided default constructor, automatic X x; leaves the int uninitialized, whereas X x{}; or X() value-initializes it to zero. Static storage has a separate zero-initialization phase. Do not read indeterminate automatic ints.

An out-of-class = default following a prior declaration makes that constructor user-provided; it does not preserve all the first-declaration-defaulting properties. The appendix’s out-of-class example blurs this distinction. Explicit member initialization is usually easier to reason about.

Version and trait cautions: the printed T& assignment return in class Y is a typo for Y&. Aggregate rules change across standards, notably in C++20. Bytewise copying and atomic<T> eligibility depend on the relevant complete type requirements (including trivial copyability), not just one trivial assignment operator. = default alone is not a universal permission for memcpy or atomic storage.
A.4 / Constant expressionspp. 324–329

Compile-time eligibility is not mandatory compile-time execution.

Array bounds and non-type template arguments are examples of contexts requiring suitable constant expressions. constexpr makes an eligible function usable in constant evaluation when the arguments and evaluation satisfy the rules. The same function can run normally with runtime arguments.

The square example gives a 25-element array for square(5); square(dummy) with a runtime dummy does not provide a portable constant array bound. Compiler extensions accepting variable-length arrays are not standard C++11.

User-defined constant values

The first CX is a literal-type illustration with a trivial default constructor. The revised CX adds a constexpr constructor and accessors, allowing make_cx, half_double, and foo_squared to form a constant computation: (10,1) → (5,2) → 7², yielding 49.

constexpr objects must have a valid constant initializer and are const. Constant initialization of eligible static-storage objects helps avoid dynamic-initialization ordering hazards for that initialization; it does not make later mutations synchronized or solve every global object lifetime problem.

Read the rules with a standard version attached

C++11 places tight restrictions on constexpr bodies and constructors. C++14 and later relax many of them. In particular, the implicit const on the appendix’s constexpr non-static accessors is a C++11 rule; add explicit const for that interface in later standards.

The appendix’s literal-type checklist is simplified and not a normative definition: a literal class need not satisfy its blanket “all members trivial / trivial copy constructor” wording. Nor is constexpr a universal purity annotation. Explain each valid constant evaluation in terms of the actual version’s rules rather than assuming every call happens at compile time.

The sum template can be used in a constant expression for ints and, in the shown C++11 setting, as a runtime operation for strings. That does not mean constexpr can be placed on any invalid template body and ignored at will. The original rejection of constexpr std::string is C++11-specific; later library support is substantially different.

A.5 / Lambda functionspp. 329–333

A short callable still has ownership and lifetime rules.

A lambda expression creates a closure object with a call operator. It can be invoked immediately, passed to an algorithm, used as a condition-variable predicate, or packaged as a thread-pool task. Its unique unnamed type can be stored with auto; std::function is an optional type-erased wrapper, not part of every lambda.

[]

No automatic-variable captures. Globals and supplied parameters remain usable. Listing A.4 reads a namespace-scope flag under a mutex, so no capture is necessary.

[=]

Default to copying automatic variables that actually need capture. A copied int is a snapshot; a copied pointer still aliases its pointee. This is not a deep copy of all reachable state.

[&]

Borrow captured locals. Calls see their current values while the objects remain alive. Returning a closure does not extend those objects’ lifetimes.

Explicit / mixed captures

[=,&j,&k], [&,j,k], or [&i,j,&k] express different ownership decisions. [this] copies a pointer, not the enclosing object; it must remain alive.

The source’s mixed-capture examples produce 1239, 5688, and 5682 after changing i/j/k to 1/2/3. The reference-offset example produces 135,135 then 111,111 as the same borrowed offset changes.

Snapshots versus borrowed state

Interactive study aid / Lambda capture model

A closure is created with offset=42 and later invoked with argument 12. Change the current offset and whether the original local is still alive.

Symbolic model of one captured int, with no actual dangling dereference and no concurrent writes. Copying a raw pointer, a reference-like view, or this would not provide the ownership guarantee shown for a copied int.

Captures do not synchronize threads. Reference captures need lifetime and access protection; value captures may still share mutable pointees. In C++11, [=] in a member function can implicitly capture this, not a snapshot of members. Explicit this capture is not ownership.

The book uses explicit trailing return types for complex lambdas. Current compilers incorporate defect resolutions and later standards broaden deduction; treat those examples as a conservative spelling, not a blanket modern restriction. C++14 also adds init-captures, including moving a unique_ptr into a closure; C++11 requires a different ownership arrangement.

A.6 / Variadic templatespp. 333–337

Expand a pattern, not just a list of types.

A parameter pack represents zero or more template parameters or function arguments. Params... can become tuple elements; Params*... forms pointer types; unique_ptr<Params>... forms a corresponding list of owners. A destination template still has its own arity requirements: std::pair needs exactly two types.

packaged_task<R(Args...)> illustrates specialization by a callable signature: R describes the result while Args describes its arguments, possibly empty. The thread constructor similarly accepts a callable plus a variable-length argument list.

std::forward<ArgTypes>(args)... expands the whole forwarding expression for each paired type and argument. Keeping that relationship intact preserves each argument’s category at the forwarded call. Naming args alone would turn each expression into an lvalue.

sizeof...(Args) counts a pack and is a constant expression. The printed count_args function, however, is not declared constexpr, so calling it is not itself a C++11 constant expression. Packs are not unlimited runtime argument lists: instantiation resources and the target callable’s valid signature still constrain use.

A.7 / auto deductionpp. 337–338

Less spelling does not mean dynamic typing.

auto deduces a compile-time type from an initializer, making long iterator types easier to use. The declaration still controls whether a value is copied or a reference retained: auto x=r makes a value, auto& y=r aliases, and qualifiers can be applied deliberately.

Plain by-value auto normally drops top-level const and references and allows array-to-pointer decay. auto& can instead bind an array without that decay. Watch the cost and semantics: auto can accidentally copy a large object, fail for a noncopyable resource, or retain a proxy object rather than the value it resembles.

Use exact types, static assertions, or an intentionally explicit declaration where an interface depends on reference/const behavior. These are the ordinary deduction examples in the source, not a complete reference for initializer-list deduction or later decltype(auto).

A.8 / Thread-local variablespp. 338–339

Per-thread is not per-task—and not unshareable.

thread_local gives a separate instance for each owning thread. It can appear at namespace scope, on a static data member, or on a block-scope variable. A function-local instance is initialized when that thread first passes its declaration; an unused instance need not be constructed.

Namespace/class TLS dynamic initialization timing has rules and implementation latitude; do not depend on one universal “at thread start” timing. Constructed TLS objects are normally destroyed as their owning thread exits, subject to the specified ordering rules. Returning from main or std::exit does not arrange orderly exit and TLS cleanup for every still-running worker.

A pointer can escape

A pointer obtained from a TLS object identifies that particular thread’s object even when another thread uses the pointer. Such access still needs a valid lifetime and the appropriate synchronization. After the owner exits, the pointer does not become a pointer to the accessing thread’s own instance; it dangles. This is the key lifetime issue in Chapter 9’s raw interrupt-flag sketch.

In a pool, a worker can run many unrelated tasks. Its thread-local state persists between them unless reset or otherwise scoped by the design. TLS does not automatically identify the pool instance either, as Chapter 9’s static local-queue examples demonstrate.

Source corrections: do not repeat static on the out-of-class definition of X::s. Also distinguish TLS initialization cases: an exception escaping initialization of a non-block thread-storage variable leads to termination, while a function-local thread_local initializer that throws can propagate and be retried on the next entry. The appendix’s blanket constructor-throws statement is too broad. Avoid throwing destructors and cross-object teardown dependencies.

Four listings and all supporting fragments.

All four numbered listings and 71 additional source passages are embedded below. Multi-page continuations are joined, whitespace normalized, typographic quotation marks converted to ASCII, and callout markers omitted. Rejected examples and printed typos remain visible with caveats. Repeated class names, alternative definitions, call-site fragments, and illustrative signatures cannot be concatenated into one program.

The appendix contains no numbered figures or tables. The capture explorer is an original study aid, not reproduced book artwork.

Listing A.1 · A resource-owning class with a move constructor

A teaching sketch, not a complete safe owning type. The int array is uninitialized; copying it before initializing its elements reads indeterminate ints in C++11. Copying from its null moved-from state is also not supported safely by this constructor. The user-declared move constructor causes the implicit copy-assignment operator to be deleted; no move-assignment operator is supplied. Prefer an appropriate standard owner, or design all special-member and moved-from contracts explicitly; mark moves noexcept when justified.

Listing A.1 · Book pp. 317
class X
{
private:
    int* data;
public:
    X():
        data(new int[1000000])
    {}
    ~X()
    {
        delete [] data;
    }
    X(const X& other):
        data(new int[1000000])
    {
        std::copy(other.data,other.data+1000000,data);
    }
    X(X&& other):
        data(other.data)
    {
        other.data=nullptr;
    }
};

Listing A.2 · A simple move-only type

my_class is a placeholder. The printed move_only m1 is ill-formed because the class declares constructors but no default constructor. Add move_only() = default; (and a complete my_class where destruction requires it) for that use. The m2 line deliberately invokes a deleted copy constructor; remove it in runnable code. Moving m1 into m3 is then permitted. Consider noexcept for these ownership moves.

Listing A.2 · Book pp. 320
class move_only
{
    std::unique_ptr<my_class> data;
public:
    move_only(const move_only&) = delete;
    move_only(move_only&& other):
        data(std::move(other.data))
    {}
    move_only& operator=(const move_only&) = delete;
    move_only& operator=(move_only&& other)
    {
        data=std::move(other.data);
        return *this;
    }
};
move_only m1;
move_only m2(m1);
move_only m3(std::move(m1));

Listing A.3 · A class with a trivial default constructor

Requires C++11 or later and is an alternative to the later constexpr CX definition. Automatic CX x; leaves its ints uninitialized; CX() value-initializes them to zero with this in-class defaulted constructor. This does not mean all constexpr-capable objects always initialize all members automatically.

Listing A.3 · Book pp. 325–326
class CX
{
private:
    int a;
    int b;
public:
    CX() = default;
    CX(int a_, int b_):
        a(a_),b(b_)
    {}
    int get_a() const
    {
        return a;
    }
    int get_b() const
    {
        return b;
    }
    int foo() const
    {
        return a+b;
    }
};

Listing A.4 · A lambda predicate with a deduced return type

Add mutex/condition_variable headers. These namespace-scope objects are statically initialized, so data_ready starts false. The producer must modify data_ready while holding the same mutex and notify appropriately. The predicate reads a global, so no capture is needed. Predicate evaluation holds m and repeats after spurious wakes; it can also be true on the initial check without waiting.

Listing A.4 · Book pp. 330
std::condition_variable cond;
bool data_ready;
std::mutex m;
void wait_for_data()
{
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m);
    cond.wait(lk,[]{return data_ready;});
}

A.9 / Check your understandingp. 339

Syntax expresses contracts; it does not replace them.

Does std::move transfer the resource?

No. It changes the expression category. A selected move operation may then transfer ownership; overload resolution can instead select a copy or reject the operation.

Why forward a named T&& parameter?

A named parameter is an lvalue expression. For a deduced forwarding reference, std::forward<T> recovers the original argument category rather than unconditionally consuming it.

Does = default initialize every int to zero?

No. Object storage duration, initialization form, member initializers, and whether a constructor is user-provided affect the outcome. Explicitly initialize state when correctness depends on its value.

Does [=] make asynchronous work self-contained?

Not necessarily. Copied pointers and views can still borrow other objects, and implicit this capture borrows the enclosing object. Captured data can also refer to shared mutable state needing synchronization.

Does constexpr always mean compile-time execution?

No. Suitable calls may be constant evaluated; other calls can run at runtime. Required constant-expression contexts enforce stricter checks, and rules vary by language version.

Does a pointer to TLS become thread-local wherever it is used?

No. It continues to point to the original owner thread’s object. Sharing it does not extend that object’s lifetime or remove the need for synchronization.

Appendix in one sentence

Understand what is moved, copied, borrowed, deduced, initialized, and destroyed before deciding whether a concurrent use is safe.

Reading the table criticallySource corrections & original context

Names correspond. Semantics must be proved.

Starting threads

Java identifier corrected from the printed java.lang.thread. A comparable role does not imply identical ownership: C++11 thread objects require explicit join/detach policy, and destroying a joinable std::thread terminates the process.

Mutual exclusion

C++ lock guards provide scoped ownership. Do not translate Java synchronized into manual lock/unlock without considering exceptions. Ordinary std::mutex is not recursive; Java intrinsic monitors are reentrant. Review lock ordering and object lifetime.

Monitors / waits for a predicate

Wait with the required lock and recheck the application predicate. Notifications are not stored as future work credits; spurious wakes are possible. Java wait releases the monitor on that object, not every lock held. C++ condition_variable uses unique_lock<mutex>; condition_variable_any supports other suitable lock types.

Atomic operations and a concurrency-aware memory model

Java volatile and C++ volatile have different concurrency meanings. C++ volatile does not make ordinary shared data race-free or establish inter-thread synchronization. This is a comparison with POSIX Threads and Boost.Thread as scoped in the text, not a claim that all C/POSIX/Boost facilities lack atomics; C11 atomics and Boost.Atomic are distinct facilities.

Thread-safe containers

C++11 standard containers are not general concurrent queues/maps. Some independent-element and read-only operations are permitted under their contracts, but structural changes require appropriate synchronization. A thread-safe operation does not automatically make a sequence of operations atomic.

Futures

Java Future is capitalized here, correcting the source. std::atomic_future never became a C++11 standard-library type; use future/shared_future as appropriate. Shared_future allows multiple observers under its contract; it does not make a referenced mutable result safe for arbitrary concurrent writes. Boost API names/options vary by version.

Thread pools

C++11 provides no standard thread-pool class. std::async is not a guaranteed bounded pool; default policy may defer execution. The N/A cells concern the compared APIs in this 2012 snapshot, not every library in their ecosystems. Choose and document resource limits, dependency waiting, result/error delivery, and shutdown behavior.

Thread interruption

These are not interchangeable “kill thread” operations. Java interruption and Boost interruption use their own cooperative protocols; POSIX cancellation has deferred/asynchronous modes and cancellation-state rules. C++11 has no std::thread::interrupt(). C++20 stop_token/jthread add cooperative stop support, not forced termination or automatic interruption of every blocking call.

What this appendix does not tell you

It does not specify fairness, lock-free progress, exception safety, scheduling policy, shutdown/draining behavior, task granularity, or cancellation latency. Consult the target API’s version-specific contract and apply the lifetime and test-design checks from Chapters 8–10.

Modern context is separate from the source: C++20 stop tokens and joining threads postdate this C++11 table; they request cooperative stop, and do not turn ordinary blocking operations into universally cancelable waits. Likewise, a table cell for std::async should never be inferred to promise a bounded worker pool.

Check your understanding / Cross-library conceptsOriginal study questions

Port the guarantees, not the spelling.

Does Java volatile translate to C++ volatile?

No. C++ volatile is not an inter-thread synchronization primitive. Choose the required atomics, ordering, or mutex protection under the C++ memory model.

Is std::atomic_future a standard C++11 type?

No. It is printed in the source table but is not a standard-library type. std::future and std::shared_future provide the relevant standard result-handle facilities, with distinct contracts.

Does N/A mean an entire ecosystem lacks that capability?

No. These cells reflect the table’s selected library scope and 2012 context. A separate library or a different standard/version can provide additional facilities.

Are thread interruption APIs interchangeable?

No. Each has rules about cooperation, cancellation points, exception delivery, masking, cleanup, and lifetime. C++11 std::thread has no interrupt member.

What should be checked when moving from Java monitors to C++ locks?

Reentrancy, exception-safe release, lock ownership and ordering, object lifetime, predicate/wait behavior, and the publication relationship for shared data. std::mutex is not a drop-in semantic replacement for an intrinsic Java monitor.

Appendix in one sentence

Use the table to locate a concept, then verify the precise contract before translating a concurrent design.

Appendix C / Complete teaching example

Messages, ownership,
and an ATM.

The full framework behind Chapter 4’s ATM: synchronized mailboxes, typed dispatch, and three collaborating state machines.

PRINTED PAGES 342–359PDF PAGES 365–38210 LISTINGS · NO NUMBERED FIGURES
The central idea

Give each service exclusive ownership of its mutable state and communicate by messages. That simplifies local synchronization—but does not automatically solve message lifetime, protocol races, distributed transactions, or shutdown.

Architecture / The Chapter 4 example completedpp. 342–359

Three owners. Three inboxes.

The appendix supplies the complete teaching source for the message-passing example introduced in Chapter 4. The driver starts an ATM coordinator, bank, and interface on separate threads, then converts keyboard input into messages for the ATM.

ATM coordinator

Owns the current interaction state, account string, collected PIN, and requested withdrawal amount. It sends requests to the bank and display/dispenser messages to the interface.

Bank machine

Owns a toy balance and answers verification, balance, and withdrawal messages. Its single run thread serializes those handlers; the ATM never reads that balance directly.

Interface machine

Consumes display and cash-issue messages and prints output. A separate output mutex prevents interleaving within the protected print sections.

Input driver

Turns i, digits, b, w, c, and q into card, PIN, balance, withdrawal, cancellation, and shutdown actions. It does not directly mutate the ATM’s state machine.

The local ownership rule reduces shared mutable business state. The mailboxes themselves are still shared synchronized objects: message passing here is implemented with mutexes, a condition variable, and copied message payloads.

“Complete ATM example” means the book’s complete demonstration, not a complete banking system. It is in-process, nondurable, unauthenticated, unbounded, and lacks transaction compensation. Never use its monetary, PIN, or cancellation behavior as a production design.
Listings C.1–C.3 / Queues & endpointspp. 342–344

The receiver owns the mailbox; senders borrow it.

A polymorphic message_base gives the queue one uniform element type. wrapped_message<T> stores the concrete payload, and shared_ptr keeps the wrapper alive while a receiving thread inspects it. The virtual destructor permits correct destruction through the base type.

push constructs and inserts a wrapper under the queue mutex, then notifies. wait_and_pop waits with a nonempty predicate, removes the oldest wrapper, and returns it. Spurious wakes are handled by the predicate; FIFO order is queue insertion order, not a global causal order across all actors and queues.

A receiver owns the queue and can convert to a sender. A sender stores only queue*: it is a send capability, not a lifetime owner. Copying one copies the address, while a default sender silently drops a message. Receivers must outlive every sender use and any active dispatcher.

Copying a message does not necessarily isolate its contents

The wrapper owns its copied payload, but pointers, references, views, and reply addresses inside that payload can still alias other objects. This API also requires copyable payloads; it does not transparently accept every move-only message.

The queue has no capacity/backpressure or explicit closed state. close_queue is an ordinary queued message interpreted by a dispatcher. Enqueueing it neither rejects later sends nor proves all prior distributed work has finished.

Listings C.4–C.5 / Dispatch chainspp. 344–348

Destruction drives the wait.

incoming.wait().handle<A>(...).handle<B>(...) builds a chain of temporary dispatchers. Chaining marks the predecessor inactive, so only the final object waits when the full expression ends. It pops messages, checks the last-added handler first, and delegates backward on a type mismatch.

A matching handler runs and ends that wait, allowing the actor to reconsider its state before waiting again. The base dispatcher recognizes close_queue and throws it. The run methods catch that sentinel exception to leave their loops.

Unmatched messages are discarded

This is not selective receive that saves unmatched messages for later. The wrapper has already been popped; if no handler recognizes it, it is destroyed and the loop waits for another. A message arriving in the wrong state can disappear, and a delayed reply can be consumed in a later state that happens to accept its type.

Elegant syntax, delicate lifetimes

The chain borrows predecessor pointers and can borrow callable state. Its usual safety depends on keeping the whole expression’s temporaries and captures alive through dispatch. Saving a returned chain past the lifetime of its predecessors can leave dangling links.

The destructors deliberately block and use noexcept(false). A thrown handler or close sentinel during existing exception unwinding can trigger termination. Marking a destructor as potentially throwing does not make a second exception during unwinding safe. For a maintainable general framework, an explicit dispatch/run operation and explicit stop result are often easier to reason about.

Listings C.6–C.9 / Message protocolpp. 348–358

The state determines what a message means.

  1. Waiting for card: accept card_inserted, remember the account, clear the PIN, and request PIN entry.
  2. Getting PIN: collect four digits, allow clearing/canceling, then send verify_pin with a reply endpoint.
  3. Verifying PIN: on pin_verified enter the action menu; on an incorrect PIN or cancellation, end the interaction.
  4. Action menu: request a balance or withdrawal, or cancel. The next state waits for the corresponding reply.
  5. Withdrawal result: approval sends issue_money and withdrawal_processed; denial displays insufficient funds. Cancellation sends cancel_withdrawal.
  6. Done processing: request card ejection and return to waiting for another card.

Balance replies display the amount and return to the menu. A PIN of 1937 is accepted by the toy bank, and one unsigned balance starts at 199. Account strings are carried but ignored by its handlers. The protocol assumes cooperating actors, not hostile clients.

Cancellation is not a transaction rollback

The bank approves a withdrawal and subtracts the amount in the same handler. The ATM may process a user cancellation before it consumes the approval. Its cancel_withdrawal message does nothing in the bank, so the balance can be debited with no cash issued by the ATM.

Even a withdrawal_processed message has an empty handler. Console output is not a confirmed physical dispense, and there is no durable commit, compensation, retry/idempotency, or reconciliation protocol.

Replies need identity, not only a type

There are no session IDs or request IDs. A delayed approval or PIN verification can arrive after cancellation and a new interaction. Depending on the receiving state, it can be dropped or wrongly accepted as the new request’s reply. Single-threaded handlers prevent simultaneous local mutation, not every temporal protocol race.

A stronger design would define per-request correlation, authorization at the bank boundary, idempotent operations, transaction status, failure recovery, and lifecycle rules. Those are requirements beyond this demonstration, not fixes implied by swapping in a faster queue.

Interactive study aid / Message-by-message ATM modelOriginal simulation

Approval can race cancellation.

Use the buttons to send a user event, process one queued bank request, or deliver one bank reply. The model makes the scheduling choice explicit. It is not the actual C++ program, real banking software, or a security test.

Try: insert card → enter 1937 → process request → deliver reply → withdraw 50 → process request → cancel → deliver reply. The balance becomes 149 while issued cash remains zero. Processing the queued cancel request will not restore the balance because its source handler is empty.

The model bundles four digit presses into one action, immediately models display/ejection instead of a third queue, and assumes all sends succeed. It retains bank requests/replies across cancellation, discards incompatible events, and reproduces the toy bank’s missing rollback. These simplifications do not prove real scheduling or transaction correctness.

Assembly & shutdown / Reading complete source carefullypp. 342–359

Complete listings still need correct assembly.

The source order introduces receiver before the dispatcher used in its inline wait body. Assemble the framework in dependency order, or separate declarations and definitions. Provide a TemplateDispatcher template declaration before its use as a return type. The interface’s iom mutex also needs a definition, along with headers such as thread, string, iostream, cstdio, and utility.

The final driver uses getchar but narrows its int result to char and has no EOF branch. In a runnable adaptation, retain int, handle EOF as an exit condition, and distinguish the prompt’s uppercase I from the switch’s lowercase i.

A close sentinel is not global quiescence

The driver posts close messages to bank, ATM, and interface before joining. These separate queues have no coordinated drain boundary. The ATM may still generate requests or output after another service has accepted its sentinel and stopped. Define whether work is abandoned, completed, or compensated before considering this an orderly application shutdown.

Thread startup and all exceptional exits need RAII ownership: a failure to create a later thread must not destroy an earlier joinable thread. Allocation, message copying, and handlers can throw; the run loops catch only close_queue. Also preserve every receiver’s lifetime until no thread or sender can access it.

Source notebook / All 10 listingspp. 342–359

The framework and ATM source, embedded.

All ten numbered listings are reproduced below. Multi-page source is joined, whitespace normalized, and annotation markers omitted. There are no additional standalone source snippets or numbered figures/tables in this appendix. Local notes distinguish the printed demonstration from a hardened implementation; the code is not silently rewritten into an alleged production ATM.

Listing C.1 · A simple message queue

The queue owns shared pointers to polymorphic wrapped messages. It serializes push/pop with one mutex and waits on a predicate. Message construction/copy/allocation can throw; there is no capacity bound, close state, or push rejection. Messages must be copyable in this interface. A sentinel does not itself close the queue.

Listing C.1 · Book pp. 342–343
#include <mutex>
#include <condition_variable>
#include <queue>
#include <memory>
namespace messaging
{
    struct message_base
    {
        virtual ~message_base()
        {}
    };
    template<typename Msg>
    struct wrapped_message:
        message_base
    {
        Msg contents;
        explicit wrapped_message(Msg const& contents_):
            contents(contents_)
        {}
    };
    class queue
    {
        std::mutex m;
        std::condition_variable c;
        std::queue<std::shared_ptr<message_base> > q;
    public:
        template<typename T>
        void push(T const& msg)
        {
            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m);
            q.push(std::make_shared<wrapped_message<T> >(msg));
            c.notify_all();
        }
        std::shared_ptr<message_base> wait_and_pop()
        {
            std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m);
            c.wait(lk,[&]{return !q.empty();});
            auto res=q.front();
            q.pop();
            return res;
        }
    };
}

Listing C.2 · The sender class

Requires queue. A sender is a non-owning raw pointer to the receiving queue; copying it does not extend queue lifetime. Default/null senders silently drop sends. Sending through a dangling non-null sender is invalid. send is non-const, explaining the mutable reply-address fields in the messages.

Listing C.2 · Book pp. 343–344
namespace messaging
{
    class sender
    {
        queue*q;
    public:
        sender():
            q(nullptr)
        {}
        explicit sender(queue*q_):
            q(q_)
        {}
        template<typename Message>
        void send(Message const& msg)
        {
            if(q)
            {
                q->push(msg);
            }
        }
    };
}

Listing C.3 · The receiver class

The receiver owns its queue. Compile after dispatcher is sufficiently defined for the inline wait body, or declare wait and define it later. The printed order C.1/C.2/C.3/C.4/C.5 is explanatory, not a valid direct concatenation: dispatcher and TemplateDispatcher declarations/definitions need ordering.

Listing C.3 · Book pp. 344
namespace messaging
{
    class receiver
    {
        queue q;
    public:
        operator sender()
        {
            return sender(&q);
        }
        dispatcher wait()
        {
            return dispatcher(&q);
        }
    };
}

Listing C.4 · The base dispatcher

The destructor deliberately blocks and can throw close_queue; it is marked noexcept(false). A chained/moved-from dispatcher must not wait. Normal use relies on full-expression temporary lifetimes. Do not save a chain that outlives predecessor temporaries or let a second exception escape during stack unwinding. Unrecognized non-close messages are popped and discarded.

Listing C.4 · Book pp. 344–345
namespace messaging
{
    class close_queue
    {};
    class dispatcher
    {
        queue* q;
        bool chained;
        dispatcher(dispatcher const&)=delete;
        dispatcher& operator=(dispatcher const&)=delete;
        template<
            typename Dispatcher,
            typename Msg,
            typename Func>
        friend class TemplateDispatcher;
        void wait_and_dispatch()
        {
            for(;;)
            {
                auto msg=q->wait_and_pop();
                dispatch(msg);
            }
        }
        bool dispatch(
            std::shared_ptr<message_base> const& msg)
        {
            if(dynamic_cast<wrapped_message<close_queue>*>(msg.get()))
            {
                throw close_queue();
            }
            return false;
        }
    public:
        dispatcher(dispatcher&& other):
            q(other.q),chained(other.chained)
        {
            other.chained=true;
        }
        explicit dispatcher(queue* q_):
            q(q_),chained(false)
        {}
        template<typename Message,typename Func>
        TemplateDispatcher<dispatcher,Message,Func>
        handle(Func&& f)
        {
            return TemplateDispatcher<dispatcher,Message,Func>(
                q,this,std::forward<Func>(f));
        }
        ~dispatcher() noexcept(false)
        {
            if(!chained)
            {
                wait_and_dispatch();
            }
        }
    };
}

Listing C.5 · The typed dispatcher chain

Requires the base dispatcher and appropriate template declarations. Matching begins at the last handle in the chain and delegates backward; the first successful match ends this wait. Unmatched messages are consumed, not deferred for a future state. The chain borrows predecessor pointers and can also borrow a handler if its deduced Func is a reference. Keep all referenced objects alive. Handler exceptions can escape the destructor and must be handled at the thread boundary.

Listing C.5 · Book pp. 346–347
namespace messaging
{
    template<typename PreviousDispatcher,typename Msg,typename Func>
    class TemplateDispatcher
    {
        queue* q;
        PreviousDispatcher* prev;
        Func f;
        bool chained;
        TemplateDispatcher(TemplateDispatcher const&)=delete;
        TemplateDispatcher& operator=(TemplateDispatcher const&)=delete;
        template<typename Dispatcher,typename OtherMsg,typename OtherFunc>
        friend class TemplateDispatcher;
        void wait_and_dispatch()
        {
            for(;;)
            {
                auto msg=q->wait_and_pop();
                if(dispatch(msg))
                    break;
            }
        }
        bool dispatch(std::shared_ptr<message_base> const& msg)
        {
            if(wrapped_message<Msg>* wrapper=
                dynamic_cast<wrapped_message<Msg>*>(msg.get()))
            {
                f(wrapper->contents);
                return true;
            }
            else
            {
                return prev->dispatch(msg);
            }
        }
    public:
        TemplateDispatcher(TemplateDispatcher&& other):
            q(other.q),prev(other.prev),f(std::move(other.f)),
            chained(other.chained)
        {
            other.chained=true;
        }
        TemplateDispatcher(queue* q_,PreviousDispatcher* prev_,Func&& f_):
            q(q_),prev(prev_),f(std::forward<Func>(f_)),chained(false)
        {
            prev_->chained=true;
        }
        template<typename OtherMsg,typename OtherFunc>
        TemplateDispatcher<TemplateDispatcher,OtherMsg,OtherFunc>
        handle(OtherFunc&& of)
        {
            return TemplateDispatcher<
                TemplateDispatcher,OtherMsg,OtherFunc>(
                    q,this,std::forward<OtherFunc>(of));
        }
        ~TemplateDispatcher() noexcept(false)
        {
            if(!chained)
            {
                wait_and_dispatch();
            }
        }
    };
}

Listing C.6 · ATM message types

These simple structs carry copied payloads and non-owning reply addresses. There are no session/request identifiers, deadlines, authentication proofs, or durable transaction records. The account fields are carried but not enforced by the toy bank. Plaintext PIN handling and hard-coded test credentials are demonstration choices, not security guidance.

Listing C.7 · The ATM state machine

One run thread owns and mutates the state pointer/account/PIN. Handle only the state-appropriate messages; unexpected messages are discarded. PIN collection/verification is a UI protocol, not a bank-side authorization boundary. Replies lack correlation IDs, so delayed replies can be misapplied in a later compatible state. Catch handles close_queue only; other exceptions escaping run terminate a raw std::thread. done_processing ejects and resets the state; it does not compensate a bank debit.

Listing C.7 · Book pp. 350–354
class atm
{
    messaging::receiver incoming;
    messaging::sender bank;
    messaging::sender interface_hardware;
    void (atm::*state)();
    std::string account;
    unsigned withdrawal_amount;
    std::string pin;
    void process_withdrawal()
    {
        incoming.wait()
            .handle<withdraw_ok>(
                [&](withdraw_ok const& msg)
                {
                    interface_hardware.send(
                        issue_money(withdrawal_amount));
                    bank.send(
                        withdrawal_processed(account,withdrawal_amount));
                    state=&atm::done_processing;
                }
                )
            .handle<withdraw_denied>(
                [&](withdraw_denied const& msg)
                {
                    interface_hardware.send(display_insufficient_funds());
                    state=&atm::done_processing;
                }
                )
            .handle<cancel_pressed>(
                [&](cancel_pressed const& msg)
                {
                    bank.send(
                        cancel_withdrawal(account,withdrawal_amount));
                    interface_hardware.send(
                        display_withdrawal_cancelled());
                    state=&atm::done_processing;
                }
                );
    }
    void process_balance()
    {
        incoming.wait()
            .handle<balance>(
                [&](balance const& msg)
                {
                    interface_hardware.send(display_balance(msg.amount));
                    state=&atm::wait_for_action;
                }
                )
            .handle<cancel_pressed>(
                [&](cancel_pressed const& msg)
                {
                    state=&atm::done_processing;
                }
                );
    }
    void wait_for_action()
    {
        interface_hardware.send(display_withdrawal_options());
        incoming.wait()
            .handle<withdraw_pressed>(
                [&](withdraw_pressed const& msg)
                {
                    withdrawal_amount=msg.amount;
                    bank.send(withdraw(account,msg.amount,incoming));
                    state=&atm::process_withdrawal;
                }
                )
            .handle<balance_pressed>(
                [&](balance_pressed const& msg)
                {
                    bank.send(get_balance(account,incoming));
                    state=&atm::process_balance;
                }
                )
            .handle<cancel_pressed>(
                [&](cancel_pressed const& msg)
                {
                    state=&atm::done_processing;
                }
                );
    }
    void verifying_pin()
    {
        incoming.wait()
            .handle<pin_verified>(
                [&](pin_verified const& msg)
                {
                    state=&atm::wait_for_action;
                }
                )
            .handle<pin_incorrect>(
                [&](pin_incorrect const& msg)
                {
                    interface_hardware.send(
                        display_pin_incorrect_message());
                    state=&atm::done_processing;
                }
                )
            .handle<cancel_pressed>(
                [&](cancel_pressed const& msg)
                {
                    state=&atm::done_processing;
                }
                );
    }
    void getting_pin()
    {
        incoming.wait()
            .handle<digit_pressed>(
                [&](digit_pressed const& msg)
                {
                    unsigned const pin_length=4;
                    pin+=msg.digit;
                    if(pin.length()==pin_length)
                    {
                        bank.send(verify_pin(account,pin,incoming));
                        state=&atm::verifying_pin;
                    }
                }
                )
            .handle<clear_last_pressed>(
                [&](clear_last_pressed const& msg)
                {
                    if(!pin.empty())
                    {
                        pin.pop_back();
                    }
                }
                )
            .handle<cancel_pressed>(
                [&](cancel_pressed const& msg)
                {
                    state=&atm::done_processing;
                }
                );
    }
    void waiting_for_card()
    {
        interface_hardware.send(display_enter_card());
        incoming.wait()
            .handle<card_inserted>(
                [&](card_inserted const& msg)
                {
                    account=msg.account;
                    pin="";
                    interface_hardware.send(display_enter_pin());
                    state=&atm::getting_pin;
                }
                );
    }
    void done_processing()
    {
        interface_hardware.send(eject_card());
        state=&atm::waiting_for_card;
    }
    atm(atm const&)=delete;
    atm& operator=(atm const&)=delete;
public:
    atm(messaging::sender bank_,
        messaging::sender interface_hardware_):
        bank(bank_),interface_hardware(interface_hardware_)
    {}
    void done()
    {
        get_sender().send(messaging::close_queue());
    }
    void run()
    {
        state=&atm::waiting_for_card;
        try
        {
            for(;;)
            {
                (this->*state)();
            }
        }
        catch(messaging::close_queue const&)
        {
        }
    }
    messaging::sender get_sender()
    {
        return incoming;
    }
};

Listing C.8 · The bank state machine

Demonstration only: one unsigned balance starts at 199; PIN 1937 is hard-coded, and the account is ignored. A successful withdraw sends approval then subtracts the amount in this handler. cancel_withdrawal and withdrawal_processed handlers are empty, so cancellation is not rollback and cash issue is not confirmed atomically. No durable ledger, per-account authorization, idempotency, reconciliation, or transaction isolation is provided.

Listing C.8 · Book pp. 354–355
class bank_machine
{
    messaging::receiver incoming;
    unsigned balance;
public:
    bank_machine():
        balance(199)
    {}
    void done()
    {
        get_sender().send(messaging::close_queue());
    }
    void run()
    {
        try
        {
            for(;;)
            {
                incoming.wait()
                    .handle<verify_pin>(
                        [&](verify_pin const& msg)
                        {
                            if(msg.pin=="1937")
                            {
                                msg.atm_queue.send(pin_verified());
                            }
                            else
                            {
                                msg.atm_queue.send(pin_incorrect());
                            }
                        }
                        )
                    .handle<withdraw>(
                        [&](withdraw const& msg)
                        {
                            if(balance>=msg.amount)
                            {
                                msg.atm_queue.send(withdraw_ok());
                                balance-=msg.amount;
                            }
                            else
                            {
                                msg.atm_queue.send(withdraw_denied());
                            }
                        }
                        )
                    .handle<get_balance>(
                        [&](get_balance const& msg)
                        {
                            msg.atm_queue.send(::balance(balance));
                        }
                        )
                    .handle<withdrawal_processed>(
                        [&](withdrawal_processed const& msg)
                        {
                        }
                        )
                    .handle<cancel_withdrawal>(
                        [&](cancel_withdrawal const& msg)
                        {
                        }
                        );
            }
        }
        catch(messaging::close_queue const&)
        {
        }
    }

    messaging::sender get_sender()
    {
        return incoming;
    }
};

Listing C.9 · The interface state machine

Supply iostream and a shared std::mutex iom definition before this class. iom is used by the printed code but not defined in these listings. It protects output, not account balances or distributed transactions. issue_money only prints a line: it is not an actual dispenser interface or acknowledgment protocol.

{

Listing C.10 · The driving code

Supply thread/string/iostream/cstdio/utility and other required headers plus the correctly ordered framework definitions and iom. getchar returns int; storing it in char loses reliable EOF handling and can leave this loop spinning on closed input. The prompt says I but the switch accepts lowercase i. Startup and exceptional paths need RAII ownership of all already-started threads. Sending close sentinels to all services before joining is not a coordinated drain; in-flight requests/replies or output can be abandoned.

Listing C.10 · Book pp. 358–359
int main()
{
    bank_machine bank;
    interface_machine interface_hardware;
    atm machine(bank.get_sender(),interface_hardware.get_sender());
    std::thread bank_thread(&bank_machine::run,&bank);
    std::thread if_thread(&interface_machine::run,&interface_hardware);
    std::thread atm_thread(&atm::run,&machine);
    messaging::sender atmqueue(machine.get_sender());
    bool quit_pressed=false;
    while(!quit_pressed)
    {
        char c=getchar();
        switch(c)
        {
        case '0':
        case '1':
        case '2':
        case '3':
        case '4':
        case '5':
        case '6':
        case '7':
        case '8':
        case '9':
            atmqueue.send(digit_pressed(c));
            break;
        case 'b':
            atmqueue.send(balance_pressed());
            break;
        case 'w':
            atmqueue.send(withdraw_pressed(50));
            break;
        case 'c':
            atmqueue.send(cancel_pressed());
            break;
        case 'q':
            quit_pressed=true;
            break;
        case 'i':
            atmqueue.send(card_inserted("acc1234"));
            break;
        }
    }
    bank.done();
    machine.done();
    interface_hardware.done();
    atm_thread.join();
    bank_thread.join();
    if_thread.join();
}
Check your understanding / Message ownership & protocolsOriginal study questions

Local serialization is not a global transaction.

Does copying a sender keep the receiver alive?

No. It copies a non-owning queue pointer. The receiving queue must outlive every send and every active dispatcher that references it.

Are unmatched messages saved for later states?

No. The dispatcher pops them and drops those not recognized by its handler chain. It is not a selective-receive mailbox preserving unmatched entries.

Why does a chained wait run at the semicolon?

The final temporary dispatcher’s destructor performs the wait and dispatch; earlier chained dispatchers are marked inactive. This relies on the temporaries and borrowed references remaining alive.

Why can cancellation leave a debit without cash?

The bank debits when it approves, but the ATM can cancel before consuming that reply. The cancellation handler in the bank is empty and does not compensate the debit.

Does one thread per state machine remove protocol races?

No. It serializes each machine’s local state. Delayed, uncorrelated replies and cross-service action ordering can still violate application invariants.

Does close_queue close the underlying queue?

No. It is a normal message that makes this dispatcher throw and leave its loop. It does not reject later producers, close other queues, or prove all in-flight work has completed.

Appendix in one sentence

Message passing clarifies who owns state; a correct application still needs explicit lifetime, correlation, failure, transaction, and shutdown protocols.
