D.1 / <chrono>pp. 360–375

Represent time with units and clock identity.

A duration is a tick count plus a ratio period; a time_point is a duration since a particular clock’s epoch. Prefer explicit initialization, and distinguish safe implicit scale conversions from deliberate duration_cast truncation. Converting 1,500 milliseconds to integral seconds gives 1; that is a unit conversion, not a timer guarantee.

Use steady_clock for monotonic elapsed time. system_clock represents wall time and can be adjusted; high_resolution_clock need not be steady. Clock period, observed precision, accuracy, and call overhead are different properties. A default time_point represents an epoch, while a default-initialized automatic arithmetic duration can have an indeterminate count in the C++11 setting.

Source cautions: duration comparisons use an appropriate common duration type; they do not require one operand type to convert directly to the other as the printed requirements suggest. The text’s to_time_point name should be from_time_t. Several clock entries contradict their noexcept declarations with “Throws system_error”; do not treat those prose claims as permission for exceptions to propagate from noexcept calls.

Subsection guide

D.1.1 · std::chrono::duration class template

Counts ticks using a representation type and a ratio period. count() exposes the tick count; duration_cast makes explicit scale conversions, including truncating conversions. Initialize counts deliberately and audit numeric range/precision.

Book p. 360 / PDF p. 383 · Embedded <chrono> source excerpts

D.1.2 · std::chrono::time_point class template

A duration since one specific clock’s epoch. The clock type is part of the type: matching-looking counts from different clocks are not interchangeable. Default time_point represents its clock’s epoch.

Book p. 369 / PDF p. 392 · Embedded <chrono> source excerpts

D.1.3 · std::chrono::system_clock class

Wall-clock time for timestamps and time_t interoperation. It can be adjusted; do not assume monotonic elapsed time. The actual conversion name is from_time_t, and precision/rounding is implementation-dependent.

Book p. 371 / PDF p. 394 · Embedded <chrono> source excerpts

D.1.4 · std::chrono::steady_clock class

Guaranteed nondecreasing clock, suitable for elapsed time and deadline calculations. A fine tick period does not guarantee equivalent measurement accuracy, zero overhead, or prompt scheduling.

Book p. 373 / PDF p. 396 · Embedded <chrono> source excerpts

D.1.5 · std::chrono::high_resolution_clock typedef

Highest-resolution provided clock; it may alias system_clock or steady_clock. Check is_steady before choosing it for intervals rather than assuming “high resolution” means monotonic.

Book p. 374 / PDF p. 397 · Embedded <chrono> source excerpts

D.2 / <condition_variable>pp. 375–390

Wait for a state predicate, not a remembered notification.

condition_variable waits with unique_lock<mutex>; condition_variable_any accepts a suitable custom lock. Waiting atomically releases the lock and enters the wait, then reacquires it before returning normally. Recheck a predicate under the protection used by its writers; a notification alone does not carry data or prove that the predicate is true.

Non-predicate timed waits return cv_status, not a Boolean application result. Predicate overloads return whether the final predicate evaluation succeeded. Spurious wakes and scheduling can delay completion; a timeout is not a hard upper bound on latency. Compute one absolute deadline rather than restarting a full relative timeout after every wake.

notify_all_at_thread_exit transfers lock ownership until exit; keep its mutex/CV alive and avoid dependencies requiring that held mutex. All simultaneous waiters on a std::condition_variable must follow the same-mutex requirements. Do not destroy synchronization objects while waiters or other accesses can still use them.

The reference contains stale exception wording, including notify functions declared noexcept but described as throwing, and oversimplified re-lock failure guarantees. The total order of a CV’s notifications and wait phases is not a global order of all application actions or a stored-event mechanism.

Subsection guide

D.2.1 · std::condition_variable class

Wait with a held unique_lock<mutex>; the wait atomically unlocks and blocks, then reacquires the mutex. Use a predicate protected by the same mutex. Notifications are not stored events and spurious wakes require rechecking.

Book p. 375 / PDF p. 398 · Embedded <condition_variable> source excerpts

D.2.2 · std::condition_variable_any class

The analogous wait interface for a suitable user-supplied lock type. Custom lock/lifetime/exception behavior is part of the contract. Predicate and deadline discipline remain essential.

Book p. 383 / PDF p. 406 · Embedded <condition_variable> source excerpts

D.3 / <atomic>pp. 390–424

Separate atomicity, ordering, and lifetime.

Generic atomics provide load/store, exchange, and compare/exchange. Integral and pointer specializations add appropriate RMW operations; bool is not an arithmetic specialization. fetch operations return the old value, while prefix increment and compound assignment return the updated value. None of these keeps an independently managed pointee alive.

CAS compares the current value against expected. On failure it updates expected with the observed value; weak CAS can also fail spuriously. Success performs an RMW; failure is load-like. In C++11, failure ordering must not be release/acq_rel or stronger than the success ordering. Validity restrictions apply separately to loads, stores, clear, and RMW operations.

relaxed preserves atomicity but does not publish unrelated data. A release/acquire handoff requires the relevant observation or release-sequence relationship; a fence needs an atomic communication protocol. atomic_signal_fence applies to a signal handler on the same thread, not general inter-thread communication. seq_cst cannot repair a dangling pointer or an incorrect algorithm.

Lock-free macros and is_lock_free describe primitives, not whole containers. Initialize C++11 atomics explicitly and publish their construction safely. memory_order_consume is a historical dependency-ordering facility; prefer a well-understood acquire protocol rather than assuming portable implementations exploit its intended weaker behavior.

Source corrections: atomic_ssize_t is not a standard C++11 alias; the generic atomic eligibility list is not normative (trivial copyability is central). The synopsis has malformed atomic_init/exchange signatures and wrong atomic assignment return types. Atomic assignment from T returns T, not bool or the void result of store; atomic_exchange requires the desired value. See the source notes before copying declarations.

Subsection guide

D.3.1 · std::atomic_xxx typedefs

Convenient names for corresponding atomic types. Table D.1 maps the fundamental integral aliases. Optional exact-width integer names depend on underlying type support; do not assume every printed alias is standard.

Book p. 391 / PDF p. 414 · Embedded <atomic> source excerpts

D.3.2 · ATOMIC_xxx_LOCK_FREE macros

0 means never lock-free, 1 means sometimes, and 2 means always for the corresponding family. is_lock_free() queries an object. A lock-free primitive does not make an enclosing algorithm wait-free or end-to-end lock-free.

Book p. 392 / PDF p. 415 · Embedded <atomic> source excerpts

D.3.3 · ATOMIC_VAR_INIT macro

Historical C++11 atomic initialization macro. Initialization is not a concurrent update and must happen before access. Prefer explicit value initialization for the intended standard; macro availability/deprecation changes in later versions.

Book p. 393 / PDF p. 416 · Embedded <atomic> source excerpts

D.3.4 · std::memory_order enumeration

Selects ordering for individual atomic operations. relaxed retains atomicity, acquire/release can publish through the required observation, and seq_cst adds ordering constraints. Not every order is valid for every operation.

Book p. 393 / PDF p. 416 · Embedded <atomic> source excerpts

D.3.5 · std::atomic_thread_fence function

Inter-thread ordering fence. It needs the appropriate atomic communication and sequenced-before relationships to establish synchronization; a fence alone does not legalize ordinary data races.

D.3.6 · std::atomic_signal_fence function

Compiler ordering constraints for a thread and a signal handler executing on that same thread; not a general replacement for inter-thread atomic synchronization.

Lock-free set/clear flag. In C++11 use ATOMIC_FLAG_INIT for a known clear state. test_and_set returns the previous value, clear is a store. A spinlock built from it remains a lock-based algorithm.

Generic atomic object: load, store, exchange, and compare/exchange, with no ordinary copying of the atomic object. Eligibility depends on the applicable type requirements, including trivial copyability, not the source’s oversimplified list.

Integral and object-pointer specializations add operations beyond the primary template. bool is not an arithmetic counter. Atomic pointers protect pointer updates, not pointee lifetime or multi-field invariants.

fetch_add/sub/and/or/xor return the old value; prefix and compound forms return the updated value. Pointer arithmetic scales by elements for supported object pointers. An atomic integer is not an automatically safe resource counter protocol.

D.4 / <future>pp. 424–446

A valid handle is not necessarily a ready result.

future is a move-only consumer, shared_future permits shared observation, promise supplies a result, and packaged_task captures a callable’s result or exception. A future can be valid but pending, ready with an exception, or associated with deferred execution. wait waits without consuming; get retrieves/rethrows. Ordinary future::get invalidates its handle, whereas shared_future::get can be repeated.

A provider’s get_future is once per state. Satisfying an already satisfied state is an error; abandoning an unsatisfied provider reports broken_promise. A packaged_task does not schedule itself: invoking it runs the callable where invoked. reset establishes a new result state. At-thread-exit setters store a result now but defer readiness until exit.

async permits explicit async/deferred policies or an implementation-selected choice by default. Timed waits can report deferred without executing anything; a non-timed wait/get may execute the deferred task. There is no standard guarantee of a bounded pool or immediate return without setup costs. Explicit async launch can fail with system_error; callable/materialization failures also need handling.

Last release of an async-launched task’s state can wait for that task. Do not generalize this to every future or assume that discarding a result requests cancellation. Separate shared_future copies are convenient observers; any mutable referenced result still requires its own synchronization and lifetime contract.

Printed issues include a move-assignment entry showing a constructor declaration, missing dependent typename in async synopsis, and shared_future::wait_until incorrectly declared bool in its detailed entry. It returns future_status. “Ready” includes stored exceptions, not only successful values.

Subsection guide

D.4.1 · std::future class template

A move-only consumer of one shared result. get() retrieves/rethrows and invalidates the future; wait() does not consume it. valid() means associated state exists, not that the result is ready.

Book p. 425 / PDF p. 448 · Embedded <future> source excerpts

D.4.2 · std::shared_future class template

Copyable handles observing a shared result. Repeated get() is allowed; for ordinary T it returns const T&, while reference/void specializations differ. Result references must not outlive their state, and mutable referents need separate synchronization.

Book p. 429 / PDF p. 452 · Embedded <future> source excerpts

D.4.3 · std::packaged_task class template

Owns a callable and result state. Invoking it captures a value or callable exception; it does not choose a thread. get_future() is once per state; reset() creates a new result state. make_ready_at_thread_exit defers readiness, not execution.

Book p. 434 / PDF p. 457 · Embedded <future> source excerpts

D.4.4 · std::promise class template

The producer side of a result: get_future(), set_value(), set_exception(), and at-thread-exit variants. Destroying an unsatisfied provider makes the state report broken_promise. A second successful satisfaction is not allowed.

Book p. 440 / PDF p. 463 · Embedded <future> source excerpts

D.4.5 · std::async function template

Creates an async or deferred computation according to policy and returns a future. Timed polling can report deferred without running it; non-timed wait/get can execute it. Default policy does not promise a bounded pool.

D.5 / <mutex>pp. 446–471

Own locks explicitly and release them reliably.

The four C++11 mutex types combine nonrecursive/recursive ownership with optional timed acquisition. Every successful recursive acquisition needs a matching release. A failed try_lock may be spurious and does not establish ownership or a successful-acquisition synchronization edge.

lock_guard provides a simple scope-bound lock; unique_lock supports empty/deferred states, moving, try/timed acquisition, and unlock/relock. adopt_lock takes responsibility for an already-held lock; defer_lock does not acquire; try_to_lock requires checking success. unique_lock::release detaches the mutex pointer without unlocking—callers must arrange the final release.

std::lock acquires a set of suitable lockables with a deadlock-avoiding algorithm and unwinds acquired locks on exceptions. It does not solve arbitrary application lock cycles or duplicate/already-held argument misuse. std::try_lock returns -1 on success or the zero-based failed argument index, undoing earlier acquisitions when it fails.

call_once with once_flag permits failed throwing attempts to retry; precisely one active invocation returns normally as the successful initializer. Passive callers observe its completed effects. “Exactly once” does not mean the callable body can never start more than once or that partial failed side effects are rolled back.

The printed variadic lock/try_lock/call_once signatures are schematic/malformed; use the real header declarations, including forwarding where specified. The recursive_timed_mutex no-relock precondition contradicts its own recursive contract. There is no guarantee of fairness or immediate completion once a mutex becomes available.

Subsection guide

D.5.1 · std::mutex class

Basic non-recursive mutual exclusion. Unlock in the owning thread; use RAII rather than pairing raw calls across exceptional paths. A failed try_lock may be spurious and establishes no successful-acquisition ordering.

Book p. 447 / PDF p. 470 · Embedded <mutex> source excerpts

D.5.2 · std::recursive_mutex class

Allows repeated acquisition by the same owner up to an implementation limit. Every acquisition must be balanced. It does not resolve cycles across different mutexes or make arbitrary reentrancy safe.

Book p. 449 / PDF p. 472 · Embedded <mutex> source excerpts

D.5.3 · std::timed_mutex class

Adds try_lock_for and try_lock_until. Failure and timeout semantics are not hard scheduling deadlines; a thread may return late. Only successful acquisition grants ownership.

Book p. 451 / PDF p. 474 · Embedded <mutex> source excerpts

D.5.4 · std::recursive_timed_mutex class

Combines timed acquisition with recursive ownership. The source’s no-relock precondition copied into its lock() entry conflicts with recursive behavior; balanced repeated acquisition is the point of this type.

Book p. 455 / PDF p. 478 · Embedded <mutex> source excerpts

D.5.5 · std::lock_guard class template

Small noncopyable, nonmovable scoped owner. Normally locks at construction and unlocks at destruction. adopt_lock requires that the current thread already owns the lock; it does not acquire it.

Book p. 459 / PDF p. 482 · Embedded <mutex> source excerpts

D.5.6 · std::unique_lock class template

Movable, optional ownership wrapper supporting deferred/try/timed acquisition and unlock/relock. owns_lock() and mutex() are different queries. release() disassociates without unlocking, transferring responsibility to the caller.

Book p. 460 / PDF p. 483 · Embedded <mutex> source excerpts

D.5.7 · std::lock function template

Acquires multiple distinct suitable lockables using a deadlock-avoiding algorithm and releases acquisitions if it throws. It is not a cure for all application lock cycles, already-held locks, or duplicate mutex arguments.

Book p. 469 / PDF p. 492 · Embedded <mutex> source excerpts

D.5.8 · std::try_lock function template

Tries lockables in order; returns -1 on success or the zero-based failed index and releases earlier acquisitions on failure. A failure does not necessarily prove another thread owns that lock.

Book p. 469 / PDF p. 492 · Embedded <mutex> source excerpts

D.5.9 · std::once_flag class

Noncopyable state used with call_once. Keep the flag alive for all associated calls; one flag represents one initialization protocol and cannot simply be reset for arbitrary repeated use.

Book p. 470 / PDF p. 493 · Embedded <mutex> source excerpts

D.5.10 · std::call_once function template

At most one invocation returns successfully as the active initializer for a flag. Throwing attempts propagate and permit retry. Returning success publishes effects to passive callers; it does not roll back partial side effects of a failed attempt.

D.6 / <ratio>pp. 471–477

Carry scale information at compile time.

ratio<N,D> normalizes a rational value: denominator positive, numerator/denominator reduced. D cannot be zero. Arithmetic traits provide sums, differences, products, and quotients; comparison traits expose compile-time Boolean values. This is how chrono periods express fractions of seconds without a runtime scale object.

Equivalent fractions can have equal num/den but originate from different ratio specializations. Use the documented arithmetic trait members and ::type rather than depending on the source’s simplified “template alias” account. Representability limits still matter, and division by a zero-valued ratio is invalid.

Naïve cross multiplication can overflow even when a comparison has a meaningful mathematical result. Do not turn the source’s explanatory formulas directly into unchecked signed-integer arithmetic. Compile-time rational computation is not arbitrary-precision arithmetic.

Subsection guide

D.6.1 · std::ratio class template

Compile-time normalized rational value with positive denominator; denominator zero is ill-formed. Used as a chrono tick period. Different template arguments can represent the same value without being the identical specialization.

D.7 / <thread>pp. 477–486

A handle’s joinability is a lifetime obligation.

std::thread starts and owns an association with a thread of execution. Callable and argument values are normally stored by decay-copy/move; use ref/cref deliberately for borrowing and retain the referenced objects. Completion synchronizes with successful join, but not with an arbitrary sleep or detach.

A thread can finish while its object remains joinable. Destroying it—or move-assigning a different thread over it—while joinable terminates. Join or detach explicitly using an exception-safe ownership protocol. Detach removes the handle association, not lifetime requirements of data or synchronization objects the worker uses.

thread::id supports identity and an ordering suitable for containers, not a chronological execution order. IDs may be reused after an execution ends. native_handle is implementation-defined. hardware_concurrency is a hint and may be zero; it does not reserve CPUs or specify your ideal worker count.

this_thread::yield is a scheduling hint, and sleep_for/until may return late. Neither creates the application synchronization needed for data safety. The source has a malformed template-pack spelling and stream insertion with ostream&&; the ordinary thread-ID stream inserter accepts an lvalue stream reference. C++20 jthread/stop tokens are later facilities, not features of this C++11 reference.

Subsection guide

D.7.1 · std::thread class

Owns a thread handle, not the lifetime of everything the thread accesses. Move-only. A finished but unjoined thread is still joinable; destroying or move-assigning over a joinable std::thread terminates.

Book p. 477 / PDF p. 500 · Embedded <thread> source excerpts

D.7.2 · Namespace this_thread

Operations on the calling thread: get_id, yield, sleep_for, sleep_until. Sleep/yield are not synchronization or cancellation. Wakeup can be late; yield is only a scheduling opportunity.

Source audit / Common reference trapsOriginal annotations

Do not turn a synopsis typo into an API.

  • noexcept conflicts: several clock, notification, or constructor entries promise noexcept while their prose says an exception can escape. Treat the conflict as a source defect, not a usable exception contract.
  • Atomic signatures: generic atomic_init takes the underlying value, not void*. exchange needs a desired value, and assignment from a value returns that value type. Integral/pointer assignment returning bool in the synopsis is wrong.
  • CAS ordering: a failed comparison is load-like, not a release operation. The C++11 failure-order restrictions include the relative-strength restriction omitted by parts of the text. A failed weak CAS does not imply that another thread definitely modified the value.
  • Time: non-predicate CV waits return cv_status; future timed waits return future_status. A timeout/deferred result does not mean application work succeeded, and requested durations are not scheduling upper bounds.
  • Async and ownership: default async is not guaranteed pool execution or an immediate zero-cost return. Provider-based futures and async-launched states do not have identical cleanup behavior.
  • Templates: placeholders such as integral-type, unspecified, and see description are not real type names. Several packs and dependent return types are schematic or malformed; the header is the declaration source for runnable code.
  • Initialization: explicitly initialize C++11 atomic state. Later default-initialization changes and macro deprecations must be checked for the selected standard.
  • Once: “exactly once” means a successful initialization, not that no throwing attempt can have run earlier.

These notes identify important pitfalls rather than claiming a complete errata audit of every printed declaration. The archive retains original errors to keep the distinction between source and correction visible.

Check your understanding / Library contractsOriginal study questions

Six distinctions to keep straight.

valid versus ready?

A future can have a shared state and still not have a result. A ready state may contain an exception. Timed polling of a deferred task can report deferred without running it.

joinable versus running?

A completed thread remains joinable until its association is joined, detached, or moved away. Destroying a joinable std::thread terminates even if its execution already finished.

release versus unlock?

unique_lock::release returns/disassociates the mutex without unlocking it. The caller inherits the responsibility to release any lock still held.

notification versus predicate?

A notification may wake a waiter, but only the protected application predicate decides whether it can proceed. Notifications are not retained credits and waking can be spurious.

atomic pointer versus live object?

Updating or loading a pointer atomically does not prevent another thread from reclaiming its pointee. Lifetime/reclamation is a separate protocol.

once attempted versus once completed?

A throwing call_once attempt can be retried. The successful returning initializer publishes its effects to passive callers; failed side effects are not automatically undone.

Appendix in one sentence

The right primitive is only correct when its preconditions, state transitions, lifetime obligations, and synchronization relationships all fit the surrounding program.

Scope and historical context

There is no further chapter after Appendix D. This Resources section is a reading list, not new library specifications or a current ranking of tools.

Reading guide / Original study notespp. 487–488

Choose a question before a source.

Can failure preserve the invariant?

Cargill and Sutter’s exception-safety material complements the lock-based interface design in Chapters 3 and 6. RAII handles resource release, but application invariants still require an explicit failure contract.

When can a removed node be freed?

Michael’s reclamation paper and the Atomic Ptr Plus project connect to Chapter 7. Atomic pointer manipulation and safe memory reclamation are separate obligations; publication, ABA, and ownership must all be considered.

How else can work communicate?

Hoare, Erlang, and MPI provide different contexts for message passing. Haskell supplies functional-programming context. Compare models carefully rather than assuming their safety or performance properties transfer automatically to C++.

Which contract is authoritative?

The GCC page, FAQ, committee proposal, and library projects document an ecosystem in transition. Distinguish proposals, implementation status, library-specific APIs, and the adopted standard. Patent and license entries require their own legal/contextual checks.

Reading checklistOriginal study aid

Keep the layers separate.

  • A historical proposal explains design intent, not necessarily final normative wording.
  • A working implementation demonstrates one environment, not universal portability.
  • A lock-free update does not by itself solve memory reclamation.
  • A bibliography citation is not an endorsement, a license grant, or current legal clearance.
  • A URL printed in 2012 is a historical pointer, not a verified current destination.

The next part of the book is its alphabetical index (printed pp. 489–506), not another chapter.

Source & scope

Anthony Williams, C++ Concurrency in Action: Practical Multithreading, Manning, 2012. Chapters 1–10, “Hello, world of concurrency in C++!”, “Managing threads,” “Sharing data between threads,” “Synchronizing concurrent operations,” “The C++ memory model and operations on atomic types,” “Designing lock-based concurrent data structures,” “Designing lock-free concurrent data structures,” “Designing concurrent code,” “Advanced thread management,” and “Testing and debugging multithreaded applications,” plus Appendices A–D, “Brief reference for some C++11 language features,” “Brief comparison of concurrency libraries,” “A message-passing framework and complete ATM example,” and “C++ Thread Library reference,” plus the Resources bibliography, printed pp. 1–488 (PDF pp. 24–511), from this repository’s C__CON~1.PDF. Summary prose and interactive walkthrough are original study aids; Figures 1.1–1.4, 3.1, 4.1–4.3, 5.1–5.7, 6.1, 7.1, and 8.1–8.3, Tables 3.1, 4.1, and 5.1–5.3, and C++ examples are reproduced from the supplied chapters and appendices A–D. The original unnumbered comparison table from Appendix B and both parts of Table D.1 are also embedded. Chapters 2, 9, and 10 and Appendices A–D contain no numbered figures. Added explanations, corrections, calculators, and walkthroughs are original study aids. Figures and source material © 2012 Manning Publications Co.
